Title page

History of the New World.

Prologue to the Reader

The diversity of opinions, prudent reader, that one finds in the chronicles of the New World, and the desire to inquire into and ascertain the truth of the matters written therein, was the principal motive that led me to decide to come to these Indies. For anyone who reads attentively the various writers who have printed histories of these Western Indies will experience what I say, and in those who agree most closely with one another in their writings, it will be apparent that some have taken from others what they say; those who wrote after the first authors followed them, trusting in their credibility and authority without troubling themselves to examine the truth of what they found in them. So that if the first authors were mistaken in certain cases, the same error spread through those who followed them. This fault cannot be presumed to lie with the historians who wrote in Europe, whose intention was to be accurate, but rather with those who sent them from here the accounts upon which they based their histories; for from the experience I have gained over so many years in the Indies, from the many accounts that have been made of new events and discoveries of lands that occurred in my time, I find that they are seldom as faithful as they ought to be; and if made so sincerely that no passion, flattery, or ambition creeps into them — those who

they send to Spain to glorify and give credit to their deeds and
enterprises; or those of the captains and governors, in whose favor
the most eminent authors write. And so that none of these considerations
may find place in such accounts, the risk is usually borne by
departing with the first news, which is always regarded with suspicion
since the bearer carries it, as experience teaches us. I could prove
this truth with many examples: and because singular cases carry great
weight, I only wish to refer here to what I read in a history of those
days written in Latin: where its author, describing the island of
Hispaniola, says it is very abundant in wheat, wine, and olive
oil; which are things that in no way grow there,
nor on any of the other Windward Islands of that
archipelago. And alongside this error, others are usually found
in some accounts that describe other regions of the New World.
But I do not wish to dwell further on this particular matter, as it is
so well known that the distinguished chief chronicler of the
Indies, Antonio de Herrera, confesses it in his history. And
having said in one place, as proof of the truth he treats therein,
that he follows the accounts and papers he has
seen gathered in the Royal Council of the Indies; in another
place he complains that it is very difficult to ascertain the truth
of events in the Indies because of the discrepancies that occur
on account of the little consistency that accounts usually carry.

And so it is that among the historians who wrote in Spain, drawing from what they gathered through particular accounts without firsthand knowledge of some provinces: in both groups I find that they lacked the most solid foundation that a history must have, which is to be supported by the public archives of the republic about which one writes. Beyond this, what is necessarily required for political and ecclesiastical history, and the course of the times and customs that have occurred in the New World since its discovery: regarding the natural soils to be found there, I have not seen that anyone has treated this subject thoroughly. For this reason, wishing to supply, as far as my abilities allow, the said deficiencies, I resolved to write this history in order to serve the common good, and it appears (though not without great labor) that I have succeeded in accomplishing it.

First, because of the many years I have resided in the Indies, which are no fewer than fifty-seven, from the year one thousand five hundred and seventy-six when I went there, until the present year of one thousand six hundred and fifty-three: aided not only by my natural inclination to learn and to probe the secrets of the lands where I have resided, but especially having experienced the diverse climates found throughout both hemispheres of the New World; for I have lived in one and the other for a long time, which has given me the opportunity to inquire into and contemplate at length the ma[tters...]

the nature of the regions, and the rare fruits they produce, which are the things that professors of natural philosophy tend to overlook and conceal.

The Spaniards, because they have been living among the Indians, have arrived at the founding of their settlements, and I can say that they entered them within the first century of the founding of a republic. For although this land was discovered in the year fourteen hundred and ninety-two, and the Spaniards returned a year later to begin its settlement, it was not until the city of Santo Domingo was founded in the year fourteen hundred and ninety-seven, that it newly gained a permanent seat and stability as a new republic. And thus, having arrived myself at the island of Hispaniola in the aforementioned year of ninety-six, within the ninety-ninth year of the founding of the said city of Santo Domingo, it is well verified that I entered among them and among the Indians in the first century of their settlement. For this reason I had the occasion to come to know some of the first settlers, particularly from the kingdom of Peru, which I entered in its sixty-eighth year after its conquest; and nearly all the sons of its conquerors, and not a few from other provinces; and a great number of Indians who remembered when those from Spain entered their land — with whom I conversed at length, and who were able to inform me of much of what they had witnessed; and what they could not reach themselves, they knew from the mouths of the first Spaniards who came.

to his homeland.

Beyond this (which is the third reason), I have found many ancient accounts in manuscript papers, such as diaries and relations written by some of the conquistadors, which their descendants now keep. Among these, I consider particularly worthy of full credence a brief account made of the conquest of New Spain by one of its principal conquistadors, called Captain Bernardino Vázquez de Tapia, which he presented to Don Antonio de Mendoza, the first Viceroy thereof. The original of this, written in his own hand by Bernardino Vázquez, was shared with me by one of his grandsons. Regarding those who wrote about the conquest of the kingdom of Peru, one of its first conquistadors, named Pedro Pizarro, resident of the city of Arequipa, gave me his account, which a descendant of his shared with me and which I now hold in my possession.

In addition to these authentic writings, I have made use of many old depositions that the conquistadors made to document their services, with witnesses who were themselves conquistadors, in which particular circumstances are found that never came to the attention of the first chroniclers. Others of these include royal provisions and letters from Viceroys and governors, many of which are kept in the public archives, and others are inserted into depositions authorized by the courts. And finally I have seen and drawn from many

things from the ecclesiastical and secular archives in the places where
I have been, which, being certain and irrefutable arguments of the truth
of what is written, are scattered throughout this history, particularly
in the second and third parts, with many documents and texts copied
formally from said archives: which in the course of this
writing serve as a guide, just as the markers of posts that
are set up along the roads that are often covered by snow
to direct the travelers. This I do more par
ticularly when it is necessary to clarify
obscure matters, or to refute those things that without foundation of truth
are told in some histories.

Having concluded, then, with divine favor this work after
forty years since I began it, it seemed right to me to entitle it the
History of the New World: because leaving aside being dazzled
by the universality of the subject, which encompasses all this land of the
West Indies and the New World. And first, because in
it are contained all the things that those fond of the new
land wish to know about universal history and erudition:
for part of this writing belongs to natural history, and part
to political and ecclesiastical history. And although from the last of these it would
rightly be called ecclesiastical history, and drawing
its name from its most noble part, nonetheless it is because
the aforementioned title is more general, and corresponds better

to the variety of subjects that are treated in it. I judged
that it was better to approve it.
divided into parts among themselves, each one in its own body: the first
deals with the nature and qualities of the New World
with all the things that it produces and brings forth, and which our
Spaniards found there. This contains fourteen books: in
the first he wrote of the world in common, with the divisions
that cosmographers and geographers make of its parts.
Because the New World being so great a part of the uni
verse, that within its limits it embraces more than half of the
terrestrial globe, it was proportionately fitting, before beginning to
write of the proper subject of this history, which is the new world,
to offer by way of prelude something about the entire universe, an account
of the description of its parts and regions, so that from this one may
understand the proportion and correspondence that the New World
has with the Old. And whoever reads what is proper to these
Indies will find, as if in epitome, what pertains to the uni
verse, and will be able to comprehend all that its breadth and circum
ference contains. In which, when arranging this, that in the description
of our Spain and kingdoms and states that are under its rule,
it will extend more broadly than what does not pertain to it:
to which I am moved, beyond the natural affection for one's home
land, by seeing that through the benefit of [illegible] this day
this monarchy stands at the highest point of greatness, that

has had.

The following eight books deal with the qualities and climates of
the New World, and all the natural things that from its land
they took, and our Spaniards found when they came to
settle it, arranged by their degrees and kinds, according to the order of merit
and nobility, as considered by philosophers and
cosmographers, and by miners for these, as well as the inanimate ones;
following through all the species of stones and metals that he has been
able to obtain: and continuing through the lineages of plants and ani
mals, which are native and proper to the land, in whose
history he touches along the way on the knowledge and uses that
the Indians had of them, which the Spaniards have learned from them, both
regarding their sustenance, in which they make use of them, and for
the cure of their illnesses, to which they have applied them for the
virtues they came to know in them as useful for remedy
ing them. In the tenth book we cover all the customary
categories of plants and animals that the Span
iards have brought from Spain, and from other regions to these Indies
since they settled them, and at present grow in them with no
less abundance than their own native ones. The last four books
contain what pertains to the nature, con
dition, and customs of the Indians, particularly those of the
inhabitants of this kingdom, along with the government that their Kings
maintained both in what concerns temporal administration,

as to the adherents of their false religion. Because it has been a republic of the Reyes, buos the most orderly in its manner of government of all those that existed in this land. Because they treat purposefully of all the other republics of the Indians that were worthy of noting: although in the other two parts of this history, the most notable customs and ways of living of some nations are also touched upon.

The second part consists of fifteen books: the first two deal with the discovery and pacification of the first provinces of the Indies and of the Kingdom of Peru; the third covers the course of the governors and viceroys who have governed it, giving a brief account of the uses and other memorable things that have occurred there from its beginning to the present time; in the fourth and fifth is set out the manner in which the republic of the Spaniards and of the Indians has been planted and established in these Indies, after the latter became Christians, and the form of government observed among them, particularly in the Kingdom of Peru; in the nine following books there is a general description of that same Kingdom of Peru by its bishoprics and provinces, and at great length that of the City of the Kings; and in the last is the description of the remaining provinces of Austral America, which fall outside the boundaries of Peru, together with everything else belonging to what of this New World falls within the Antarctic hemisphere.

The third part and volume contains fourteen books: the first two deal with the qualities of New Spain, and its discovery and conquest; the third with the governors and viceroys it has had: from the fourth onward, an account is given of its provinces, and of all the others of North America; and an account is given of the founding and present state of the city of Mexico, and of its settlers and families descended from them: and in the fourteenth and last, the islands of both seas, the North and the South, are described, as far as the Philippines and the Moluccas: and a brief treatise is included on the voyages of all the Indies and the new world.

At the end of this prologue it seemed right to me to offer the reader two advisories. The first is that although I personally observed each region during the time I resided there, for greater verification of what I relate, as one who understood the present matter, it does not mean that the history follows the time in which each thing was written; rather, some things are placed first that were actually written later, following in this the order that the subject matter itself demands, and not the chronological order in which they were written: as can be seen in the first part, which I finished perfecting after the other two, given that its subject required greater experience and knowledge of the matters it contains.

The second advisory is that in describing the city of Mexico I treat of its founders, and I do not return to do the same in the description of Lima, not because the latter is inferior to the former

in the nobility of its settlers, but rather because when I began this history I had no intention of dwelling so long on this part, and principally because, having resided many years in Mexico, I had great opportunity to write about this matter, since I found all those conquistadors and settlers with descendants in that city — which would have been very difficult here in Lima, both because many of the conquerors of Peru returned at once to Spain, content with the great riches of gold and silver that fell to them from the spoils of war, and because others scattered throughout the whole kingdom to populate the other cities that the king has been founding — so that today in this city there are fewer families of such settlers than in that of Mexico, and to draw from those known to me and not from others would be to slight those who would find no place in the history.

Finally, the reader will find here no few things added to what he will have read in other chronicles of the Indies, for had we not gone beyond what is said in them, my work would have been spared — though certainly it has been no small effort that I have put into inquiring after the truth of everything written here. And with all that, I do not doubt that it will carry many defects, which this reader is kindly asked to attribute more to the common failing of short human foresight than to any lack of diligence and desire to get it right — for that I have

...the North Star which I have always kept before me, and principally to render some service to God our Lord in pro[moting] this history, which manifests His infinite power and Wisdom in the marvels which He had hidden in the New World from the people of the other [world]: and His great goodness and mercy in having deigned that in our age His holy faith should be amplified in these last regions of the universe, from which so much glory has followed to His divine Majesty, and immortal honor to our nation Spain, which He was pleased to take as His instrument to achieve these sovereign goods. Farewell, 7th of July, 1653.

History of the New World. First Part. Book 1.

Chapter 1. Of the Universe.

The ancient philosophers gave various names to this universal machine of the world, calling it at times Heaven, at other times Universe, and at other times World. The first of these is no longer in use in that sense; the other two are used interchangeably; given that "World" is the most frequent and common, by which we mean the gathering and joining together of all created things, which amounts to the same as saying Universe. Aristotle defines it in this manner: the World is a gathering composed of heaven and earth, and of all the natures contained within them. Or in other words: the World is an ordered composition of all the things that God has brought to light, and by which they are animated. It may well be that the philosopher speaks here only of the corporeal world, which consists of the four elements and of heaven; but in the chapter he uses the name in a broader sense, insofar as it encompasses all created things that are contained within the Universe.

Which is one alone, and not many; and its shape is spherical, resembling a perfectly round ball, like the principal parts that compose it, which are the simple bodies of the heavens and elements. In the sacrifices called Orgia, which the ancients performed in honor of the god Bacchus, Macrobius relates that they gave special veneration to the egg, honoring it as

History of the New World.
In the image and likeness of the world, both in its roundness and principally in its composition: taking the white to represent the sky, the yolk the globe of the earth, and the white the region and element of air. A comparison, though humble and domestic, that well illustrates the figure. Because of the three parts that make up the egg — the white, the shell with its hardness, whiteness, and shining luster — and because it embraces and encloses within itself the other two, it ought to be attributed as the symbol of the celestial sphere. The yolk, which represents the earth, by virtue of its position in the middle and center, surrounded and encircled on all sides by the white and the shell, and because its substance is less transparent than the white, and not so white, and denser than the shell. As for the white — who cannot see how aptly it represents the other two elements, water and air, by its fluidity and transparency? Where one can see how wisely those ancients depicted the form and fabric of the universe in an egg: which figure is all the more fitting when we consider the world in that imperfect and chaotic state it had on the first day of its creation, when, according to the most probable opinion, there existed in it no more than three simple bodies — sky, water, and earth — as we shall see in the following chapter.
The greatness of this world is so incomparable and immense that, although it does have its limits and bounds, as may be inferred from its shape, which it could not have were it not finite and limited, it not only exceeds the faculty of the bodily senses, which are measures far too small and short to measure it,

embrace its extent and circumference: but also the human understanding, which, stretching the sight of the imagination across so vast a magnitude, becomes daunted and surrenders, acknowledging its own limitations. For this reason it is necessary to approach it gradually, part by part, exploring and uncovering it through much reflection in order to come to know it. Just as (to give an example) we behold a towering mountain range, full of the highest peaks, whose length runs for many hundreds of leagues; such as the great cordillera that crosses all of this South America: and from this range the mind rises to consider the great body of the land, which contains within itself many other mountain ranges and peaks of equal magnitude: and when we find ourselves in the middle of a broad and open plain and flatland, which is clear and unobstructed on all sides, giving a free view to the horizon: such as the great plains and flatlands of the provinces of Tucumán and Paraguay; and marveling at such extensive flatlands, we consider that the surface of the earth does not end with them, but rather embraces many others no less spacious than they: which together with the mountains, hills, and valleys make up all that of the whole globe of the earth that lies above the water. So too is the reflection, especially the one we make when, placed in the middle of the open sea, we cast our gaze in all directions and discover nothing but water and sky: and we understand how great a part of the land is covered by the waters of the ocean, and by the many arms and inlets that proceed from it.

History of the New World.
Known in this way, the greatness of the element of earth, one must give the imagination to measure it, so that by means of it we may go around circling how great the whole of the universe will be, going around it, and using as our guide the smallest star that our sight can reach, which to the senses appears no more than a tiny point: and persuading ourselves from its rays that it is a greater star than the entire lower globe composed of water and earth: and that just as seen from here below, though it is in itself so large, it appears to us as small as a dot: so also the lower globe, viewed from well before reaching the place where it is, will appear no more than another point; and from the starry heavens all of this can be seen in its entirety — the understanding is left stunned and astonished at the consideration of so immense a greatness: and more so if thought penetrates all the way to placing itself upon the summit and convex surface of the empyrean heaven, reaching so far out that there is no human force sufficient to go around and measure them. There are the final limits and boundary markers of the universe; up to there its domain and jurisdiction extends, and goes no further, because beyond what I have marked there is no longer any structure or building — beyond the outermost heaven is nothingness, where there is no body, no movement, no time: and so the world has no other boundary or border than that which it and the last sphere enclose: from which arises the meaning that the name Universe denotes, as Aristotle holds: coming to understand that, comprehending and enclosing within itself all bodies and giving each its order as its nature requires, it itself is not comprehended by anything else.

some other body, which would remain indeterminate, would be called a part,
and the name Universe would not suit it.

Having considered its greatness, it is well worth noting that its marvelous
beauty and capital nature declares to us the name of World, which
the Latins gave it, as Pliny says, for its extreme beauty
and consummate elegance. The Greeks called it cosmos, a name
of order, and taxis, for the singular order with which it is com-
posed of all its parts, which enrich and adorn it.
Plato called it the fullness of forms and species, on account of the many
that are found within it. But since its beautiful composition results
from the admirable parts it contains, and from the connection, order,
and harmony that those parts maintain among themselves: from this it follows that one must not
understand that all its beauty and loveliness is only the exterior kind, which
delights all bodily senses: but rather that the principal beauty is the interior,
which is the object of the understanding, through whose knowledge and
contemplation the soul is calmed and delighted, contemplating
the perfection and essential goodness of the Universe, and of all
its parts: and the order in which they correspond to one another, and all
to their ends: for which reason Saint Dionysius teaches that beauty
and perfection are names that signify one and the same thing, that
there is no distinction between them: that what the understanding
imagines insofar as it considers it under various aspects, and so the
most perfect as such, insofar as it is complete and not lacking
in what its being and essence require: and that which is thus perfect is given the
name of beautiful insofar as through its natural perfection, and the

History of the New World.
radiance nourishes, and enamors the sight of the body, and of the reason of those who look upon and know it. Plato said that beauty was the luster and splendor of good that those things possess, which are perceived through all the senses and through reflection. This beauty makes the perfection of the Universe consist principally of three things, which we equally find in it. The first is the beauty and perfection of the things of which it is composed; the second, the distinction and variety of its natural elements; and the third, the disposition and order of its parts.

Speaking of the essential perfection of things, which cannot be distinguished from their essences, it is clear and manifest that the world cannot exist without it, since the things that compose and form it cannot lack their own essences. The Universe must also be said to have accidental perfection, which arises from the form of each thing as its inseparable property; and no less certain and notable is the perfection that derives from the variety and distinction of the natures it contains. For it contains all the grades of beings, at least the primary and general ones, as Saint Thomas teaches, for it embraces the supreme genera into which being is immediately divided. Likewise, material and immaterial substances: among the latter, the three Hierarchies of the Angels, which are divided into nine choirs. Those are the classes of sublunary beings, which, as if by degrees, surpass one another in nobility. In the first degree are placed the simple bodies of which the Universe is made, as the foundation and whole of that which

First Part. Book 1.
The other creatures are contained and presented in the following order: the second belongs to imperfect mixed things, which are generated in the region of the air from the exhalations and vapors that, rising from the others, ascend from the earth and the water. The third contains the perfect mixed things, which lack life. The fourth contains the plants. In the fifth, irrational animals have their place. And in the sixth and supreme place is man: who, beyond being a sum and cipher of all the perfections shared by all the bodily natures of the other beings, surpasses them so greatly with the faculties proper to the rational part — understanding and will — that on account of these it is said that he was created in the image and likeness of his Creator, and as lord and master of His creatures; capable of free will, virtue, and merit, of praise and reward.

Beyond this, it was fitting that beneath each degree (except the sixth) there should be many species, through which various perfections would be spread and dispersed for the greater abundance and adornment of the world. In these we experience such different effects and properties that, by noting well the diversity of substances from which they flow: in the elements we see some heavy, others light and airy; some high, others low; some dark, others clear; some dry and others wet. In the imperfect mixed things, such a great multitude and diversity of impressions as appear in the region of the air; and in the mete-

History of the New World.

Some are resplendent, others dark; some precious, and others
worthless. Among plants the difference is no smaller, as can be found in
different parts of the world — those that are fruit-bearing and garden varieties differ from others. Some
grow in water, and others on land; some rise up
tall, while others spread along the ground and grow among it. Some
are medicinal and healthful; others are poisonous and deadly.
Some bear fruit, others only flowers; some produce worthy
flowers and fruit, while others yield nothing but wood and timber.
Finally, among animals, some are born and raised in water;
others inhabit the air, and others the land. Some are wild
and carnivorous, others tame and domestic. Some go crawling
along the ground, others stand upright on their feet. Of
all of them there are almost countless numbers, such are the differences that
are found in various regions. All this variety and distinction
of things nevertheless produces in the world a harmony and
consonance as well-ordered as that which in music is
composed of diverse voices, well attuned. Wherefore
Pythagoras said that in the composition of the Universe one perceives only
the order and correspondence that the strings of a lute
hold among themselves. And Saint Augustine compared it
to an elegant and measured verse, composed
of short and long syllables artfully
arranged.

Chapter 2. Continues the same subject as the previous chapter.

But so that the beauty and perfection that flows from this well-ordered arrangement may be more clearly understood, it will be good to explain in greater detail the order and subordination that all things existing in the world maintain among themselves. This order shines forth first in the place and position that each thing occupies, being content with that which best suits its nature; and in it, as in its own homeland, things remain calm and quiet, without desiring any change of place. The second way it appears is in the great subordination and harmony by which lower bodies receive from higher ones their movement and influences, through which they are ruled and governed by them; and the higher ones in turn by spiritual substances: among which there is also their own order and harmony, for the highest and most sublime announce to the others the divine mysteries. The third way this order is known is through the way all things attend to their particular ends, as well as to the end of the Universe.

And coming to man, who is the lesser world, for whose sake the greater was created: all his faculties, senses, and members are arranged with marvelous design and artistry for their operations and ends; down to the very source from which all of them spring, which is the soul. To the soul was given its being on account of the most excellent operations that it achieves with its most noble powers.

History of the New World.
of the understanding and the will, and these are spiritual forces
independent in their being from the body; yet because
the understanding, in order to act better and more in keeping with its na-
ture, has need of species and material and
corporeal forms; it was necessary to unite the soul with the human
body, which was created for its sake, and not the contrary. From
which it follows that the soul is the end of the body. And so for the minis-
try of the operations of the understanding, there were given to it fa-
culties and sensitive internal powers; and on account of these,
the external sensitive powers as well; and for the use of both the one and the other,
all the other faculties, organs, and material virtues:
which are ordered one to another in exchange, as to related things;
and because the superior and more perfect ones are looked to
by the inferior ones as their end.

From what has been said, it clearly follows that all the powers and
senses of the human body have such correspondence
and proper subordination that some look toward and bear relation
to others; and finally all are directed and serve
the understanding and the will, so that with their operations
they assist those of the understanding, either mediately or immediately.
From which it is concluded that if all the powers of
man, as well as their acts, exist for the sake of his end; and because
the body was composed and fashioned in the form that
those same powers required, so that it might be an apt instrument
for its actions: from each one of the powers, and from

The functions of these things show that in all of nature, there is no thing, however small it may be, that does not have its purpose, and is not ordered in such a way toward its end that no wise craftsman could find anything to add or remove, nor could the imagination conceive of inventing or improving upon it. For nothing is to be found in so marvelous and complex a structure that is superfluous, lacking, or defective: from which one might say that it could have been made better according to some other design.
In the same way we see in the other animals and in plants, that all the faculties they share with man exist for the sake of some end toward which they are directed. And from such faculties and virtues one can readily see that the whole structure and organization of their bodies exists by reason of the purpose for which they were made. Especially if we turn our eyes to the particular ends of each one, for the reason they were created was to serve mankind. Because, as one can see, in keeping with its purpose, nature contains within itself such a diversity of forms, and so great a variety of instruments, as we see in animals — in birds adapted for flight in one way, in land animals in another way, and differently in those that walk and live in the water — and all of it contrived to be most suited to their respective ends.
By the same path one may proceed, going through the...

History of the New World
other kinds of natures, and showing us how all the
things that are found in the universe have their own
ends: so that if we observe them carefully, we will
find that all of them serve their purpose. Both those that partake
of life, and those that lack it, are nothing other
than a well-provided storehouse and pantry, which the Creator
abundantly filled with everything that man needs
for his service, sustenance, and pleasure. For
some things help him in his labors, carrying his burdens:
others provide him with clothing and sustenance: others
delight him with their variety and vividness of colors: they entertain
him with their sweet song: and they refresh him with the delicate fra
grance that they release and spread: from some he benefits
in the study of the sciences: others serve him as instruments
of alliances, and exercise the virtues: and finally
all of them bring him various utilities and benefits, of
which it becomes clear that all of them exist for the sake of reason.
Aside from the consonance and subordination referred to,
which all created things maintain among themselves; of no lesser
consideration is the order that their maker, as efficient,
exemplary, and final cause, gives them. For which reason it is said
that the Creator made them with measure, species, and form,
lib. de nat. as Saint Augustine teaches. For insofar as they look
Boni. c. 3. to God as efficient cause, measure belongs to them;

First Part. Book 1.
them, having been given being, and by the bond they have to a limited and certain modification: insofar as they refer to God as their exemplary cause, the species belongs to them, that is, their specific, formed, and perfect being; and lastly, insofar as they bear an order toward God as their final cause, there belongs to them the order, which is the inclination of being, and the proper end of each one. These three circumstances are signified in those words of Wisdom, which say that God has set all things in number, weight, and measure. For number denotes species: since, according to the doctrine of Aristotle, the species of things are compared to numbers. By weight is understood order: because just as a body is carried by its weight, so the natural inclination and propensity of each thing carries it toward its own good. Measure denotes the mode, because measure is that which modifies and limits the essential perfection of a thing.
There also shines forth in this order that which the Universe expresses toward God in the participation of the supreme good: because, as Saint Dionysius teaches, although God is equally present to all things, they do not draw near to Him equally, because not all things participate in the same degree in the divine perfection, but rather in a certain order and distinction. For just as being, life,

History of the New World.
and knowledge, both of intelligible beings and of sensible ones: the things that partake most of perfections, we say come closer to God, and those that partake least are more distant and removed from Him. And accordingly, those that do not participate in life are placed in the last and most remote degree; those that participate in it, together with knowledge and immortality, are in the first and most proximate to the Creator; the rest stand in the middle, distinguishing themselves from those of the last degree, yet falling short of those of the first. And not only in the genera and species of things do we find this order, but it also reigns among the individuals of each species: for the individuality that each one has, being itself, and though distinct from another, represents the unity of God; beauty, divine wisdom, and utility, His goodness.

This admirable order and subordination that shines throughout the Universe, both among its parts with one another and of all of them with their Maker, implies that those parts that compose it must be almost infinite in number, distinct and of measured natures; so that the harmony by which they all agree and are unanimous, and are directed toward the common good of the Universe itself, may be called one. And because by the benefit of order the world is called One, from this arose that illustrious tribute: that without order there would be, and could be, no world.

Chapter 3. On the beginning and origin of the world, and how all the simple bodies contained within it were created and produced.

For greater ease and clarity regarding the many difficulties that are obscured in the matters already addressed,

The Most High God brought to light this marvelous work of the Universe, which He had drawn in His divine mind from eternity; when and as it pleased His infinite goodness, one thousand one hundred and ninety-nine years before the birth of His only-begotten Son and our Redeemer Jesus Christ. Giving beginning to the times and creatures that are measured by them, at the instant from which began the primordial age of the world, which was a Sunday; and over the following five days He was creating and placing in due proportion all its parts. For although it is true that for divine wisdom and omnipotence it would have been no less easy to create in a single moment, and from nothing, all that He made over the space of

Yet with all of this we see that it was not instantaneous; but rather successively, and in parts, he was fashioning and perfecting the universe, for the reason that his divine wisdom held, which we also understand. Given that the sacred doctors bring forth some suitable arguments of which one may here cite others.

And let the first be that which says that God, in the formation of the world, did so that its beauty and perfection might better be perceived. For just as an object placed against its opposite stands out more clearly, as white does against black; so by creating the world in darkness, and imagining it anew in his understanding in that darkness without any light, he better knew the great perfection and beauty that he bestowed upon it with the benefit of light. And in the same way, considering the state and condition that it had on each of those days that preceded the sixth; without the perfections that, like vivid tints and colors, were being added to it; the order, brilliance, and perfection with which the wisdom of the divine Architect arranged and adorned it shone forth all the more. Beyond this, it was fitting to the nature of the author of creation that he should maintain the same order and style in fashioning the world and giving being to nature; so that it would be proper and connatural to nature itself.

First, for the effect

These three bodies were the foundations, and with them

The empyrean sky served as its secure roof, and the element of earth as its floor and foundation; and all the remaining space filled with waters, from which, as from primary materials, the other parts of the great edifice were afterward fashioned.

The earth was created perfectly round, without the hills and valleys it now has: pure in its substance, though mixed with other things such as rocks, minerals, etc., yet without the accidental hardness that its essence required, as it lacked full dryness on account of being covered with water. Fitting to it are those words of the Royal Prophet: the deep covered it as if it were its garment. And because it lacked the ornament and perfection that it looked toward, still at the end for which it was created, the divine scriptures say that in that rough and crude state it was empty and imperfect, and so without appearance and luster that with good reason it could be called invisible matter; which name is given to it in the Book of Wisdom, where it is said that the hand of the Lord fashioned the orb of the earth from an invisible matter, or without form and without perfection. For being covered on all sides by an immensity of waters, it was not suited to be inhabited by men and animals, which was the purpose for which it was created. And all that abyss of waters, which was to yield the space

At the end of which, the first light and perfection that God placed in the world he had created in that imperfect state, began to emerge, by which his works were illuminated and made manifest; and the days began to be counted, in which God continued producing and perfecting what remained so that the Universe might attain its proper perfection. This light did not proceed from any body, but rather God himself produced it directly, in the manner in which it might derive from some luminous body, moving swiftly from one place to another across the entire circumference of the world: so that those first three days of time were one continuous and brilliant production of light. This light illuminated one hemisphere of the world from the surface of the earth to that of the water and the vault of the Empyrean heaven, penetrating all the depth and multitude of waters that lay between. And with a uniform motion it went leaving the eastern hemisphere and passing to the western, in the manner that the Sun now runs its course; and in the same space of twenty-four hours it made one circuit of the world, causing by its presence the day, and by its absence the night; and with three turns

Chapter 4. How God perfected and populated the world with the innumerable species of things that passed through it.

The world being now fully formed and composed of all its parts and intrinsic bodies, the divine artificer began on the third day to arrange it and accommodate it for the purpose for which He had created it. And since water still covered the entire surface of the earth, following its natural inclination, He separated these two elements, gathering the waters into one place so that the land would be left uncovered and made ready for the habitation of men and animals, and everything else that was necessary for the service of mankind. To bring about this separation He raised the earth in many parts

And because all the springs and gatherings of water called seas are connected and communicate with one another, as the experience of modern navigations has discovered; yet Holy Scripture says the contrary, that the waters were gathered together into one place: although the sea is not just one single body, nor is this part that lies between the dry land and the other part; but rather many, distributed throughout the whole earth. The waters of the sea being gathered together in this manner, God mixed into them many terrestrial exhalations, dry and parched, though He made them salty for their preservation and other purposes; and it is understood that perpetually the power of the sun and of other forces kept producing these same exhalations, and restoring to the water those parts which through various causes continually decay within it: because before the waters retired to the sea, they were not salty, given that God had not yet created any living thing, but all things were in their pure simplicity, and the elements preserved their purity. The circles of the sphere are some greater and some lesser: a great circle is one that divides it into two equal parts, or halves; and a lesser one is that which cuts it into two unequal parts. That which consists of the two equal parts into which the great circle divides the sphere is called a Hemisphere, because this name, which in Greek means half-sphere, is the same as half of the world. The great circles are six: the equinoctial, the horizon, the meridian, the ecliptic line of the Zodiac, and the two circles called the colures.
The equinoctial line is one of the great circles of the sphere, equidistant on all sides from the two Poles of the world: which are the limits and points at which the axis of the sphere ends. It has various names: one is called the North Pole, or Arctic, Septentrional, Boreal, and Aquilonal; and the other, the South Pole, or Antarctic, Austral, and Meridional. By this circle the sphere is divided into two.

equal parts, or hemispheres; each of which takes its name from the Pole that falls on its side. From the said Poles to the equinoctial line there are ninety degrees of latitude, out of the three hundred and sixty into which these Astronomers divide the entire circumference and circuit of the sphere. The Horizon is another great circle of the sphere, which divides it equally on all sides from our zenith, which is a point we imagine in the sky directly perpendicular above our heads; and from the Nadir, which is another point corresponding to the zenith directly below our feet on the other part of the sphere that we cannot see. From each of these points to any part of the horizon there are ninety degrees. Each location has its own horizon, which divides the part of the world we can see from the part we cannot: that which we see we call the superior hemisphere, and the other the inferior hemisphere.

The Meridian is the third of the great circles of the sphere, which passes through the North and South poles of the world, and through our zenith and Nadir. When the Sun reaches the feet of this circle, falling into the superior hemisphere, it is midday; and when it crosses through the inferior hemisphere, it is midnight. Chapter 6. On Climates.

Some cosmographers use the circles called parallels, while others use them to divide the world into climates. They call these circles parallels because each one runs around the sphere at an equal distance from the equinoctial line on all sides. A climate is the space in which there is a difference of half an hour in the longest day of the year, beginning from the equinoctial line and proceeding toward either pole of the world. And because those who live beneath the equinoctial line have days equal to twelve hours throughout the entire year, and from there the days gradually differentiate by another twelve hours up to the altitude of sixty-six and a half degrees — up to which altitude there is throughout the year a distinction between day and night — they count twenty-four climates in the following manner.

The space from the equinoctial line to eight degrees and three, not four minutes of latitude, where the longest day of the year is twelve and a half hours, is the first climate.

The second climate begins at eight degrees and thirty-four minutes, and ends at sixteen degrees and forty-three minutes; at which altitude the longest day of the year is thirteen hours, and the shortest is eleven.

It is worth noting here that the equality of climatic zones does not imply uniformity of temperatures in different hemispheres: inasmuch as the sun, being at the same altitude in the Southern hemisphere, aligns and interacts with different signs and stars than when it is at the same altitude in the Northern part: from which arise diverse and very dissimilar influences. Hence arises the difference in temperatures that we experience in the regions of this Southern hemisphere, compared to those experienced by other regions that lie at the same polar altitude in the Northern hemisphere.

History of the New World.

As proof of this we can give as an example two provinces of equal climates in both hemispheres, from experience: let them be that of Charcas in this Southern hemisphere, in the kingdom of Peru; and that of Mexico in the Northern hemisphere, in the kingdom of New Spain. Both fall under the third climate zone and at the same latitude, yet despite this they are very different in their qualities and products. For the province of Charcas has drier air; its high, cold mountains are bare; and in the deep valleys and ravines where groves of trees grow, they are of very different species from those found in New Spain, such as quinine, soto, villa, and other hardwoods of that same kind. And those same valleys are very well suited for vineyards, and thus a great quantity of excellent wine is harvested there.

On the contrary, the province of Mexico has more humid air, with denser forests, found on the high cold mountains near the snowy peaks, and the trees that grow there are pines, junipers, cypresses, oaks, and other kinds, so that apart from the cedar, which grows in both climates, no other species of the same kind is found in both. And the warm valleys of the province of Mexico, such as those of the Marquesado, are not suited for vineyards, but rather for sugar cane plantations.

The tenth heaven is what the astronomers call the prime mover, because it is the first that moves, and with its movement it carries along and draws after itself those that are beneath it. It completes its movement, which we call diurnal, from East to West over the poles of the world, and in the space of twenty-four hours makes a full revolution, so uniformly and regularly that it never moves at one time more quickly than at another. The speed of this movement at its outermost sphere is so great that it equals thought itself. In the lower heavens it grows greater the more they are separated from the tenth; as we see in any wheel that turns. Each of the ten heavens is attended and moved by an Angel, whom the ancient philosophers called Intelligences.

The empyrean heaven embraces and encompasses within itself all the other heavens, and surpasses them all in greatness, brightness, and beauty; and chiefly in the dignity of its nature; as befitted the office and purpose for which it was made, to be the theater of the celestial court and the dwelling of the blessed. It does not move, because it is a place of quiet and rest; and yet for all that it sends its influence down to the lower heavens; and many learned men are of the opinion that the diversity of conditions seen in some parts of the earth within the same climate arises from the influence of this heaven.

Chapter 8. On the aspect of the Southern sky, and the stars we lose sight of there.

I have not been able to consult with anyone on earth about the observation of this southern hemisphere's sky as much as I would have wished, because very few people devote themselves to its study, from whom one might gather the particular observations there are to be made regarding its appearance, and the many stars that we left behind on the voyage as we came to this southern part of the world, which the inhabitants of Europe do not know. And so what I have been able to learn about the matter has come through my own labor alone; for which reason I do not have the satisfaction I would have had, if what I write in this chapter had passed through the scrutiny of persons knowledgeable in astronomy. This is reason enough for me to be forgiven, if in treating these matters by my judgment alone, I should fall into some errors.

This part of the Southern sky is the most beautiful and clear, not inferior in beauty to the other, that of the North: rather it seems to me that it surpasses it in brightness; as we experience in those lands that enjoy a clear sky, free of clouds; which is the case in part of the plains, which lie away from the sea, at the foot of the mountains; and on the slopes facing the Southern sea of the same mountain range. Of the finest quality are the valleys

History of the New World.

of Chincha, Lunaguaná, Ica, and Nasca in the bishopric near Lima; and all those of the plains situated six to eight leagues from the seacoast. And of the second, the provinces of the highlands bordering those same plains, such as the city of Arequipa, which lies at sixteen degrees South. In that city, where I resided for three years, I made the observations contained in this chapter, owing to the very great purity and serenity of the sky that city enjoys every night of the year.

The beauty and clarity of the sky are caused, first, by the signs of the Zodiac, which fall nearer to us than to those of Europe. Second, and more principally, by that part of the Milky Way which in this region encompasses two particular constellations, and other large stars, and certain brilliantly shining parts of the sky that we have discovered here.

The Milky Way is a part of the firmament and the eighth heaven, which girds it all around, or from one side to the other, like a sash or band; or, better said, in the manner of a baldric — a splendid band, sparkling with precious stones, which lend it remarkable ornament and beauty. The source of its brightness is a matter of debate among astronomers, whether it comes from a multitude of tiny stars with which it is packed and which our sight cannot reach; or from being

First part. Book 1.
that part of the Milky Way which we can observe, toward the sun's light, outstanding and more intense. Whether this brightness comes from its own nature or from another source, what we observe is that the part of the Milky Way that falls in the Antarctic hemisphere, with its many more stars and brilliance, exceeds what falls in the northern part. For looking from our zenith toward the southern pole and the other pole, we discover the entire semicircle it makes on the southern side; and on the northern side, just a little past our own zenith, it disappears and we can no longer distinguish it from the rest of the sky. And viewed from the northern hemisphere, as I myself observed many times while residing in New Spain, we experience the same thing: that the part of the Milky Way contained in the Antarctic hemisphere is much brighter than what is included in the Arctic hemisphere. It does not end in a perfect semicircle within the hemisphere, but rather in an oval shape. And it begins to show itself with greater brightness from the sign of Gemini; which increases the closer it approaches obliquely to the Antarctic pole, declining somewhat toward the east through the following signs, up to that of Scorpio, where it ends at the foot of the Southern Cross, thirty degrees before the south pole; and from there it turns back toward the equinoctial line, and the northern part through the

other winds that follow, forming the semicircle described above.

Of the two constellations, or notable figures, that we observe in this hemisphere; the greater and most principal is the one we call the Southern Cross; which consists of four stars arranged in the shape of a perfect cross; which straightens and rises when our Meridian is such that the two stars forming the foot and head of the cross stand North to South; these stars are a little farther apart from each other than the other two that form the arms: so that all four display the figure of a cross raised upright. The star of the right arm, being the most easterly, is somewhat farther from the line we imagine running from foot to head than the star of the left arm; and thus one arm is a little longer than the other. The magnitude of these stars appears to be as follows: the star at the foot, which is the largest and closest to the Antarctic Pole — from which it is thirty degrees distant — is of the second magnitude. That of the head and that of the right arm are both of the third magnitude; and that of the left arm is of the fourth. Near the star of the foot another star of the fifth magnitude appears, almost equally distant from both. By the star at the foot of the Cross, navigators take their altitude at night using the cross-staff; and that star together with the one at the head serves as a clock by night.

Once the hour is known at which they align North to South, one can determine the bearings just as with the North Star. It has its station in the sign of Scorpio, and the Milky Way is found there; and so the Southern Cross appears to it like a jewel of very fine and circular diamonds, as if hanging from a necklace of precious stones.

Chapter 11. On the winds of the Indies.

The matter of the winds, which was already discussed in the previous chapter, pertains to these: the winds take on much of the character of the lands and seas through which they pass. Those that blow ordinarily in the region that falls within the tropics and the Torrid Zone are of two kinds: some are common and general throughout the entire year along the sea coasts, and others blow in the interior lands. At sea, and along the coasts, easterly winds blow most frequently, particularly offshore, and these we call Brisas; they are very favorable for sailing from Europe to the Indies, and from here to China, the East Indies, and for returning from there to Europe, because they always travel around the world from East to West, in which they appear to follow the diurnal movement of the heavens. Along the coastal lands, the South wind and the North wind are almost continuous, one on some coasts and the other on others. Along all the coasts of the mainland and of Peru, the South wind — which we call Sur — is the most frequent throughout the year; and sometimes when it ceases, the North wind takes over. When this happens, it is most often at night and in the mornings, and as midday approaches, the South wind rises again from the land.

On the coasts of the northern hemisphere, the North wind is more frequent; and between these two winds one experiences

History of the New World.
There are notable differences; the first is that the South wind in the climates of the Southern Hemisphere, which is its native region, is very gentle, pure, and mild; it crosses the equinoctial line, and entering the opposite hemisphere it becomes stormy and hot. On the contrary, the North wind in its Arctic hemisphere is cold; and as it passes beyond its limits and enters the other, it turns either cold or warm depending on the land that tempers it with the great coldness that the ocean water along the coast always holds. The South wind in its hemisphere communicates this to it and makes it unhealthy; and the North wind likewise in its northern region; and the others from the south cause sickness that unsettles the body and causes headaches. Beyond that, the North wind in its hemisphere, particularly in the Sea of the North, tends to be so vehement and furious that it causes terrible storms and shipwrecks; for which reason the fleets of New Spain are compelled to winter in the port of Veracruz from September until February, which are the months when the Nortes reign along those coasts; and even within the port itself the ships need to be well anchored and moored to defend themselves from its fury. But once past the equinoctial line into the other Antarctic hemisphere, the weather becomes well tempered.

Water is naturally heavy, though not as much so
as earth; cold and moist. And it is divided into
seas, lakes, bays, springs, and rivers. The sea is the place
where the Creator caused the waters to withdraw and gather,
waters which at the beginning of the world covered the land.
Which land occupies not one side of the world alone, and on the other side the land

History of the New World.

discovered, but rather that water and land are found everywhere together. Because in the way that God divided the two elements, they remained intermingled equally, with the sea making many inlets with its bays and arms into the land; and the land jutting out into the sea in many places with its shores, promontories, islands, and peninsulas; so that all the uncovered land remains on all sides neighboring the sea, and enjoys its comforts and riches; the winds and tides refresh it; and it is watered by the rains, which originate from its waters.

The sea is the beginning, end, and destination of all waters: because from it come all the rains and springs, and to it, as to a center, they all return. So that although the rivers that flow into the sea are innumerable, and some of prodigious size, as we shall see in this work, the sea neither grows nor overflows, because as much as it receives, it sends back in the form of vapors, which the power of the sun, and of the other stars, constantly draws up from its entire surface: in the same way that, through the heat of fire, the vapors rise from liquids that are distilled. And these vapors that rise from the sea turn into rains; with which the rivers are fed, and the earth, being moistened, generates in its depths and pores the water that flows from springs. From this it follows that the rainiest lands are the most abundantly supplied with springs and lakes, as occurs in

First Part. Book 1.

The general cordillera of mountain ranges of Peru, which, due to the great amount of water that falls from the sky, springs forth everywhere with fountains and piquios [small irrigation channels or springs]: from which all the rivers that flow from this southern America to the North Sea and the South Sea take their source. And at whatever time it rains, the springs produce more water than in the dry season. And just as the rains are more plentiful, so too are the springs: while on the contrary we see that the lands where it never rains lack springs entirely; as happens in these plains of Peru, which, for lack of rainfall from the sky, have no springs in them, except near the rivers in the valleys that are cultivated and irrigated: for the water there seeps from the rivers themselves and from the water used to irrigate the estates.

We also find by experience that during the season of the garúas [coastal mists and drizzles], which will be discussed in its proper place, in the plains that are watered by them, small springs and fountains tend to appear; and once the garúas have passed they dry up entirely. It is true that in those parts and seasons where that moisture is most abundant, these springs tend to last longer. But in most of the plains, where this rain does not reach, the land is so dry that springs never appear, and for lack of water it is entirely useless, and barren of men and animals.

We give the name Ocean to the sea in general, particularly to the wide and deep gulf that, with its profound bays, touches all parts of the world. And that portion we call the Mediterranean Sea: that arm of the Ocean which, breaking through between Europe and Africa by way of the Strait of Gibraltar, pushes inland to bathe the coasts of Asia. Apart from all these we have the various gulfs and inlets into which the ocean divides and spreads. The most common and well-known division in use today is that which is made of the sea into the North Sea and the South Sea. This division, as befits cosmography, is customarily made along the equinoctial line, so that all that part of the sea lying in the Boreal hemisphere takes the name of the North, and that of the other hemisphere, the Antarctic, takes the name of the South. Geographers and historians do not divide it strictly by that circle, but rather in such a way that a great portion of the sea lying in that hemisphere is counted as the South Sea, and conversely many stretches contained in the Austral hemisphere fall into what is called the North Sea. And there is no fixed mark that defines the limits of each of the seas: some are accustomed to extend them, others to narrow them. The most common way in which this division is made today is this: all the sea that lies to the West of the Americas, and runs from its shores turning westward until

First Part. Book 1.
the Philippine Islands, we call the South Sea; because it is that very great stretch of sea of the Western hemisphere: which is that which bathes the coasts of Terra Firma, and of New Spain; and what corresponds along that parallel as far as the aforementioned Philippines; and so too what lies on the ocean that falls to the east of America itself, and which has been called until the east, we name the North Sea, notwithstanding that it enters into the great expanse of sea of the Southern hemisphere, such as that which borders the coast of Brazil, and the other eastern coasts of America as far as the surroundings of Magellan Strait, and of San Vicente, where these two seas, the North and the South, meet and communicate.
On the coasts of the South Sea we observe that the tides — the rising and the ebbing — are very unequal; for on the coasts of Terra Firma and Nicaragua the sea rises and falls four or five fathoms; yet on the coast of Peru the tide is so slight that it is barely noticeable, not reaching half a fathom. And in those tidal flows and ebbs, the perfect correspondence and agreement with the movement of the moon that those who have written about this in Europe set down is not found to hold everywhere, as experience here shows.
And so we find in these seas of the Indies great diversity and variety of qualities in the gulfs that fall within the same climate, as is experienced on the coast of Peru, where the water of the sea so cold held the years

which can barely be swum in, being that of other parts of the same sea, and a climate so temperate that it partakes more of warmth than coldness. Beyond this, almost all year the current they call self-sustaining, or which it receives from the southern part toward the northern, runs so continuously that sailing in its flow one makes one's way toward the north; and on the contrary it overturns navigation toward the south, so that in less than two hundred leagues between the port of Payta and that of Callao, ships sometimes take five or six months; it being a journey of no more than six to seven days from Callao to Payta. And the same is experienced on the coast of New Spain on the North Sea, where the waters perpetually run toward the north, as can be seen in the Bahama Channel.

It is a matter very worthy of notice that, although the floods of the rivers on this coast of Peru come in summer, which is the time when it rains in the mountains, from October to March, and these same rivers diminish so greatly in winter that many dry up before reaching the sea — despite all this, the sea shows no change in rising more at one time than at another, but always remains the same. Inquiring into the cause of this admirable constancy, I found it to be the wonderfully ordered arrangement with which God composed the waters of the rivers that feed the sea, so that it might never lack sufficient nourishment: and it is that just as on this southern coast they are the fore-

the rivers of Summer are full and those of Winter ebb; and likewise in the other Arctic hemisphere, and on the coasts of New Spain; but in opposing months: so that when along the coast of Peru the rivers run fullest during the months of October, November, December, January, February, and March — at that same time on the other side it is winter, and the heat and warmth pass over; while when on those coasts of New Spain it is summer and the rivers rise, on those of the south it is winter and the rivers' rising ceases. And so, the waters of one hemisphere compensating those of the other, the sea comes to receive an equal quantity of water at all times, so as never to diminish.

The nature and properties of the particular springs, rivers, and lakes that we find in this New World are treated in the second and third parts of this history. I think it worth noting here only two things observed in that part of the Indies which falls within the Torrid Zone: the first is that inland one finds very few wells of brackish water, but rather that nearly all those dug yield fresh water, good for drinking. The second is that I have not observed the difference found in Spain in springs and wells with the changes of the seasons of winter and summer — whereby in winter the water flows warm and in summer cold — but rather that here the water is found the same at all times of year.

Chapter 13. On the Element of Earth.

The element of earth is somewhat rough and coarse, it occupies the lowest and central place in the world. Its natural qualities are dry and cold, and whereas the two superior elements are transparent, it is turbid and opaque, unable to be penetrated by light. The earth remains still and immobile by reason of its natural gravity and weight. It and the element of water together form a perfectly round globe, which is suspended on all sides, surrounded by air, and equally distant from the heavens — its properties and attributes being those that Holy Job indicates in those words: qui appendit terram super nihilum: meaning that God placed the globe of the earth in the middle of the universe, and keeps it there fixed and immobile, without resting upon any other body, for its natural weight and inclination — by which it seeks what is lowest and farthest from the heavens — suffices to hold it firm. This inclination is expressed in those words of the Prophet: fundabit terram super stabilitatem suam, nun inclinabitur in seculum seculi: and by this the earth is so still and stable that it never inclines to one side or another, for to do so would be to act against its own nature.

History of the New World
it does not argue against the roundness of the globe of the Sea that the land, being covered by water higher than the plains, has some parts raised into high ridges and mountains, and others low and sunken into valleys and plains. Because these ups and downs in so great a body are of such little consequence, just as a very large ball covered with cordovan leather, with the grain facing outward — the raised and sunken parts that show in the grain would not take away its roundness in that case, even if it would not be as perfect in the strict reckoning of mathematicians as it would be if the surface of such a ball were smooth. The same holds for the globe of the world, which would have a more perfect mathematical roundness if it lacked the high and low places that the land has, and if its surface were so even that all lines drawn from the center were equal — as indeed it was when it was first created. But it suited the purpose of the Lord that it should have mountains and valleys, for the benefits that this unevenness provides to the universe.
For, setting aside the beauty and adornment that the lofty mountains bring to it: from them principally comes the diversity of climates that we experience within a single region, which are so necessary for the production of plants and animals of different natures; in them rivers have their source, and flowing down to the sea they fertilize along the way the plains and valleys,

First Part. Book 1.
through which it passes: they serve the roads, and mineral deposits of metals: in them is found the healthiest and most convenient dwelling for human life: they are the wall and defense, without which we would be laid bare to the fury of the winds, to the floods and currents of the rivers: and finally for the benefit of the land, and for a thousand other advantages: all the more so because, as has been said, their unevenness does not affect the roundness of the Universe, as experience shows us in the eclipses of the moon, where we see the shadow of the earth as perfectly round, without the height of the mountains departing from this to alter its shape. It is true that the surface of the sea is more perfectly spherical than that of the land, because, being a liquid body, it spreads out evenly, and its surface turns at an equal distance from the center of the world.

This globe, composed of water and land, has a circumference of three hundred and sixty degrees, which by the great circle amounts to six thousand three hundred leagues. Until now it has not been possible to determine what proportion the surface of the water bears to that of the land that lies uncovered, nor which of the two elements occupies the greater part of the terrestrial globe; owing to the scant knowledge we have of that part which falls beneath the poles in the frozen zones. But speaking of what other more learned men have found, the Torrid Zone has no more surface of water than of land that is fertile and habitable; and in the austral regions, from the voyages made in our own times, both in the northern and southern parts, it appears that the ocean occupies the greater part.

But if we compare the two elements with respect to their quantities, it offers no help, for the land exceeds the water to such a degree that, if all the waters of rivers, springs, lakes, and seas were gathered and heaped together in one place, they would not cover so great a body, nor would they amount to much over the element of the earth. And because it is found by experience in the seas that are navigated, that when we take soundings they barely reach a depth of two miles; and if it sometimes seems that no bottom can be found in the open sea, it is because the longest sounding lines they carry are not more than a mile in length; and those who out of curiosity have sounded some very deep gulfs have found the result that I have described.

The task that this man came to undertake on these voyages was to find a way by which degrees of longitude could be measured in voyages made from East to West with the same ease and certainty with which degrees of latitude are obtained by measuring the Sun with the astrolabe; and it truly seems that he succeeded in his scheme, according to the demonstration he gave one day at noon in our house of Tante before all the friars who were there present. Of this scheme I thought it worthwhile to give here a brief account, since it has not yet been published, and in case it should never come to light, some knowledge of it may be preserved. This invention consists in knowing how the meridian is marked on a given day, and from it determining what the compass needle reads in the course of navigation from East to West, or the reverse. For this purpose the author of this device said that the world must be divided by two meridians that cross at the poles into four quarters of ninety degrees each. And that he had found by experience that at these meridians, which divide the world into four quarters, the needle points true north at the pole; and that passing from one meridian to another, the needle goes

Chapter 16. On Asia.

Asia is the largest of the three parts of the Old World, for
Asia alone is larger than Africa and Europe combined. Its
latitude begins at the equinoctial line and extends toward
the North as far as eighty degrees; and so the whole of it
falls within the Arctic hemisphere. In longitude it spans one
hundred and twenty-four degrees, which in terms of the
greater circumference amount to two thousand one hundred
and seventy leagues. It is bounded on three sides by the ocean;
and on the west it joins Europe through Tartary, and
Africa through Egypt. It is divided into seven parts: the first is the
one closest to Europe, from the Northern Ocean to
the Caspian Sea, which was formerly called Sarmatia
and is now called Muscovy or Moscobia; the second is Tartary, which
borders the Caspian Sea, the ocean, and Moscobia;
the third is the Turkish territory, which is the western part of
Asia, comprising the region between the Caspian Sea, the Persian Gulf,
and the Tigris River; the fourth is the kingdom of Persia; the fifth is the
East Indies from the Indus River to China; the sixth is the great
kingdom of China; and the seventh comprises all the islands adjacent to
Asia.

History of the New World.

The southernmost land of Asia is a peninsula called Arabia, which possesses the Third; it is divided into four great provinces: one is called Trogloditica, which belongs to the description of Africa; the second, bordering Mesopotamia, Syria, and Judea, is called Arabia Deserta; the third is Petraea; the fourth is Felix, which is the largest, most abundant, and most populous; full of incense, myrrh, and of precious and notable provinces; and the kingdoms of Sael and Aden are not without importance: from Arabia to Judea runs the province of Idumea, a land most abundantly rich in palms, and containing within it Gaza, a most ancient city, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and others.

The province of Syria is very large, lying between Arabia, the Euphrates, and Cilicia: it is divided into these five provinces — Palestine, Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, Syria, and Commagene. Palestine is divided into three parts: one properly called Judea, another Samaria, and the third Galilee. The capital of Judea is Jerusalem, the city of God, more exalted than all the cities of the world. Never was there seen a province in the entire universe that was, in proportion, as populous as Palestine when it was at its height: for although it measured no more than one hundred and sixty miles in length and sixty in width, in the census carried out by order of King David, one million three hundred thousand fighting men were registered, not counting among them the tribe of Levi.

Asia Minor is a great peninsula of land between the Black Sea (Pontus Euxinus) and the Sea of Cilicia, which they call Anatolia. The remaining western lands of Asia are all the provinces lying to the west of the river Tigris and the Caspian Sea, namely Mesopotamia, Greater Armenia, the Georgians, Mingrelia, and others encompassed between the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Sea of Azov. The Caspian Sea does not connect with the Ocean; it is eight hundred miles long and six hundred miles wide; and its water is not as salty as that of the other seas.
Mesopotamia lies between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris; it is rich land and of incredible fertility. Its principal cities are Urfa, Caramit, which in former times was called Amida, and Mardin, and Mosul. Further below, where the Tigris and the Euphrates meet, see—
