Chapter 1. On the names of the West Indies
and the New World.

To the last two parts of the earth, which we call America
and the Southern Land, and which by the proper subject of the history of the beginnings
of this second book, and where it will be treated even more, regarding
the greatness, situation, and nature of the New World, which
comprises the said two parts of the earth, and the great archipelago
of San Lazaro extending toward Asia — it is fitting to clarify first
the various names that the Spaniards have given it since
they discovered it in the year fourteen hundred and ninety-
two, and the one by which it is most commonly known at present,
and in what sense that name is taken, broadly, amplifying or restricting
its meaning, along with the reasons and motives that led the discoverers
to give it such names. For which purpose it is necessary

History of the New World.

One of the reasons that led our Spaniards to give new names to the lands they came across was that none of the native peoples of those lands had a general name by which they could be called. This was because knowledge extended no further than one's own homeland and province, and those that bordered it; to these they had assigned particular names. And since among the Indians there was in ancient times so little trade and commerce, they not only did not deal with anyone beyond their neighbors and nearby peoples, without venturing to distant lands; from this it followed that they came to know not only not all the land that lay adjacent to their own, but not even the provinces and kingdoms somewhat farther away, of which they had little or no knowledge.

The most general name that they commonly gave to the lands was to signify the district and province that was governed by a lord and cacique. And at most, the inhabitants of islands would name the whole island in which they lived with a single name, even if it encompassed many lordships. But the inhabitants of the mainland named it, as has been said, by small provinces; some of ten leagues in length, and others somewhat more or less, according to the extent of the lordship. The most extensive kingdom we find to have a general name given by its own people is the empire of the Inca kings of Peru, called by them Tahuantinsuyu, which measured some eight hundred leagues in longitude and a certain amount in latitude.

Within which there are many provinces, both small and medium-sized, each with its own particular names.

Four are the names that from the beginning of its discovery were given to this New World, namely: the Islands of the West, the West Indies, the New World, and America. Although when taken in their full breadth and broad meaning, these names all refer indifferently to the same thing — that is, all the land newly found by the Spaniards on this side, in the western hemisphere of the world — yet in their proper and more precise meaning they differ considerably, as I shall explain by going through each one in turn. I will begin with the first name, which is at present the least used, or better said, already entirely out of use and even forgotten: Some called this new land the Islands of the West, because the first part of it to be discovered was the Windward Islands, and for some years no mainland was found. And even after the mainland was found, because it could not be determined for a long time whether it was mainland or a large island, it was also called by the name of Island. And so in those early years, those who came and went from Spain used to say they were coming from and returning to the Islands.

And likewise in letters and public and private documents written at that time, it was given the same name of Islands; as we see was done by the Supreme Pontiff

Concerning the West: the name itself says it no less clearly, and if by the second reasoning — that it was thought to be continuous with the eastern land — they were no less correct; for we see that this land extends so far toward the West, and lies so far, that it is very probable it joins with Asia, whose province is the East Indies, according to what we famously stated in chapter 14 of the preceding book. And that name fits it perfectly, as is shown by the things found there, so novel and strange, and so contrary to all the doctrine of the ancient masters of philosophy.

Chapter 2. On the boundaries, size, and location of America.

Just as the Old World, which is divided into Europe, Asia, and Africa, has its length running from east to west, and its breadth from north to south: so this new world of the Indies, called America, extends and stretches in the opposite direction, from one pole to the other, and its breadth runs from East to West. On the southern side it shares its borders, by way of the Strait of Magellan, with the fifth part of the universe called the Austral Land; on the northern side it borders, and is even joined to, Asia; to the east it faces Africa and Europe, from which it is separated by the North Sea; and toward the west it runs until it meets Asia and approaches the Austral Land, with the South Sea lying between them.

This fourth part of the world begins on the southern side from the aforementioned Strait of Magellan at fifty-two and a half degrees south latitude, and runs northward to seventy degrees north latitude, which is the furthest point that has been discovered on that side. It does not run in a perfectly straight north-south longitude, since the southern part inclines somewhat to the east and the northern part to the west, so that its length runs in a northwest-southeast direction. Taking in this entire great land between two meridian lines, drawn so that the eastern one touches the island that faces east and is closest to it, which is that of Brazil,

and the western end being the farthest and most remote from the first, which is the coast of North America that faces Asia toward the West, comes to span from one point to another, from north to south, one hundred and twenty-two and a half degrees, which make two thousand three hundred and forty-three leagues; and one meridian is distant from another one hundred and seventy-six degrees, which along a great circle make three thousand one hundred and fifteen leagues: so that reckoning the length and breadth of it in accordance with that of the world, it comes to measure in length, that is from one meridian to the other, three thousand one hundred and fifteen leagues, and in breadth, that is from pole to pole, two thousand one hundred and forty-three leagues in a straight line drawn from North to South: where it must be noted that within these two meridians are included part of the Austral land, which will perhaps be counted here, and great expanses of sea, both of the South and of the North.

In proportion to the amount of water from the sky, the waters of the earth are ordinarily abundant as well: the very copious rains cause there to be so many springs, rivers, lakes, and swamps, that they make the Torrid Zone the most humid, pleasant, and plant-abundant region in the entire world. It is true that although this reasoning holds generally throughout the entire space falling within the tropics, it fails with respect to the plains of the kingdom of Peru, where it rains neither in winter nor in summer; and yet for all that, its heat does not exceed that of other provinces in the same climate. For this reason I say that rain alone is not by itself sufficient to temper the fierce heat of the sun; rather, other factors working together with others produce this effect. Of all of these, the most general one, which operates throughout the middle region, is one I will now describe. It has great power to mitigate the terrible heat of the region; which is in itself so excessive that, were it absent along with the other causes that combine to reduce it, the opinion of Aristotle — that the Torrid Zone would be uninhabitable — would undoubtedly prove true.

At one and the same time it is hot in some places and cold in others; some here enjoy a perpetual and pleasant spring; others at a short distance from them are stiff with cold, and still others a league away are scorched by heat: it is necessary that we seek other particular causes for this great variety.

The first and most principal cause of this variation I hold with certainty to be the cool winds that blow in some places and not in others, as is seen by experience not only on land but also at sea. And the plains of Peru, with their very great dry sand flats where it never rains, although they should be the hottest and most scorched land in the Indies, nevertheless, on account of the cool south wind that perpetually blows through them, are cold in winter; and the year there is more temperate and pleasant than in any land as low as it.

The following case, which happened to me personally, occurred while on a mule-driving journey. I recall that the lay brother in charge of supplies at the college of the Society of Jesus in the city of Lima used to make very thick woolen leggings for the black muleteers who transported the wine from our vineyard at Ica to the port of Pisco. I asked him why he made such heavily padded garments for them, given that the sand flats between Ica and Pisco are extremely hot. He replied that the cold which sets in there during the winter nights is so intense that the blacks would freeze, and they needed all that warm clothing plus a fire to warm themselves. This was so hard for me to believe that I decided to experience it for myself. And so, after having traveled the road from Pisco to Ica many times, I arranged to go with the muleteers during the month of July, which is the heart of winter. We spent the night in the middle of the road on a broad, flat stretch of ground. The south wind blew so keenly that the muleteers lit a fire, and I myself had to wrap up as best I could. What is more, when we set out at two in the morning in order to arrive early at Ica, the cold I felt was so intense that my hands went numb and I could not bring my fingers together until ten o'clock, when I reached Ica — something that had never happened to me on any of the many high passes and snowfields I had crossed in the kingdom. It happened that while sailing from Nicaragua to the kingdom of Latin Bermillo, six hundred and forty-two passengers were on the ship who had never been to that land; and since the heat of that island was so unbearable, they were all of them eager for the expectation that the heat would soon end, and that we would enjoy the fresh wind of Peru upon reaching the equinoctial line (which according to the general rule should have been the opposite, that the closer we came to the line the more the heat would increase). The reasons given by those of the Mediterranean as to why the islands of the Windward region are more temperate, and the heat is less intense than on the mainland, is because, being surrounded by the Ocean, and all of them being narrow, though some quite long, the sea winds notably cool them, especially the sea breezes and trade winds that blow from midday onward; and not only are they very pleasant and delightful on account of this, as I myself experienced during the year I spent on the island of Hispaniola. This is an opinion I consider very probable, because it satisfies as many doubts as may arise on this subject.

Chapter 5. That the division of the year as practiced in
Europe also holds true in the Torrid
Zone.

The reason why the change and inequality of qualities with the variation of seasons of the year, as experienced in Europe, is not felt in the Torrid Zone is a source of very great discrepancy and confusion among common people regarding how to count and distinguish the seasons. For since the Spaniards are accustomed to the reckoning used in Spain, where winter brings with it cold and wet weather, and summer brings warm and dry weather — not stopping to recognize two qualities but rather their opposites, so that dryness is joined with the cold of winter, and humidity and rains with the heat of summer — some rely on one quality and others on the other to orient themselves and distinguish the seasons of the year. Learned men, guided by the cold and warmth that result from the Sun drawing closer to or moving away from our hemisphere, follow the true reckoning, calling summer the warm period when the Sun moves through our Southern hemisphere, and winter the cold, or less warm period, when the Sun moves away from us and passes to the opposite hemisphere. But common people and those without letters, who are ordinarily the greater part of the republic, guided

History of the New World.

Regarding the rainy seasons, and running counter to the standard reckoning, they call the rainy season winter and the dry, clear season summer. In this they are not only plainly mistaken in calling those months winter when the Sun is directly overhead and the heat is at its strongest — simply because the rains come then — but they also call it summer during the cold period when the Sun is farthest from us, merely because it does not rain. From this reckoning many absurdities follow.

The first is that in the Indies, winter ought to be warmer than summer, and summer colder than winter. The second is that in the Kingdom of Peru, at the same latitude and altitude, people call it winter in one place and summer less than four leagues away: because since in the highlands it rains in summer and not in the lowlands, and these two lands of such different character border one another, they say that when it is winter in the mountains it is summer in the lowlands, and vice versa. The third absurdity is that, the year being divided into only two seasons — namely winter and summer — they lengthen one and shorten the other within a single climate according to how much time the rains occupy in one place versus another. For where it rains no more than four months of the year, people call those four months winter and the remaining eight summer. And where the dry, clear months number no more than three or four and the rest are rainy, they make summer no more than three or four months and winter eight or nine. But where

The error is most clearly seen in lands where it rains all year long, where people find themselves stumped by this reckoning, unable to distinguish between winter and summer.
But the truth is that in dividing the year into two seasons, winter and summer, this division and reckoning must be made according to the approach and withdrawal of the sun, calling it winter in the hemisphere when the sun travels on the opposite side, from one equinox to the other; and summer, from when it enters our hemisphere until it leaves it. These seasons are followed, as their proper qualities, by cold, or a more moderate warmth, from the sun's absence; and with its presence, more intense heat. From this it follows that rain or lack of rain, making the weather wet or dry, is something incidental to winter or summer. From which it becomes clear that because it rains in the Torrid Zone when the sun is in our hemisphere and summer arrives, and because the weather turns cold and clear when it is far away and most distant from ours, one must say absolutely that rains and wet weather belong to summer, and drier, clearer weather to winter.
The division that in Europe is made of the year into four seasons — spring, summer, autumn, and winter — also applies to this middle region and Torrid Zone; this division arises from the four notable points that the sun marks for us at the two equinoxes and two solstices in the movement it makes in a year. And even though these seasons are not distinguished here by the qualities that those who make this division in Europe attribute to each of them — who make it in the following manner —

Because the Sun reaches the equinox on the twenty-ninth of March, the three following months are called spring until the northern solstice, because when it reaches the tropic of Cancer on the twenty-second of June: From here, for the next three months until the equinox of the twenty-third of September — that is, from that point until the Southern solstice of the twenty-third of December — is autumn; and from this solstice and tropic of Capricorn until returning to the equinox of March, is winter. Astrologers and philosophers assign to each of the seasons two qualities, belonging to the two symbols that Aristotle attributes to each of the elements; and they compare these four seasons to the four ages of man, to the four humors of the human body, and to the four elements. Setting aside that in all those lands there is only one wind that blows throughout the year, we observe that it rains there during one season and thunders in another, as happens in the lowlands of that kingdom, where the rainfall comes in winter and not in summer, with the wind of that name blowing every year across these southern lowlands. At night the air becomes turbid, the weather closes in, and the sky discharges heavy rains, and especially around midday in autumn those clouds rise and dissolve into rain, since when they withdrew at dawn the horizon remained clear and free of clouds. It seems to me that in what has been said above, the reasons previously given — that some believed the Torrid Zone received its rains in summer and not in winter — are sufficiently refuted and dismissed.

What I feel regarding this difficulty, and others no less significant, which present themselves at every turn when considering the strange and admirable effects of nature that we have experienced in this New World, is that no matter how much the human understanding may toil and exhaust itself in inquiring and tracing their causes, it cannot grasp them all, since many of them are secret and hidden from the senses. I hold it as certain, for instance, regarding those that cause the summer rains: the supreme and lofty wisdom of the sovereign Creator of the world ordained that these should occur in this place, in order to provide for the needs of the Torrid Zone so that it could be habitable — for otherwise it would not be, or would be most uncomfortable for human habitation. The reason is that this entire middle region, as we shall presently see, has on one side iron and sand, which is very vast and hot, and very high mountains, dry and cold; and although between these two extremes there are some intermediate and temperate lands, the southern side

Those that occupy the greater part of what has been seen in the world within the tropics. Of these, some lands were made useless and barren, one by excessive heat and others by their rigorous cold; if in the first the summer heat were not tempered by rains; and in the second, the intemperate and cruel cold of winter were not counteracted by the continuous sunshine and the dry, clear weather that prevails at that season.
In order to understand this better, it should be known that the cold of the lands of Peru is so excessive that, while the valleys formed within them — which, being low and sheltered, are temperate — the remaining terrain cannot be traversed without people placing themselves in the sun during the day and gathering near fires at night. So it is that although the heat of the sun is very great, being so directly overhead, the cold of the land on the other hand is so rigorous that it tempers and mitigates it in such a way that one can walk and work in the sun all day without feeling heat or sweating at any time of year. And it is very common and customary for those who live in the highlands, when the midday sun is at its most intense, to expose themselves to its rays, covering only their heads with some shade so as not to be burned. From this it follows that since the cold of the highlands remains so constant throughout the year, if the rains came in winter, the land would undoubtedly be entirely uninhabitable for many reasons.

History of the New World.

The first reason is that whatever fell there would come down frozen in snow, and cold, as experience shows with the snow that sometimes falls at the beginning of the season, or at least surrounding areas at other times, with which men could not endure the terrible cold that would result; nor would the land be cultivated and produce fruits; nor would the livestock have pastures; the cold would be intolerable, because snowing every day, such a quantity of snow would pile up on the land that it would last throughout the entire winter, and with the cold that comes from it increasing, and the icy winds that would blow, to the extreme that I say the region already reaches — who could live there? For even in summer, when the weather is by nature milder and more temperate, though it may be warm during the day, the cold is still distressing; on days when it snows, rains, or is cloudy, because the sun does not warm the earth with its rays, one feels greater cold than in winter; so much so that it is necessary to stay by the fire all day long; but as the weather clears and the sky brightens, and the sun comes out, it becomes notably more temperate. From this one can gather how great a role rains play in refreshing the land.

That during the snow neither would the land be sown, nor would the livestock have anything to eat, is very clear, as we find ample experience of this in the sierra itself.

Because going around toward the south as far as the Strait of Magellan, and already leaving the tropic of Capricorn, those regions in winter have, for six months of the year, such an immense quantity of snow upon them that they are not only uninhabitable by people, but not even by animals or birds. And what is more, the roads that connect the kingdom of Chile to the province of Tucumán cannot be traveled in winter at all, until the sun and clear weather of summer melts the snow from the mountain passes and ravines through which the roads are cut, and it becomes possible to travel them. The second reason why it would be uninhabitable is that even if something were sown, the seeds could not possibly germinate given the intense cold and frosts that occur every night, which scorch and wither the plants. The third reason is that even if winter were past, and there were time at the end of summer, one could not sow crops in the rainy season because there is no water, as is currently done; and even if in some places crops were sown under irrigation, they would wither upon sprouting. For every night of the year, both in winter and in summer, whenever the sky is clear and free of clouds, frosts fall. For this reason God arranged that rains should come in summer, so that through them the earth would be watered and sweetened; and with the mildness of the season, which is not as harsh as winter, the crops could grow.

And what is most important, and in which divine providence shines no less, is how the clouds calmed and prevented the crops from being lost to the frosts: because, even though it may be summer, any night that clears up and the sky becomes serene is likely to bring a frost as a matter of course. To address this danger, the Lord arranged the winds and atmospheric influences in such a way that from December through March inclusive — which is the season when the crops are most at risk — there is scarcely a night when the sky is not covered with clouds, without clearing away entirely. During these months the inhabitants of the land are also so wary of the sky clearing and a frost falling that before going to bed they customarily go out to see whether it is cloudy or clear; and if it happens that on some night the sky clears so thoroughly that no clouds can be seen, a great wailing arises, and the stars shine bright and clear — it is a great pity and sorrow to hear the cries and weeping that rise up in the Indian towns. For, forewarning themselves by these signs that a frost is certain on such nights, they do not wait for daylight to learn of the damage, but go out before dawn. And the damage is truly incomparable, what a single night of frost can do, because when it freezes it is commonly so widespread that it may extend over a hundred leagues or more, destroying many thousands of ducats' worth of crops. Chapter 6: The sierra of Peru depends on having its rains in summer.

It remains now to show how the rains are also the cause of the highland being settled and cultivated. But it is clear enough, and needs no further proof beyond the experience we have had, that in the sierra during the rainy season it is felt to be colder in summer than it normally is in winter. From this we can make the following argument: if the rains in the sierra cause such cold in summer — when it would otherwise be temperate — as great as that brought by winter, then likewise in the hot lands they must have great power to moderate the heat of summer, so that the land is not scorched as it would be without them. And so I conclude this question by saying that I find no other reason for the summer rains in the Torrid Zone than that it is thus fitting so that it may be inhabited, and no less for the health of its inhabitants: because both in the sierra and in the lowlands the rainy season is the healthiest time of the whole year. When the rains are late in coming at their usual time, acute illnesses tend to break out, such as fevers and pleurisy — of which there is experience both in Peru and in New Spain, particularly in the city of Mexico, where when by May the rains do not come —

Chapter 7. On the situation of the Kingdom of Peru.

The Kingdom of Peru runs north to south seven hundred and seventy leagues in length, and in width reaches up to one hundred and thirty leagues at its widest, and about eighty at its narrowest. Its farthest limits are, on the northern side, the province and diocese of Quito, and on the southern side, the Archbishopric of Charcas. Because this region encompasses, and all of America experiences, all the qualities and varieties of cold and temperate climates found in the Torrid Zone of this New World, its consideration is very important, because upon it depends the full understanding of the nature of all these Indies. The diversity of climates in this kingdom proceeds from one of the greatest mountain ranges known in the world, which runs along its length, and which we call the sierra, or the general cordillera of Austral America, or of Peru; because it begins and ends with this southern part of America, from the Strait of Magellan at fifty-two and a half degrees of latitude from the Antarctic pole, and runs to the coasts of the North Sea of the provinces of Santa Marta and Venezuela, where it ends at ten degrees of the Arctic hemisphere, in which span, although by a straight north-to-south line there are no more than one thousand and ninety-four leagues; nevertheless, in all

First Part. Book 2.
This great Sierra did not run always in one direction, but rather turns in three directions, and thus its length is more than one thousand five hundred leagues. And there have been no shortage of learned men, moved by its extraordinary height and grandeur, who hold this Cordillera to be the spine of the world, which branches out and joins everything in a circle, so that rising up from the ocean, where it ends to our sight, it continues beneath the water, its height exceeding all the floor of the sea, just as it exceeds all other land beyond it; and that it continues from there to other regions of the world. But this is uncertain, and has no greater foundation than the contemplations and discourses of some philosophers of the Indies. What is established and verified is that it embraces and encircles all of this Southern America, not through its middle, but along its western side, standing no more than about fifty leagues from the South Sea at its farthest, and no more than eight at its closest. And the same distance from the North Sea in the said provinces of Santa Marta and Venezuela.
The two slopes and flanks of this sierra are of a very complex nature in all that falls within the tropics, setting aside the western slope of the kingdom of Peru, which has very particular and strange qualities such as are not found elsewhere in the Indies. For this reason we shall divide the land of Peru into three parts or regions, which are like three narrow strips running the whole length of the kingdom; and each is of such different and contrary qualities from the other, that

History of the New World.

By way of introduction: The eastern region and strip embraces the slopes and foothills of the land that face east, which we call the Andes and the yunca lowlands. The second strip is the sierra itself, which by excellence we give the name of sierra, and cordillera in general, to distinguish it from the other mountain ranges found in the land. The third encompasses the western slopes and foothills of the same sierra, and is the region we call the llanos.

These three strips and regions differ from one another in the following ways. The first is that, granted that in all three there is both hilly and flat terrain, the sierra and cordillera still surpasses the other two in height to such a degree that the middle region of the air, and the clouds of both of the others, remain far below its peaks. The second difference is that the yunca lowlands are very hot and humid throughout the year; the sierra very cold and dry; and the llanos moderately warm and humid, with no more notable difference between winter and summer than the other two. The third is that in the yunca it rains in some parts all year, and in others for the greater part of it; in the sierra at set times, which is during the summer; and in the lowlands we have little rain, and in a certain part of them what little there is falls in winter. The fourth difference is that the yunca has many swamps and marshes, great dense forests and woodlands, and resembles the torrid zone in form. The sierra, though it is abundant in rivers and lakes, is bare and treeless and healthier than those parts of the New World that lie within the tropics; and the land of the llanos is dry, without water or forests, and not as healthy as

sierra, nor as clearly defined as the yunca land. Finally, within these three regions, despite being neighboring and sharing the same climate over so short a distance, there are such strange and different qualities to be found, as will be seen when treating each one in particular.

Chapter 8. On the qualities of the yunca land of Peru.

The Indians of Cuzco and its surroundings called by the name of yuncos those lands that lie on the eastern side of the great cordillera, which are directly opposite that city, being principally the provincial land called Anti; a place of very hot and humid climate. From this, the Spaniards, extending these names to all lands of the same character, call them yuncos, and Andes, a corruption of the name Anti; and they call the natives of those lands Indios yuncos, distinguishing them from those of the sierra, whom they call Serranos. The yunca land, as it falls within the boundaries of Peru, is that which lies at the foot of the great cordillera, on the far side of it; and it begins some five or six leagues below the summits of the cordillera, which space consists of very steep, cold, and bare slopes, like the rest of the sierra in general, until one descends five-sixths of its great height.

Although from where the yunca land begins, it extends with the same properties described here all the way to the shores of the North Sea; and in that stretch there are more than five hundred leagues of

History of the New World
unknown lands, inhabited by innumerable nations of gentile Indians, and the kingdom of Peru has no designated limits on this side, nor are its boundaries and borders fixed; some cause others to extend them, and others to shorten them: it seems to me that we can assign forty leagues of width to this strip of yunca land that belongs to the kingdom of Peru: its length runs the full extent of the said kingdom. Because on the side where some provinces have already been pacified by Spaniards, all of the above is true, as in the bishoprics of Quito and Trujillo, whose boundaries extend a number of leagues into the interior: in the rest that borders other provinces of the highlands, almost from whatever direction one enters these Andes and the yunca land, no warring Indians are encountered throughout this entire breadth. And so the first region, or strip of the three into which we divide Peru, which is the eastern part of the yunca land, has a width of the said forty leagues; and in length from the bishopric of Quito inclusive to the Tropic of Capricorn, where Peru ends on this side, and the province of Tucumán begins. For this reason, this first strip is more than fifty leagues shorter than the other two: because Peru does not extend as far south on this side as it does along the highlands and the sea coast.

Of those eighty-odd leagues of land, the first twenty leagues from the foot of the main mountain range toward the east, which is its width, consist of very rugged and folded hills and ridges, rough and craggy, covered with very dense groves and forests, and there are only some ravines and small valleys formed by the rivers, and even these are bare and narrow, rising

closes and enclosed outskirts. Coming down from those mountain ranges, the rest is flatland; though there is no shortage, here and there, of some hills and small ridges that cut across wide plains: these parts being highland and lowland; and partly made up of large and spacious savannas and meadows, which the Spaniards name after the flatness they judge them to have, calling them open plains. Some of those savannas are so large that, leaving the boundaries of one, one descends into the interior of the land for more than a hundred leagues without finding any hills to block the view. From what is known through accounts of persons who have entered the lands of the gentiles bordering this territory nearby, the greater part of the plains is occupied by dense woodlands; and where the land is open it still has, at intervals, some patches of highland, which, in relation to the open plains surrounding them, look like islands. In the rest of those open plains free of woodland, there grow in great abundance grasses suitable for large cattle; which the Spaniards call pajunales, because they stand so much taller than other plants, and in such great quantity — because of the lack of animals to graze them — that, the dry growth of one year reaching that of the year before, the amount of dry grass is ordinarily as great as the green. The sierras, or ridges, that rise among those open and highland plains share the same character: part of them are outskirts, and part rocky, though they are generally rough, and more so in their slopes than in the flatlands. As regards the soil, situation, and lay of the land in general:
As for the climate and quality of the soil, it is all very hot and humid; and it partakes of moisture not

History of the New World

carried by the very humid air (for it is from this quality that a region is principally called temperate, humid, or dry), but also because its soil is notably moistened both from above and below: for in some parts it rains all year long, in others more or less, and where the rains are most concentrated they fall in the months of peak season, during which time there are many thunderstorms, lightning, heavy downpours, tempests, whirlwinds of fierce winds, lightning flashes and thunderclaps: never at any time does snow fall, nor hail, nor is there any frost or ice. With the heavy rains the rivers rise continuously, and overflowing their banks and shores they flood much of the land, forming great pools and lagoons because the rainwater cannot drain away in many places. And so there are very large stretches of land covered by lakes, marshes, swamps, bogs, and flooded areas.

The heat of the air is so intense that the natives go about naked and unclothed, having no need of garments to cover themselves by day or by night. The Spaniards go about sweating most of the time; and the heat would be even more unbearable were it not tempered by the fresh breezes that sometimes blow. So that these breezes may circulate and cool their houses, the Indians build them without walls all around, but only on wooden posts, open on all sides to the winds. One can also observe the humidity of this land in the fact that food cannot be kept, as it quickly rots; iron becomes corroded; meat goes bad by the second day; salt in saltshakers dissolves and turns to water; and when goods arrive they can scarcely be lifted in sacks.

because it folds like wet paper. It is very unhealthy and sickly land; the Indians have teeth the color of cooked quince, and the Spaniards, even if they arrive there with good complexions, soon lose them and turn yellow, looking like sick men. For this reason it has always been the least populated land among the Indians, as it still is today, both among the natives and the Spaniards. In the end it is better as a place for those who come to live there, because it has a most beautiful appearance, being at all times clothed in greenery and covered with groves of trees, so that one does not know what winter is, which elsewhere strips away their beauty, owing to the continual humidity of the climate. The best and healthiest time of year is winter, because the rains cease, the weather becomes clear and dry, fresher breezes blow, which diminish the excessive humidity of the soil and air, and the heat moderates. With all this it seems that the Creator compensates for the intemperate nature of this region and, together with enriching it with natural goods, grants it favorable winds above all the rest of the new wealth in variety of plants, animals, and abundance of gold mines, which are found throughout it. The Indians had no tame or domestic animals other than guinea pigs and ducks, but this land breeds wild and fierce ones such as tapirs, deer, small cats, wild pigs, armadillos, hares, rabbits, guadatinapos, lions, tigers, bears like those of Europe, and besides those, what we call anteaters, pericuigera, foxes, vicuñas, wildcats, ferrets, weasels, squirrels, innumerable different kinds of monkeys, and many are born

Animals and venomous creatures: mosquitoes, though smaller in body than all the rest, surpass them in being bothersome and harmful; there are innumerable ones, of four or five species, as well as various kinds of ants, all manner of vipers and snakes, notably those we call "bobas" which are as large as great beams; bees that make honey in the hollows of trees and underground. In the rivers, which are very mighty where they descend from the main mountain range and cross this land, great numbers of fish are found. The variety of birds that inhabit the forests and woodlands is beyond counting, particularly those of beautiful colors, which the native peoples prize most for the fineness of their feathers: some are entirely red, others green, others blue, others yellow, and others of every other color. There is plenty of game birds in the lands: pheasants, parrots, macaws, herons, turtledoves, doves, ducks of various breeds, and others of different kinds. Birds of prey: eagles, condors, hawks, choice falcons of every kind. Finally, so great is the variety of birds found in the mountains and ranges of the Andes that their species and kinds cannot be counted.
Beyond all the fruits of the land found in other parts of the Indies, outside of this territory only a few fruits grow; and there are the various kinds of resins that are brought from the Indies to Europe, such as balsam, liquidambar, dragon's blood, anime, oil of Mary, incense of the land, copal, caraña, rubber, tecomahaca, and many cedars and countless other trees of prized timber, brazilwood, and others.

The coastal mountain range, though from time to time it has very tall and rugged, snow-capped peaks — such as the one that stands directly opposite this city of Lima, which we call Luna, and the range of Pariacaca, named for a great snow-capped peak it has by that name, which can be seen from this city on clear days — in many places it descends and forms wide passes, such that it rarely snows there throughout the seasons, although it is always a very cold highland, and snow-capped peaks are never out of sight. It has many very tall volcanoes that are continuously smoking, and not infrequently launch fire; and when one of them erupts it causes incomparable damage to all the surrounding lands and provinces, as we shall shortly describe.
The Eastern range, or that of the Andes, is higher, with more towering, rugged, and snow-covered peaks. No volcanoes are seen in it, nor is it as broad as the coastal one, since its common width is only six to ten leagues of crossing, whereas the first is fifteen to twenty. In places this eastern range is so tall and snow-covered that seen from afar it looks like nothing but a string of sugar loaves, on account of the many tall, snow-covered peaks it has.

Because this great mountain range is divided throughout, it is the most abundant land in springs and fountains in all of Peru, and indeed in all the Indies. In effect, this is such a folded land that of every eight parts, no more than one should be flat; and this flat land is distributed among certain valleys, which are formed where the mountains open up, between the peaks that surround them: and in spacious plains and plateaus that are also found upon the mountains themselves. The most important valleys are those of Huanca, Cajamarca, Jauja, Sangaro, Andahuaylas, Jaqui, Jaguanal, Yucay, Cochabamba, Cliza, Misque, Tarija, and others of lesser note found in the dioceses of Huamanga, Cusco, Chuquiabo, and Chuquisaca. Of the high and cold plateaus, the most extensive are those of the provinces of the Collao, which run along the length of the mountain range between the two snowy cordilleras for about one hundred and fifty leagues, between the provinces of Cusco and Chuquisaca.

All of the sierra region is in general bare and treeless land, with no woodland except in certain valleys and deep, sheltered ravines. Its climate, generally speaking, is dry and cold throughout the year to an extreme degree, especially during the three winter months. For this reason, fruits and seeds can be kept for a long time without rotting or being eaten by worms; nor does moth damage come as quickly as in humid lands to clothing and books; at least while I was residing in the sierra, having gone through many books, I never found

History of the New World.

some eaten by moths. Dead meat keeps without spoiling for two months in winter, and somewhat less in summer. However, throughout the whole year, due to the intense cold and dryness, the pot that is to be eaten at midday must be put on to cook from the night before. The air is so dry that when a person sneezes, and when shaking out the bed blankets, sparks ignite and fly about. And to say mass, one must be very careful in breaking the host, because it is as dry as tinder. And particles are wont to fly off. The salt in the saltcellars never cakes or gets damp. In short, the dryness in winter is so excessive that it makes this season the least healthy of the year, and when some acute illness strikes, everyone hopes the rains will come soon, because with them the severity eases and fewer people are in danger. Thus the healthiest time of the year is summer, or autumn, on account of the rains, which moisten the air and temper its great dryness.

What also helps to make winter less healthy are terrible winds that blow during the months of June, July, and August, which they call throughout the region Tomahelas, because they come from Haina, a village of that name; and in the rest of the land of the province and diocese of Charcas they give them the same name. They are very dry, harsh, and dark; they raise great whirlwinds of dust, with which they notably muddy the air, soil and coat clothes with dust, so much so that one is hard pressed to protect oneself from the dust that this season brings; and with them

First Part. Book 2.

winds cling to clothing, and have a very singular property, different from the dust of other regions, because it cannot be removed from garments however freshly washed or cleaned with brushes; rather, it is necessary to dampen them first so that the dust will come off; which is done by watering the ground well and hanging the garments out overnight, and by morning the moisture that has acted on them allows them to be cleaned easily.

But of greater consequence is the harm that the winds cause to human bodies than to the clothing that covers them; because they notably dry out the brain, and kindle the temper in such a way that on the slightest occasion men lose their composure greatly; and so in the highland towns, ringworm is common at certain times, and even more frequent are scabs, and acts of violence; and this harm would be greater were it not somewhat remedied by the sky, through the snows that come in the afternoons, which partly temper and moisten the air. With respect to this extreme dryness, it has been found by experience that the dwellings of houses situated lower are healthier to live in, and whatever vapors come from above; because although the sky is almost always clear, the ground is moist, though not as much as that of the lowland soil, whereby the moisture of the ground in the lower dwelling somewhat repairs the harm of the dryness of the air. From which it is clearly inferred that the temperate quality of a region being humid or not does not arise from whether the soil is so or not, but from the ambient air; because where there is greater humidity than in the water and in all the air, the climate around the highland lakes is as great as that which the land of its shores enjoys; as those who sail the great lake of Chucuito experience, which lies in the coldest and driest part of the land.

The rains are not uniform, because in some places they come earlier and last longer than in others: in the province of Quito it rains almost every month of the year, with no more than three or four dry months, during which it still rains on some days; so that throughout the whole year there is no certainty of enjoying a single clear day. The same happens on the peaks of the two snow-capped mountain ranges, where one can hardly travel without encountering snow or hail. Even so, the most common and general pattern throughout the land is for the rains and seasonal storms to last from December to March, except in the temperate valleys, where they usually begin one or eight months earlier.

The sky is extremely changeable and variable; for the day often dawns clear and calm, without a cloud in the sky, and within about eight hours the weather turns, the air grows troubled, the sky covers itself with dark clouds, and furious downpours fall with great storms of thunder, lightning, and flashes, as if the clouds were splitting apart; and then the storm ceases as suddenly as it began, and the sky clears again. At other times, it dawns snowing, with the weather closed in on all sides, the fields covered in snow, and as far as the eye can see — hills and valleys alike — blanketed from having snowed all night, so that it seems impossible for so much snow to melt except over many days; and then suddenly the weather clears, the sun comes out, and within about eight hours not a trace of snow remains on the ground, nor does anything white appear across the whole expanse that, two hours before, showed nothing but snow to the eye.

So ordinary are these sudden changes in summer

The downpours usually begin sometimes with hail accompanied by fearsome thunder and frequent lightning; and then afterwards, when the storm ceases, the rain continues gently. Although, as has already been said, the whole mountain range in general is cold, taking its name from the greater part, nonetheless because of the inequality it has in some parts being higher than others, one finds in it a great variety of climates; which arise not only from the high mountain range being very exposed to the winds, and the deep valleys sheltered by hills that surround them and cause greater reverberation of the sun's rays; but mainly because the air is by its nature colder the higher and more distant

History of the New World.

Of the land, of which the low-lying territories give sufficient proof, being found in low positions and surrounded on all sides by hills, and the high plains that form above the mountain ranges enclosed on all points by ridges and peaks: of these, those that have no surrounding hills to shelter them and cause the sun's reflected rays to warm them are very cold, and these are exposed to all the winds, and the sun strikes them with direct rays, and on account of the reverberation that comes from the mountains surrounding them, they are extremely frigid. Of this diversity, another explanation may be offered beyond that of the coldness of the high region of the air: from this it follows that as we descend from the summits of the high mountain ranges, which are extremely cold, we experience that the climate changes perceptibly the closer we come to the bottom of the valleys that form between the mountains, which are many, and some of them, being very deep, are for that reason very hot; and between these two extremes of the cold of the high places and the heat of the low ones, one finds all the differences in climates that we observe: cold, temperate, and warm.

Chapter 10. On the first difference in climates found in the highlands of Peru.

Because all the variety of climates that we experience in the highlands of Peru arises from the fact that certain lands are higher and more elevated above the interior of the earth than others, it is necessary that we divide the entire highland into certain grades or terraces, according to

First Part, Book 2.

The altitude and character of each zone, from which division the different climates that this land possesses may be understood. Taking it from the highest peaks down to the lowest and most sheltered of its valleys, it seems to me that we can divide it into six degrees, orders, or climates, according to the plants that grow, or do not grow, in each climate — which I believe is the best means available for conveying the qualities of each degree and climate. In the first, then, beginning from the high parts of the land, we shall include all the barren and sterile land that is neither cultivated nor sown, on account of its being extremely cold and intemperate plateaus; this is what we call in Peru Puna brava, meaning roughly the coldest and most sterile moorland that exists. Into this degree and climate fall the two snow-covered mountain ranges — that of Lamas and that of the Andes — the peaks of the hills and high ridges of the entire mountain range generally, and certain flat stretches that form on top of them, along with the open slopes and hillsides of the same range, where the same climate and harshness of sterile moorland persists. The greater part of these mountain ranges is entirely useless and without any benefit for the sustenance of men or animals, being made up of crags and inaccessible cliffs always covered in snow, which sweeps across the bare hillsides and slopes, leaving no room for grass to grow, because whenever there has been burning and the frost and ice come, no other fruit is obtained from the snow-covered ranges than —

All the land of this first degree and climate is generally cold and dry, even though it is the most abundantly watered by rain and by springs of the entire sierra: because in it are born all the rivers that cross Peru and flow to both seas, the North and the South; it has many very large and deep freshwater lakes, so cold that frogs produce no fish in them. From the peaks of the snow-covered mountain ranges flow innumerable streams formed from the snow, which continually sno

History of the New World.

Running with only the rays it has, which are agitated and vehement, seeming to combat the ardent heat of the sun and the intense cold of the land; from which comes the notion held in Peru that it is something to be feared; and the Sun of the puna is confirmed in this, for although it cannot impart its warmth because of the excessive cold of this region, it is nonetheless harmful, and is wont to cause spotted fevers and other fevers.

From this arises the resolution of two doubts that commonly present themselves to those who experience these great colds. The first, how it is that, the land being so cold, the lakes and rivers do not freeze; and the second, from whence it comes that, though it snows so much, and snow falls well upon the ground, and more snow besides, it does not last long upon the surface without melting, as happens in Europe. To both questions, the answer is that the cause is the great intensity of the sun's rays, which throughout the year remain near our heads, and at times pass directly over them. It is also true that it helps greatly in preventing the water of rivers and lakes from freezing, that the nights are so equal to the days, and not so long at any time of year as winter nights in Europe; although they are colder than the coldest nights in Spain, and the days consequently longer. Nevertheless, it still happens that some of the streams and small pools of standing water, and some little watercourses that carry enough water to turn one or two millwheels, do freeze; but notwithstanding these mills

past borni, which clearly show the excessive cold of the high plains: once while I was traveling in the company of a German, who had just arrived from his homeland, from the town of Oruro to the valley of Cochabamba, we spent the night in the harshest part of a high plain and moorland that lies along the road; the two of us slept in a thatched house, and although it was small and sheltered, we felt very great cold throughout the night, and in the morning we found that the urine had frozen in the chamber pot, and that all the surrounding countryside was white with the frost that had fallen that night, because it was the heart of winter; which frost, two hours after the sun came out, had all melted away. A similar thing happened to me crossing the coastal mountain range in the year sixteen hundred and eighteen, traveling from the province of Collao to the city of Arequipa, which I recount for the month of December, which is summertime in this hemisphere, and while I and another friar, my companion, slept beneath a canopy and a pavilion we had set up inside the canopy, the urine also froze, because the cold was equal to what I had experienced on the road to Cochabamba.

the intemperate air, and I being moved to seek out a more benign one, I found myself suddenly well, and rid of the discomfort.
And it is that just as this indisposition is sudden, caused by the thin and intemperate airs of the puna, once one leaves that harsh climate it goes away instantly.
And not only do the highlands so affect men's bodies, but there are places where men are accustomed to die suddenly, pierced by the very cold winds that blow there, as happens in the páramo of the province of Los Lipas, and in that which lies between Quito and the New Kingdom of Granada. The manner in which they remain dead is with the appearance of the living, seated with their eyes open and their teeth showing, always leaning against a rock, so that when people have gone to look for some individuals who had frozen to death while passing through, speaking to them in the manner described, those searching believed them to be alive, and drawing closer and attempting to move them, found them stiff. This is because when the cold and the sinews are gripped by the rigidity of the frost, the lips draw back and they remain with their teeth exposed.
As I was describing to the Archbishop of Nira the great harshness of the high mountain ranges, at the time he was beginning to cross them through the valley of Ica in the year sixteen hundred and twenty-three, he replied that having himself seen and traveled the mountains of Armenia and Persia, he did not believe there could be others in the world more rugged and lofty. And when afterward, upon his entering these plains, I visited him and asked him what

It had seemed to him regarding the general mountain range of his kingdom, he responded to me that I had been very right in what I had told him about it: because it far surpasses in height and harshness of climate all those he had seen, both in Asia and in the other parts of the world he had traveled, which was a good portion of it. And the same has been affirmed to me by persons who have seen the high mountains of Germany.

Although the sterility of the puna is so notable that it produces no kind of plants or vegetables for the sustenance of men, the divine distributor of natural riches compensates for this by creating there such great abundance of silver mines and other metals, that almost all the hills and bare slopes of gravel and rocks of these desolate moorlands are laden with silver. From here has been extracted the inestimable treasure of this metal, which has been sent to Spain from its kingdom of Peru. And so great is the number of mines that are discovered every day in this first degree and climate of mountain range, that it is considered certain that these rich metals will never run out, as long as the Indies endure. And likewise from the moorlands comes the benefit of mercury, upon which the silver is refined, and what these metals and rivers, and lead bestow upon this kingdom. But none of those of this kind manage to go to seed and produce grain, except for Clover, Cress, and Chamomile; the last does not wither throughout the year from frosts, as the others do. In the same sheltered places there also grow some stalks of maize, barley, wheat, broad beans, flax, turnips, and almost all the flowers of Spain, such as roses, carnations, lilies, wallflowers, the herb of Saint Mary, and several others. Fine domestic and wild animals thrive there, as do chickens, domestic pigeons, wood pigeons, and many other species of birds. The pastures are better, and so abundant that they do not run dry all year long, since the climate is not so harsh, and for this reason — just as we also call the first zone purea — we turn now to the lands of this second zone, because it does not generally support wheat, nor many other seeds and fruits that grow in temperate lands: and because it has the same character as the first, cold and dry, though to a lesser degree, yet not so much as to prevent it from yielding quite well; and in many hollows the sown fields of quinoa, potatoes, and the other vegetables grown here are affected by frosts.

In this regard a remarkable thing occurs: although the hillsides are colder than the plain lying at their foot by virtue of being higher, nevertheless the crops on the plain are more exposed to frosts than those on the hillsides; and

History of the New World.
Reasons why frost settles more when the night is calm and without winds, and while it falls on the flat ground and the slopes of the hills, a continuous wind blows from somewhere, and by means of it the frost on the crops is broken up. The same happens in the flatlands, which are windy with respect to the thickness of the frost, so that although it occurs many times as a second frost there, it does not come in as the first, because the winds do not allow the frost to settle. It also happens that in one year all the plots of a great plain are struck, yet a patch remains in the middle, or survives the frost, because at the moment the frost fell, some cloud had positioned itself over that place, sheltering and protecting it against the frost.
A great deal of land participates in this second highland climate, because the great plains of Collao are included in it, as well as many valleys and hillsides of the same quality; and they are called the Peru region, where men live long, both Spaniards and Indians: because in no part of this kingdom have I seen fewer sick people, nor a greater number of old Indians of more than ten years of age, who remembered the time of the Inca kings and the arrival of the Spaniards in their land. For this reason this second region of the highlands has always been, and still is today, the most populated by native people of all the highlands: who, because the high moorlands and pastures of this region and of the first are not theirs, raise there a great number of

This land differs from that of the second zone in that it is suited for grain-bearing and farming. And it differs from the fourth zone, which will be discussed shortly, in that although it is abundant in wheat and other legumes, it does not produce fruit trees as does the fourth zone that follows this one. For although orange trees, peach trees, and other fruit trees grow here, their fruit does not reach full ripeness and maturity, except for some Castilian grapes that do ripen; and so we say that this third climate zone lacks fruit, because the fruits of trees do not ripen here. The climate is cold and dry to a greater degree than in the second zone; so much so that although the cold does not compel one to sit in the sun at all times, nor to draw close to a fire, one still needs all the warmth one can get, and it is not necessary to change one's habits between winter and summer.    The land of the fourth degree and climate of the sierra is temperate, without notable cold or dryness; the winter cold is mild, and the summer is cool, so that because the heat never reaches a fatiguing level throughout the year, its climate is said to be absolutely cold, or better said, cool. In this fourth region grow all the plants, vegetables, seeds, and animals found in the third; except for llamas, or sheep of the land, which are not found in the valleys and temperate lands, but only in the cold lands of the three preceding degrees. Within this fourth climate fall the best, most fertile, and most well-watered valleys of all the sierra, such as those of Jauja, Andahuaylas, Yucay, Cochabamba, and many others of the same character. There grow in abundance all the fruits of Spain from cold and temperate regions, such as almonds, cherries, plums, peaches, nectarines, apricots, pears, apples, and pippins, and from warm-climate fruits, quinces, pomegranates, and several others.
   The climate of the fifth degree of the sierra we call chaupiyunca, which means "middle yunca," for it is so mild and pleasant that it feels neither cold nor hot. Although it is true that we may say it leans more toward warm than cold, since for a good part of the year a moderate warmth is felt, yet it is not so much that it brings on a chill, nor does the water ever fail to be quite cold at all times. In this fifth region and climate grow all the seeds, vegetables, fruits, and animals that

History of the New World.
In the fifth zone: all the fruits of Castile that have so far been brought to the Indies, such as figs, grapes, oranges, limes, and all juicy fruits; avocados, pacaes, papayas, and many other local fruits; though dates and some other fruits, both from Europe and from the land, that require a warmer climate do not fully ripen here. Within this fifth zone are found the cities of Arequipa, Guamanga, and Huanuco, along with several other Spanish settlements, and many valleys and mid-level hillsides. The dwelling of this fifth zone, and of the fourth, is the most pleasant, delightful, and comfortable not only in the Indies but in all the world, on account of the perpetual and agreeable spring that prevails here without variation of heat and cold through the changing seasons. Particularly in this fifth zone, many trees never shed their leaves, and what is most remarkable is that in some places they are continually putting forth both flower and fruit, one following the other throughout the entire year. Grapevines and trellises yield grapes at whatever time they are pruned; fig trees never lack both green and ripe figs; and the same holds true for many other fruit trees. These five zones and ranges of the sierra produce very few crawling creatures and venomous animals, such as vipers and other serpents that breed in the lowland yunca lands. The Spanish who live in these zones are healthier than those in the rest of Peru; they never lose the color they brought from Spain, nor do they feel the re-

the weakness and frailty of the stomach that occurs in the hot and humid lands; it produces a more inflamed color, and those who live at a higher elevation of the sierra, as can be seen in those who dwell in the first and second grades.

The sixth and final grade of the Sierra includes the deepest and most profound valleys found within it, and the slopes of the same character, which are extremely hot, as much or more so than the Yunca land, and moderately humid. The reason this region is so hot, and for the air that comes down from the sierra, is because it sits at the same level and height within the sierra as the plains which we shall discuss presently, and the Yunca lands, which are the most base of Peru; because from the valleys of this sixth grade the rivers carry very little current until they enter the Yunca lands. The heat is greatly increased because they are hollow and very deep ravines surrounded by the highest mountains; whereby the rays of the sun have very great intensity there; the winds that blow are few, and not as fresh as those that blow in the high places. And for this reason it is the least healthy land of the sierra. Within this grade fall the valleys and rivers of Vilcas, Auancay, and Apurimac, which we cross when traveling from the city of Lima to that of Cuzco; which travelers endeavor to cross quickly, and in the cool of the morning, because as they come from very cold highlands to enter them, the sudden change from one extreme of cold to another of heat greatly fatigues them, and its excessive heat unsettles them, if they

they pass with the face of the sun.

Although the climate of this last degree of highland is not much like the lowland and the equatorial heat, it differs greatly from it in not being so humid, and in other qualities: and thus there grow abundantly in this region all the fruits, vegetables, and animals as in the fifth: and the plants of the land, and of Castile as in the lowland and equatorial zone, along with the insects and abundance of mosquitoes that are born there: dates ripen perfectly, and wine and sugar are made; only sheep do not breed well. Likewise wheat, maize, rice and plantains, melons, and other similar fruits are harvested in land of this character. In this climate are the towns of Mizque, Palcpaya, Pilaya, Tarija, and other Spanish settlements.

Chapter 12. On the altitude that the
above-mentioned degrees of highland possess.

Because it would be of interest to whoever reads this division which we have made of the general highland of Peru into six degrees, which we have just described, to know how great its altitude is from the summits of the highest mountains and ranges down to their foot and base: and also how great is the portion that, divided among the six degrees and orders mentioned, falls to each one; I will set down here what I know with certainty about this point, which is quite difficult to determine—

The first observation and argument, which shows its height to be extraordinary, is taken from the slopes that are climbed in many places to reach the top, which are four, six, and more leagues of very steep ascent; and these are where the roads cut through, which ordinarily pass through the gaps and lowest passes: from where, looking up toward the summits of the snow-covered cordillera, one can see that a good stretch of climb still remains. The second is the great distance that the rivers run, which are born in this mountain range, until they reach the North Sea, which is one thousand six hundred to two thousand and more leagues. The third, and most compelling observation, is from when we climb from the plains to this mountain range, before reaching half its height, if we turn our eyes downward, we find that not only are the mountain ranges and hills of the plains region lower, but also the clouds that sit above them: so that looking down at them they appear very deep, like a white veil spread over the land, like another lower sky covered with clouds; and from there upward the air and sky appear pure and clear, with no vapor exhaling into it to refresh it or trouble and thicken it: and the same is experienced climbing

On the provinces of the Andes along the Eastern cordillera of the great mountain range, where the clouds also remain below the treetops and lower peaks of the Andes, below half the height of said cordillera.

From experience, then, and from what I myself have observed by sight on the occasions when I have stood upon its summits and looked downward along the straight slopes and combed hillsides, and from what knowledgeable persons have made known to us about its difficulty, I conclude that this mountain range has a height, measured by a perpendicular line, of a league and a half from its highest peaks down to the base, which comes to stand at almost the same level as the banks of the sea. Dividing this league and a half of altitude into the six degrees or tiers into which we have divided it, the first zone of exposed, barren páramo heights must be given half a league by perpendicular measure, and the second degree a quarter of a league; so that the first three quarters of a league of this inaccessible mountain range consist of extremely cold páramo, where no fruit trees grow, nor is wheat cultivated, nor other Castilian crops. The other three quarters of a league are fertile land for grain and cultivation, which is tilled and sown, and these are distributed across the four remaining degrees and terraces in the following manner: to the third, fourth, and fifth degrees the half league shall be apportioned in equal parts, so that each of the three degrees and climate zones comes to hold one eighth of a league. The remaining quarter league goes entirely to the sixth, and

the last terrace, with whose height the tallest mountains of the yunca land and those of the plains are matched. From which it follows that this general sierra of Peru is, out of six parts, five parts higher than the land on either side of it, which forms the two strips of the three into which Peru is divided.

Beyond this division, in which we have assigned to each of the six degrees and regions of the sierra the height they possess — measured vertically and by perpendicular lines — it remains for us now to divide the surface and floor of the said sierra across those same six degrees, and to see how much space belongs to each. To do this, the entire sierra must be divided into four parts: two of those parts belong to the first degree and region of the punas, which are barren moorlands; another quarter belongs to the second degree; and the last remaining quarter, which is the fertile land suitable for grain-bearing crops, is divided equally among the remaining four degrees. It should be noted, first, that much of this last quarter has not been cultivated, since roughly half of it remains unworked — partly due to lack of people, and partly because much of it is very rugged terrain, full of rubble and rock. As a result, of all the land in the sierra, no more than one-eighth part is currently cultivated and sown with wheat, maize, and other seeds and fruit-bearing plants. The second point is that when the sierra is divided into six degrees and regions, one should not understand the sierra of each one to be joined and continuous, but rather interrupted and broken up among itself, according to the arrangement of the hills and ridges. The third and final point is that the climate of each zone is of such a nature that what we call cold is to be understood as cold throughout the entire year, and the same applies to the warm zones; and no less so for those we designate as temperate. For throughout the entire highlands there is no variation of heat and cold with the changes of winter and summer that one experiences in Spain and in the other lands that lie outside the torrid zone.

Chapter 13. On the third belt or strip of Peru, which is the region we call the lowlands.

Of the three regions and strips into which we divide Peru, the third and westernmost is the maritime one called the lowlands, which lies between the sea and the main mountain range. This name was not given to it because all the land it encompasses is flat; rather, it was because the Spaniards who discovered and conquered the kingdom entered it and began its pacification along the northern coast of the province of Piura, in the diocese of Trujillo, which has very large stretches of dry sandy wastes, which they called llanos. Afterward this name spread until it came to encompass the entire coast of Peru, which shares the same climate as those sandy wastes; although the greater part of this region is hilly country. Of the roughly seven hundred leagues of coastline that this kingdom has, the first hundred toward the North are land of the same character and qualities that we said the first belt possesses.

This is not found in any other part of the middle region that lies within the tropics, because all the other provinces of it maintain throughout the year a uniformity with only a perceptible variety; in such a way that what is cold is always cold, and what is warm is always warm, having no other variation with the changing seasons except that the cold regions ease their coldness, and their dryness, in summer; and their heat and humidity in winter.

Secondly, encompassing the whole Torrid Zone, which abounds with waters from above and below, and with moist soil: on the contrary, these plains are by their nature so dry that, were it not for the rivers that come down from the main mountain range, they would be entirely barren and uninhabitable; because they have no other water from the sky or from the earth except what those rivers supply them. For it never rains there, nor for more than ten leagues inland along its entire coast: nor are there any thunder, lightning, or flashes; and its soil is extremely dry, with no wells, lakes, or springs. I say it does not rain on these plains, for this is the general rule, though in certain parts of them there falls a kind of dew, which we call in this land garúa, of which I will speak presently: which is yet another wonder no less remarkable than those of this land, in which it also differs from the rest of the Torrid Zone; for whereas in that zone the rains come in summer, here the dew comes in winter: it differs from all other regions of the world in that, being made of barren sands and lying beneath the Torrid Zone, without rains to temper the heat of the sun, which strikes it with direct rays, and

Chapter 14. The description of the land of the plains continued.

The settlements of this lowland territory are found only in the valleys, along the banks of the rivers that flow down from the main mountain range; these rivers rise on the slopes of the cordillera of ci

History of the New World.
Short, and running from east to west from their headwaters until they enter the Southern Sea, spanning twenty to thirty leagues, depending on how wide or narrow the lowlands are, and the rivers run straight or winding. Where the main mountain range is closest to the sea, the rivers are smaller but carry more water than where the range is farther away. In winter they carry nine-thirds less water than in summer, because the heavy rains that fall upon the main mountain range during that season cause them to swell considerably. They come with great current and are very turbid, and for this reason they cannot be forded. Their nature is not to run clear water, and they are all crossed by ford. Some, having run not a few leagues, sink into the sandy ground before reaching the sea, especially in winter. All of them make a great noise on account of the rocky and gravelly ground. And even though they are the lifeblood and soul of the lowlands, they do not fail to cause great damage with their swift current, carrying away with their floods and freshets a large portion of the cultivated lands of the valleys that are irrigated by them. They do not breed caimans as do the other rivers of the northern coast of Peru and those of the rest of the Torrid Zone, which is a very great blessing. The fish caught in them are pejeyes, bagres, cachuelos, shrimp, carachás, and others of their kind.

The valleys of the lowlands are separated from one another according to the rivers, some by four, eight, or ten leagues, and others by fifteen, twenty, forty, or more leagues; and the space in between consists of barren sandy stretches and hills of rubble and crags. Not all of these valleys run lengthwise along the rivers from the seacoast to the mountains; what happens is that the reed beds open up and give way to the formation of valleys a few leagues before the sea, as we see in this great valley of Lima, which is one of the largest and most fertile of the lowlands. There are also rivers that in their course form other valleys, opening up and narrowing between the mountains and hills that surround them, and it is through these narrows that the valleys are divided from one another. The most common situation is that the valleys lying away from the sea are long — from three to six leagues along the rivers — and wide from a musket-shot to one, two, four, or more leagues, as we see in the valley of Ica. And those that lie along the coast are the opposite, having their length extended along the seashore and their width running inland. All of these said valleys constitute the farmland of the lowlands; and reckoning proportionally, according to their number and size, it seems to me that they occupy a tenth part of the lowlands, and that the other nine-tenths are barren and uncultivated land. And even though the fertile land is so much less than the barren land, not even half of it is cultivated, for lack of water and people; because not all the rivers carry enough water to irrigate the valleys that are formed along them.

These plains extending to a latitude of twenty-five degrees South, we must distinguish the climate of those lying outside the Tropic, which is temperate, from that which covers the greater part of this region of plains, which falls within the Torrid Zone. The climate outside the Tropic of Capricorn differs from that which lies within the Torrid Zone in that it is uniform and mild throughout the year; one feels neither cold nor heat, nor is it excessively humid or dry, but rather of a marvelous temperance; so that if the land were not almost entirely barren and dry, these would be among the most agreeable climates in this new world for human habitation; as those who live in the province of Atacama, which occupies this stretch of land, can attest.

The remainder of the plains is, generally speaking, of a somewhat humid and cold climate in winter, and warm and less humid in summer. This does not contradict what has already been said about the land being very dry overall; for the climate is determined by the quality of the air and sky, and that of the plains inclines more toward humidity than dryness: yet so great is the dryness of the soil that it tempers this humidity to such a degree that this region is not nearly so humid as the lowland coastal territory. For this reason, the dwellings and lodgings of the valleys are just as healthful as those of the highlands.
