of greater and lesser Castile: goats and pigs sustain themselves better here, because of the abundance of carob for the former and of maize for the latter. As for wild animals, none are found other than foxes, and some deer that come down from the highlands; domestically, rabbits and guinea pigs are raised. The entire lowland territory is very free of vermin and poisonous animals: so much so that travelers, growing tired at night, lie down to sleep and rest on the sandy shores of the ports, safe in the knowledge that no animal of the kind that is dangerous in other regions will trouble them, for not even a mosquito or an ant is to be found there.
All the fruits, seeds, and vegetables of Castile and of this land that grow in the highlands and in the yunca regions are produced here in great abundance: except that among the native fruits of hot lands, coconuts, pineapples, and some others requiring a very hot and humid climate do not grow here; and from those that belong to the highlands, the lowlands produce almonds and plums of Castile. But all the other fruits of this land and of Europe are produced in great abundance, and are of better flavor and quality than those of the highlands, inasmuch as there they ripen in the rainy season, while here, where it never rains, the pears are more — we see this advantage in the pears, quinces,

Chapter 15. On the Garúas, and the highland ridge that in the lowlands we call Lomas.

We have said how in a certain part of the lowlands there falls a fine drizzle, or mist, which in Spain we call mollina, and in this land garúa: which, both because of the place where it falls and because of other properties it has, causes greater wonder than if it had rained fully there during those months. Regarding the length, which we have seen the lowlands of Peru to have, from the port of Tumbes to that of Copiapó, it should be known that although the hills and ridge found within them run from the sea along the entire coast inland until they join the main sierra and cordillera, still in the first hundred leagues from Tumbes, going toward Trujillo, they lie at a distance of eight to twelve leagues from the sea: however, from the boundaries of the said city of Trujillo as far as Copiapó they continue along the entire coast, except that at intervals they are broken by the valleys and flat lands that form along the banks

From the sea, then, among the hills and the maritime land stretching inland one league, or lacking three or four leagues of width from the seashore toward the interior; and the garúa from where it begins near Trujillo, two hundred leagues remain before the cape and end of the plains, where only the garúas fall. The seasons in which these occur we call in this kingdom lomas; and the time in which this dew falls we call the season of lomas, because during it one lives amidst greenery and abundant pastures are raised. So the lomas, and the land of garúas, extend some three hundred leagues more or less in length, and no more than three or four in width. For this reason it is generally said that it does not rain in the plains of this kingdom of Peru; partly because the rains, or garúas, of the lomas are very scarce in comparison to what falls in the climates of the Torrid Zone; and principally because, falling only in this narrow strip running along the coast of the sea, the greater part of the plains receives no rain at all — those being the two extremes, where there are three hundred leagues of coast at their greatest width; and the range, or turning sierra, that lies between the lomas themselves and the main cordillera.

The garúas usually begin around the month of May and last six months more or less. They fall very unevenly, because in the valleys that form between the lomas, and in the sandy flats along the seashore, they are thinner and scarcer than in the hills and lomas, where they are all the heavier and more abundant as the hills are higher; as we see in the sierra of the sand, which lies six leagues from the city of Lima, on whose summit the garúas are most copious and greatly grown

The grass that grows on these hills: on the slopes of the same mountain range, and even from halfway down it, as we described going down to the plain, the rains are so scarce that they do not provide enough moisture to sustain the grass; and so the slopes of the said mountain range closest to the plain remain bare of it. Although it is true that in many low and flat ravines that open up in the midst of the ridges, it tends to rain as much as elsewhere, and the grass grows no less thickly, as we see on the ridges of La Chay and La Chacama in this diocese of Lima.
This rain is not as fine as some who write about it describe; rather it is so abundant in some places that in them alone grass grows so tall that it hides the cattle within it; and in others not so much, and in those where it is least, still sufficient for the livestock to graze; and it lasts long enough for many kinds of flowers and wild herbs to grow, mature, and produce seed, which falling on dry ground sprouts and grows the following season. There also grow some thickets, which are plants that require more plentiful watering than the grasses; and they serve for firewood and fodder. During the time that the garúas last, these hillsides appear green, flowering, and delightful, clothing themselves in new livery; for I have not seen, in all my travels through the Indies, nor even in Spain, more pleasant fields and meadows. In the midst of them there are some valleys and lowlands with such abundant and tall pastures that they look like barley gardens. I wondered whether the moisture from the garúas would be sufficient for them to

they could sow wheat in season on those lomas, and the other seeds that grow there, and other plants rise up to great abundance; I have been assured by experienced farmers that this is so, and they confirm that one can find in them certain plots of cultivated land, with raised beds, where the Indians formerly sowed and harvested maize and other vegetables with nothing but the dew from the sky, which at times comes as such a fine rain that it soaks without actually raining, and drenches clothing, with drops as heavy as the good downpours of that land, and causes streams to run quite swollen; all of this falling gently and slowly.

During the time of the lomas, springs and freshwater sources appear in many places, which last throughout the winter, from which the livestock drink; but once the garúas end and summer arrives, they dry up at once. It is true that some of those springs last for several months after the garúas have ended, the longer in proportion as the rains were more abundant, for they are not the same every year nor equal in every place. The most abundant lomas, and best pasture of all the coast, where the most rain falls, where it is most plentiful and lasts longest, are in the diocese of Arequipa, the hills of Ilo, Atico, and Atiquipa; and in the diocese of Lima, the sierra de la Arena, and the lomas of Pachacama, and La Chay. The pastures in those lomas begin one or two months after the garúas have set in, and they last as long as those rains do, and a little beyond, which is until November and December, rarely failing to appear.

History of the New World.
In summer they dry out and wither in less than two months, and the hills return to their natural dryness and barrenness; so that whoever saw them during the season of garúas so clothed in green and in bloom, and comes back through them within two months, does not know what to marvel at more: whether at how hills so dry and barren, and largely covered in sandy wastes, could produce such abundance of grass and pasture as they had before; or at how in so short a time so much greenery and flowering growth has dried up and withered as there once was on them. Truly both things are admirable; the first being that, since almost all of them are flat, dead sandy wastes, wherever they are reached by old water, or from the sky, or from rivers, the dry sandy wastes are made so fertile that abundant pastures grow in them, vineyards and olive groves are planted, and all kinds of vegetables are sown and cultivated. The second is that the dryness of the soil is so extreme that within two months of lacking irrigation, so much and such tall grass withers away as the garúas had produced on the hills, leaving nothing but a few dry scrubby pastures; this being so even though in the sierra, where it rains no more than four months, the grass stays green all year long without any irrigation for the other eight months: which indicates the great moisture and richness of the soil of that region, and the remarkable dryness of the soil of the coastal plains.

The livestock fatten greatly in those rivers for six months, and when the highland rains come to an end, with this abundance of food and range they maintain many large herds, estimated as the greater livestock found on the plains. And if the pastures of the plains were to last for the months they endure, they would last the whole year, and would be an inestimable wealth for the inhabitants of those plains. In the most abundant lowlands, such as those of the bishopric of Arequipa, though it is true that the pastures dry out once the sea mists pass, still so much dry straw remains that everything is clearly laid out for some tame livestock, and a good number of mares, donkeys, and mixed mules, and their owners, which are found there.

The sea mists that fall in the coastal valleys, set back a little from the hills and ridges, are very fine and so brief that they are not sufficient to produce grass; nor do the houses need rooftops. The Indians therefore make the roofs of their houses flat, without slope, and covered with a mat of woven reed with a layer of earth placed on top, which is the Indian custom. The Spaniards at first followed their example and used this same manner of roofing, but since then, as the buildings have continued to improve day by day in refinement and strength of construction, and also because in some years when the winter brings heavy rains these flat roofs leak badly — not being suited to the houses they were using — they have gradually introduced the practice of replacing them with well-timbered plank roofs, and with Florentine-style tiled roofing.

The ordinary thing was that nothing prevented people from traveling outside the town, nor from walking through the streets, and frequenting the plazas and markets, as if it were not raining. Although it rains in the valleys very lightly, these rains are most beneficial for the crops, and when they do not come, or are delayed, they are notably missed: for which reason processions and prayers have been held in Lima, though in other parts they are not usually held for the rains. Because given that the planted fields are irrigated, the garúas (coastal mists) are still so important, that by means of them the crops sprout and ripen until harvest with only two or so waterings; and without them, many more would be needed; as we see happens in the valleys that lie outside the hills, for which there would not be sufficient water in the rivers, since many yield little at planting time. And in the times of the Inca kings, much more land was irrigated than now with the same water, because the Indians did not then have the farms and gardens that the Spaniards now have, in which much water is consumed; besides sugarcane fields, olive groves, plantain groves, and alfalfa fields. And also because, in towns where one can plant at all times of the year in the lowlands, the Indians used to sow in summer when the rivers ran full and flooded; despite all this, the Spaniards generally sow in winter because the labor is more temperate, and to enjoy the benefit of the garúas, which not only fertilize the land with the water that they

The garúas are more frequent at night and in the mornings than in the afternoons; they fall very gently, without storms or violent whirlwinds of wind; carried only by the soft south wind, which blows throughout the year across those plains, and which also serves many uses worthy of admiration. Among the things that occur with these garúas, one is particularly worth noting: they only gather over the hills of the sea coast, and not over those that continue inland from them, even though all of them are of equal height, and the inland ones are even higher. So that whoever travels in winter across those plains, from the sea coast to

sierra, crosses through the first three or four leagues along ridges that are green, covered with flowers, and shrouded in thick fogs; and upon leaving them, continuing along land of the same quality, elevation, and mountain ranges, one sees it all bare and dry, without any woodland at all, and the sky clear and serene.

The dew and mists so well known, which fall in the morning hours of the coastal plains; and beyond them all the land is dry, with no rain whatsoever. Notwithstanding what has been said, there are times when, during Summer, when it rains heavily in the sierra, in those plains nearest to it, one can hear the thunder from it as if from a distance, see the rainbow likewise from afar, and feel a few drops of water fall, as if strayed from the clouds of the sierra.

Since the Spaniards settled this land, it has happened that it rained a few times on the plains, and it has always been considered unusual and outside the ordinary course of things. The second was in the year fifteen hundred and seventy-eight, when it rained in the valleys of the bishopric of Trujillo. A dark and heavily laden cloud broke near the royal road and unleashed a great downpour over the small area below it; it served to wash some things that had remained there for several days; and as I myself passed along that same road a few days later, it was as if it had never rained.

Also, in the year sixteen hundred and twenty-four, it rained prodigiously in the town of Jaño, and in other parts of the diocese of Trujillo; and afterward it rained in those same valleys two more times. Most recently, in the present year of sixteen hundred and fifty-two, on the third of February, a great downpour fell upon this city of Lima, and because of the damage feared from it, the archbishop ordered all the churches of the city to ring their bells in supplication, asking God to stop the rain, because since the rooftops of the houses are not built to withstand downpours, the water caused no small damage to the houses it soaked, and the damage would have been far greater had the rain continued. These rains that fall on the plains tend to come with lightning that ignites, descending from the sky while it rains, thanks to the season.

We were going very slowly, and night was drawing near, with nowhere to shelter ourselves; I persuaded my companions to quicken our pace in order to get out of the coastal hills before nightfall, and to reach dry ground. We did so, and before the sun had set we came out of the hills and the thick cover of mists, arriving at the high ground, which was the top of the slope we had been climbing, and which in that area is very flat. Likewise upon reaching it, we lifted our heads above the clouds that had been covering us; and we noticed that the clouds had their upper surface level and even with that great plain, so that it seemed the flat land continued right into the high surface of the clouds. The air from there upward was clear and calm; the sky open and cheerful; and the ground of that plain dry and parched — for although it was raining right alongside it, the garúas did not cross the boundary and limits of their district. And we resolved to spend that night there, and we slept on that plain under the open sky, with as little fear of getting wet as if we had slept under a roof. And we lay the whole night under a clear, starlit sky, at less than a musket-shot's distance from the clouds or mists, which were rolling over the coastal hills all night long.

But returning to the reason why it does not rain on these plains, due to the lack of vapors — given that on the lower land

Thus, because of their great dryness, the vapors that rise from the land are very thin and fine; along the sea coast of that region I see no sound reason — for I ask myself — why it never rains there. Setting that aside, it is well known that clouds not only water the lands from which the moist vapors rose, but also, after condensing in the middle region of the air, the winds carry them from one place to another, watering different lands. According to this reasoning, the rains that formed from the sea vapors could well fall on the nearby shores, just as we see them moving inland from the sea, passing beyond it toward the sierra, which is the origin of the plains. I myself observed this one year when there was a great deal of rain in the sierra, while I was visiting the town of Pisco: each morning I would see great quantities of vapors rising from the sea in the form of mists, rushing swiftly toward the sierra, and upon reaching it they would condense into thick clouds, so that by two in the afternoon one could already see from the coast itself that it was raining in the sierra.
    Others also wish to give as a reason the lack of winds to press and squeeze the vapors and resolve them into rains, on account of the shelter that the main mountain range provides to the lowlands. This argument is without doubt more often used by authors who wish to prove their point with it; because we see, on the contrary, that the coastal mists are all the more abundant

History of the New World.
The closer the mountain range runs to the sea, and the greater shelter it provides to the plains, the more people live on the coast of the dioceses of Lima and Trujillo. And where the main mountain range most distances itself from the sea — a stretch of thirty to fifty leagues — the garúas are entirely absent, and the land is the driest and most barren of all the plains. This can be seen in the districts of Porta in the diocese of Trujillo, and Atacama in that of the Charcas, which are the extremes of the plains. From this one may conclude that the lack of rain on the plains, and the falling of garúas only along the strip or belt of the lomas, and not in the rest of them, is one of the greatest secrets of nature that we humans have experienced, whose causes we cannot comprehend; and thus we must place it in the catalogue of the other marvels of nature that we have found in the New World.
Chapter 17. On the Huyas and Mahamaes of the Plains.
Another particularity no less marvelous than those mentioned in the preceding chapters is what we find in the history of the plains — namely, the method the Indians used to make productive for their crops land that was by nature barren and fruitless. They did this in two ways: the first by digging and opening large holes; and the second by making use of humid places, either by means of some river's flow, or by having water within themselves very near the surface:

The hoyas of Chilca, ten leagues from this city of Lima, which are
among the most well-known in this kingdom, run along the edge of

sea that I have seen in the said valley of Chilca, as in

History of the New World.
not so much that it cannot be drunk, and being so shallow that even at the deepest point down to the water's surface level, one encounters it, which ordinarily occurs at one of two depths.
The lowlands of Villauiri in the province of Ica, no less famous than those of Chilea, are the most inland of any I know of; because they are four to five leagues from the sea, in which case there is greater reason to doubt whether the moisture they receive comes from the sea or from elsewhere. An argument that it comes from the sea could be that they produce, as they do, saltpeter on the surface of the earth, as do those of Chilea and the other coastal lowlands. But it seems to me, with all due respect to better judgment, that such moisture does not come from the sea; first because these lowlands are so far from it; and second because they are not on the same level as the sea itself, but rather considerably higher, as one can verify by experience, in that traveling from the sea toward them, one is always going uphill somewhat, though gradually. Therefore I maintain that all the moisture of the lowlands of Villauiri, and much of that of those situated on the coast, comes from rivers that descend from the mountains; because all of them, from the moment they reach the dry flatlands, steadily diminish, owing to the fact that their water is being absorbed and seeping through the sand and gravel that form the riverbeds, so that many of those that are not very powerful sink into the ground and disappear before reaching the sea, whose water

it spreads through the bowels of the earth, and in the places and channels it runs very shallow; of which the abundant grass and groves that we see in some places are quite sufficient proof, and these are what we properly call Mahamaes. The dust of the earth rises higher, even though the surface is covered with dry sandy wastes; if the moisture coming from the rivers does not sink as deep as in other states, it still tends to produce large, leafy trees; such are the guarangos and carob trees, which grow in the sandy stretches between Piru and Ica, which is in the same area as the above-mentioned hollows of Villacuri. These sandy wastes are so dry, due to the scarcity of rain, that the winds shift the dunes and heaps of sand from one place to another. And it frequently happens that the sand carried by the air piles up around these trees, until it buries some of them completely, and others for the greater part, leaving only the very top or some of the highest branches uncovered; and in this way many of them come to dry out. And all the land that lies between here and Pisuacla, which is two leagues, is of this same condition and quality, such that wherever one removes the sand, fertile earth with its own moisture will be found beneath. And those parts that are entirely free of sand dunes, or do not lie on low ground, enjoy such great moisture that they become Mahamaes, growing grass and other plants, and they even tend to issue forth such quantity

The same fruits grow there as in the rest of these valleys, and all the fruit of the low-lying hollows ripens well enough to supply the irrigated orchards. And although the hollows have the depth we have described, travelers cannot make out from a distance what lies within them, and so those who do not know them assume that everything stretching before them is sandy flatland, like the surrounding terrain, until, upon reaching these hollows, they find in the midst of such solitude one of these groves and lush depressions, so green and beautiful, with such abundance of trees and pleasant greenery. In the hollows that are not cultivated, much grass grows, which serves as pasture for the animals of travelers, and is no small help to the muleteers.
From what has been said in this chapter, one may understand well enough what Mahamaes are, and there is no need to dwell further on explaining them. I will only note that what grows best in the Mahamaes is melons. As we see in the valley of Ica, the melons that grow there during winter are exceedingly fine; but as summer comes on and the river begins to recede and to provide less moisture to the Mahamaes, the melons decline in quality. Beyond this, it should also be noted that the flooded lands along rivers are also commonly called Mahamaes — that is, the land along their banks,

that bathe and cover them in their floods and freshets, when they overflow their banks; the land thus always retains that moisture. Grapevines and other fruit trees are also planted in them, and wheat and other seeds and vegetables are sown.

And because it seems that the excessive moisture, both in the hoyas and in the Mahamues, would have hindered the ripening and seasoning of the fruits; the most wise maker of all things provided that in winter, when the plants require more moisture, and the rivers of the plains carry less water, the hoyas and Mahamues retain so much humidity that they seem to be springing with water. And in summer, when the rivers swell and overflow because of the rains in the mountains, which would seem to cause the moisture of the hoyas to increase excessively and rot their fruits instead of ripening them; we observe the contrary — that the water they hold within drains away and dries out in such a way that the surface of the land becomes dry, which allows those fruits to ripen most wonderfully. This I take to be attributable to the fierce suns and heats of that season, which dry out and parch the surface of the land: just as in wintertime so great a supply of moisture

Chapter 18. On the Volcanoes that exist in Peru,
and the great damage they are accustomed to cause.

The two largest and principal parts of Peru, which are
the lowlands and the highlands, are subject to two plagues and
hardships most burdensome, which tend to bring notable
damage to their inhabitants. Both arise from one and the same
principle, which are the mouths of fire, or volcanoes, found along
the main mountain range: which cause very frequent earth-
quakes. And when they erupt, releasing from their
entrails an immense quantity of fire, ash, and
boulders, they tend to devastate and destroy the lands around
them, and even those quite distant and far away. Those
who suffer most from these hardships are the inhabitants of
the lowlands; although the people of the high-
lands do not fail to receive their share, especially
during the eruptions of the volca-
noes. There are a great number of these throughout all the Indies: they are
mountains of admirable size, which dominate
the highest ranges: nearly all of them have their peaks perpetually
covered with snow, and in them a great
mouth, or opening, that descends to the depths of the.

The other volcano, which most recently erupted in the year sixteen hundred, caused such great ruin and destruction throughout all of Peru, and beyond, with swift damage across two hundred provinces according to their distance; that one cannot find recorded in the ancient or modern histories anything that occurred anywhere in the world that was more fierce and terrifying. For this reason, having been present myself at the time of this event, and having been an eyewitness to part of that terrible tempest — even though I was more than one hundred and seventy leagues distant from the volcano — I will take it upon myself to give some account of it; and it happened in the following manner.

In the middle of the province of Collaguas, which belongs to the diocese of Arequipa, there are two volcanoes, at the beginning of

The general mountain range enters on the eastern side, one of which is ten or sixteen leagues from that city, which is the day of Pinate, named after a village of that name that stood on the slope before it erupted. Five leagues from there, further inland, and behind the said city, stands the second volcano, which we call that of the Ucinas, also taking its name from the nearest village to it, called the first, which is the one that erupted in the aforementioned year of sixteen hundred. It is not a single peak, but a long mountain range of seven leagues, which, although not of excessive height, has such a great base that it spans thirty leagues. Its summit ends in several peaks which, seen from outside, have the form of a crown; the one in the middle is smaller than the others, and in it is the vent. It is considered very probable that underground this volcano communicates with that of the Ucinas, and that the ash, rock, and fire that it cast through this opening or vent came from the interior of both. The indications that persuade one that this is so are two: the first is the infinite quantity of ash and rock that came out of it, for it seems a prodigious thing, exceeding the natural course, that it should have had within itself so much material as it vomited forth, and that if it were gathered and piled up it would without doubt form a mountain two or three times greater than that of the volcano itself. The second, and more certain indication, is to see that after this one erupted, the other did not emit smoke for some years.

The volcano of the Voinas, having previously been continuously smoking, the Spanish settlement closest to the volcano of Omate is the city of Arequipa; and for that reason its inhabitants received the greatest blow of this calamity: although because of the darkness and shadows with which it came upon them, they did not know for several days where it was coming from. Those who witnessed it and experienced most closely all the miseries and damages that occurred were the ones who noted it with the greatest detail and wrote down this torment as it unfolded, and it happened thus.

On the eighteenth day of the month of February, a Friday of the first week of Lent in the year sixteen hundred, at around nine o'clock at night, some tremors of the earth began to be felt in that city, which lasted until the following Sunday. From the hour they began they grew more rapid and stronger, so that they not only increased in number but also in force. Everyone from that hour abandoned their houses, because some were falling. Shortly afterward there were heard very large and frightful sounds, as if they were being fired from within the city, and in such rapid succession that one overtook the next. The following day, which was the nineteenth, at five in the afternoon the sky began to become covered

A great and zealous one came seeing the mildness of the stretch that promised more than a dark overcast sky, bringing threats of a downpour. Although the particle that fell was a white ash as coarse as mustard grains, and in such excess, that the fear of the ash served to replace that of the thunderbolts; and though they were further alarmed by other crests, the roar of the storm kept growing in such a way that from ten o'clock until morning it continued without pause; and ever greater was the noise of the thunder, and the force of the trembling, with a great quantity of lightning flashes and other lights through the air like shooting stars, passing from one place to another with great and terrifying force, such that it had never before seemed so beyond natural. What fell from the cloud was the aforementioned ash, for it covered the plains and the mountains, the trees, the branches, and the animals of every kind; so that their bellowing, their shaking, and their calling to one another all happened at the same time; which was itself a notable source of fear, because what could be a remedy for one was a greater danger for the others.
Sunday dawned in the same manner, the ash having rained down throughout the night without ceasing; and it was so much that had accumulated, that it was necessary to quickly clear the rooftops, lest the houses collapse under its weight. From midday onward it grew ever darker.

So it was that at two in the afternoon the day was so dark that no one could recognize anyone they met; and to remedy this, large men walked through the streets carrying torches. At four o'clock the sky cleared somewhat, and ash began to fall again, lasting three hours. Twenty-one days later the ice was entirely covered with mounds, raised and protruding, which were horrifying to look upon; because of this it was necessary to carry lights for any task whatsoever. That day the sky darkened again, though not as much as before, and ash fell for another three hours. A few days later the dawn came with the lost color and hue it had before, and ash began to fall again from nine until three in the afternoon, in the manner of a white powder that made the hair and beard rough, as if it were ground pumice stone. The following two days, although they were not very dark, the sun was not seen at all. On Friday the twenty-first, the air became turbid again and a hot wind came in, around the hour when dusk falls at the end of twilight, and the closer it came to night, the greater the darkness grew, with some thunder and tremors. On the twenty-sixth there was no day at all, for the entire day was as dark as night; a bolt of lightning struck, and so much ash fell in the manner described that it was necessary to clear the rooftops frequently, lighting torches in order to do so. And on top of all this there came

First Part, Book 2.
so many, and such cruel explosions, and tremors of the earth, that all the creatures came out of their holes, and many wild animals came looking for people in the city, as if needing their help, and lacking the spirit to endure such a frightful storm, and terrified by so great a calamity. Sunday the twenty-ninth the day cleared somewhat, enough that people could go out; although the ash from the volcano and the trembling of the ground did not cease. It grew dark again at four in the afternoon; and from that hour certain rumblings were heard coming from the earth, so horrible that they caused great dread. On the twenty-eighth the day dawned somewhat clearer; but soon a terrifying tremor came; and so the gloom returned anew; and at three in the afternoon it was already as dark as night, with as great a storm of lightning and thunder as the most terrible of the previous ones: it lasted an hour and a half, because a strong wind carried the storm toward the sea. On the twenty-ninth, over three drops, the next day there was some quiet and calm, and all day it kept darkening again, and the ash falling as before. From the day the storm began to subside, the ash continually diminished, although not so quickly that many remnants of the calamity do not remain to this day in Arequipa and its surroundings.
The people of that city soon understood that

It began to rain ash, the cause being, as people said, some volcano within their district. For the first two days it was thought to come from a very large one that lay six leagues from the city, but they soon realized this was not the case. They suspected it must be the one called Obinas. In the end they could not determine with certainty where the harm was coming from, until after ten or twelve days had passed, when the weather cleared somewhat, and some Indians came to the city — those who had saved themselves from six towns that had been destroyed by being closer to the volcano — and from these, as well as from many other persons, both Indians and Spaniards, who had been at a distance of six to twelve leagues from the volcano and had witnessed the eruption from afar, it became known that it was the volcano of Oñate that had erupted. This caused little surprise at first, because no one had ever been wary of it, since it had never been seen to emit fire or smoke, and also because it was so many leagues distant from the city.

And it was learned that on the first afternoon of the storm, upon erupting, it sent forth such a quantity of black smoke together with the crashes and thunderings already mentioned, that it darkened the sky and plunged ten or twelve leagues around it into profound darkness, which lasted fifteen days, during which one could not distinguish day from night. Out of the smoke there burst a column of fire of such prodigious greatness that it seemed to reach from the earth to the sky, and after it came the ash and

A stone of great size split open at the foot of the hill, and from it burst forth a great and furious river of fire, which ran for about a league and a half, burning everything it touched, so that it turned all the trees to charcoal and the ground over which it passed was left smooth and as hard as bare rock. So great was the quantity of burning stones, and so high did they rise, that looking at the sky it seemed as though the whole of it were ablaze, turned into a sea of the innumerable stones flying through the air. For the fifteen days that the eruption lasted, the volcano did not cease roaring day and night, throwing out ash and stones, and the earth shook frequently. When these days had passed, although the violence diminished somewhat—

heavy, and the air cleared, but not enough that the sun could be seen clearly for many months, nor for more than eight days did the earth stop trembling three or four times a day, nor did the thunder and ash cease coming from the volcano from time to time.

The confusion and astonishment of the people while these things were happening was so extraordinary that it cannot be expressed in words. From the moment the storm began with such tremendous roaring and trembling of the earth, everyone ran to the churches, dumbstruck and pale, to beg for mercy from God and to implore His forgiveness for their sins and wrongdoings. No one gave a thought to their estates and riches, nor paid them any mind, believing that the end of the world had come and that their days were numbered. Persuaded of this, some Indians, forgetting their Christian obligations, sat down at their leisure to eat and drink until they were drunk, in accordance with the barbarous custom they had practiced in their pagan days; eating, even though it was Lent, the chickens and sheep they owned, saying that since they were going to die anyway, there was no point in saving them. Others among the inhabitants of the villages near the volcano hanged themselves, to be free from the ash and from a more painful death. But the residents of Arequipa

Spaniards, and a great part of the Indians prepared themselves to die as Christians, receiving with great sorrow and tears the holy sacraments of penance and communion. The churches remained open day and night, with the Blessed Sacrament exposed within them. All commerce and public offices ceased, as both great and small attended to nothing other than offering prayers to our Lord, and to processions every day, some of them bloody. The people walked in a state of perpetual alarm, for the continuous earthquakes gave them no chance to rest at night, and those near the volcano were so afflicted and broken that they considered it a better fate to end their lives at once than to prolong them, and to torment their souls further with the sight of such pitiful and extraordinary events.

The damages and calamities caused by this terrible storm were of inestimable worth, although it is true that what caused the least physical destruction was what produced the greatest dread and terror among the people, namely the horrible thunder, the roaring of the volcano, the continuous and rapid earthquakes, the darkness, and the lightning in the air. Chapter 20, On the Earthquakes of Peru.

The land most troubled by earthquakes in all of America is the coastal plain and coast of the kingdom of Peru, where a very remarkable phenomenon is experienced. The frequent tremors that occur here are caused, according to the most common opinion, by the many volcanoes in the highlands and by the general turmoil of subterranean fire, whose flames run beneath the western mountain range, as said above, and being much closer to the highlands than to the far side of the same mountain range, these coastal plains are nonetheless incomparably more subject to tremors than the provinces of the highlands. Paraguay, which is free from the torments of thunder and lightning that afflict the inhabitants of the highlands, does not spare its own residents

History of the New World.
to fear, and wherever we turn our eyes there are officers and executors of divine justice: compared among themselves to all types of storms, of which I have had experience of both during the years I have resided in the highlands and on the plains. I consider more formidable the storm and pursuit of the wind than that of the earth. Because to save life from that threat, the remedy is for people to go out to open places, away from hills and buildings; but from the storm of lightning there is no safe place in a town or outside of it: which is made all the more horrible by its blow being so sudden, that the harm is felt before the sound reaches the ears; which does not occur with earthquakes: although it is true that the damage and loss of property caused by these is greater than from lightning.
Earthquakes are so frequent and common along the coasts of Peru and the kingdom of Chile, running more than eight hundred leagues from north to south, that not a single year passes without several occurring: which follow one after another in sequence throughout this whole expanse; the smaller ones reaching a hundred leagues along the coast, and twenty to thirty leagues inland; and the general and notable ones, which tend to come less frequently, four to five hundred leagues along the sea, and from fifty to eighty leagues inland; such that this entire vast tract of land moves and undulates with a trembling agitated by the waves of the enraged and tempestuous sea.
Since the Spaniards settled this land it has been reported that

First Part, Book 2.

There have been some very notable earthquakes, worthy of memory, beyond what occurred in the kingdom of Chile in past years, which was so terrible that, overturning and joining two mountains together, it dammed and blocked the river of Valdivia, which had been a mighty river; as the floodwaters rose, the stopped trees were held back for many days, coming to burst forth, and the rains swept away the rivers — admired by all who witnessed them — causing notable harm to towns and people alike, flooding settlements and lands, causing the sea to rise and overflow its boundaries by a great distance, pushing back far from where its waters had been. In many other such instances similar events occurred.

Then followed, in the year fifteen hundred and sixty-two, the earthquake of Arequipa, which completely leveled that city. And then, four years later, came that great earthquake of the city. The tremor of the year fifteen hundred and eighty-six, on the ninth of July, struck — whose damage was beyond reckoning — yet it was fortunate in that not many people perished, owing to the earthquake not catching them asleep, and the noise having given them warning as it approached, so that they fled into the open plazas, streets, gardens, and away from the houses; and thus no more than thirteen to fifteen persons died. But its force and great fury were so terrible that it greatly ruined the city, bringing down many buildings, and obliging the citizens to set up tents and pavilions in the plazas to keep away from the walls and roofs of the houses; and there they remained for many days without daring to trust the shattered supports.

History of the New World

The sea, on the contrary, made the same movement it had made in Chile, attacked the land, and going beyond itself entered far inland, covering the fields and estates with great fear and harm to their owners.

All these torments and calamities were forgotten because of the terrifying earthquake that occurred on the twenty-fourth day of November of sixteen hundred and four, at around one-thirty in the afternoon, which was without doubt the greatest that had ever been seen in this kingdom, and is still regarded as one of the rarest and most prodigious that is known to have occurred in the world. Its extent was so great that at the very same time it shook more than three hundred leagues of land in length, running North to South along the coast of the sea, and entered inland in its width more than seventy leagues. To the city of Callao, which is sixty leagues from the sea, it arrived with such force that men could not remain standing, and it shook the buildings violently, though they did not fall because they were strong and well-founded; only the outer wall of the church of the Company of Jesus fell to the ground. Its duration was more or less, according to the force with which it struck each place. Here in this city of Lima, where I happened to be at the time, in the church of our house with some other religious men, it lasted about four or five — it was not very great here, nor yet so small as to cause no fear. We came out with this fear

First Part. Book 2.
fleeing to their patios, as soon as they saw the walls of the church beginning to shake, and the roof timbers cracking loudly. Although it caused fear in Lima in this manner, there was no damage there, but we all feared that the force had gone elsewhere, and consequently the damage as well, as indeed it had.

In the city of Arequipa it lasted half a quarter of an hour, and altogether it went on for half an hour; though, as commonly happens with large earthquakes, many smaller ones followed it, which continued for the next ten days or so. It was all the stronger the further one went from Lima toward the south, as far as the port and city of Arica, where, as in Arequipa, it had its greatest force and violence. The residents of Arequipa had suffered, since the volcano erupted, almost continuous years of harsh calamities from ash and sterility, great want and poverty. But as the ash diminished — for the constant winds, since it was so light, had carried it from one place to another, and a great part of it had blown out to sea — the sun began to show itself more clearly, and with its rays more unobstructed, it warmed the earth more, and through its heat and influence began to fertilize it again. The land enjoyed this benefit, so long denied to it by the heavy, dusty ash clouds, so that it seemed the fields, vineyards, and other properties were coming back to life; and the people, with these good hopes, began to recover

they caught some breath, and gathered together lamenting their past hardships and losses, when there came upon them the fearful and tremendous earthquake, which began to shake the entire city from one hour to the next, and caused as great a devastation in the towns and fields of its surroundings as the eruption of the volcano.

It began gently, and with little noise, which, together with its occurring during the day, was the reason it did not kill many people, as it would have done had it struck at night. It kept growing in such a way that men, thrown to their knees and clinging to one another, could still not hold themselves upright. The fields began to resound with a deep rumbling that gave warning: the mountains moved so violently that they seemed to be crashing into one another; the houses were so shaken and battered by the waves and shuddering of the earth, as ships are by a stormy sea; collapsing, they broke apart, and the force of the tremor hurled their ruins aloft with a horrible roar, as much from the buildings as from the mountains that were crumbling. Such a thick cloud of dust rose up that it darkened the sun, leaving everyone buried in a narrow and dark space, with no one daring to move from the spot where they stood, for fear of falling into greater danger. In all of Arequipa, within half a quarter of an hour, not a building remained standing except the churches of Saint Francis and Saint Augustine. Many came out of the ruins with broken legs, battered heads, and mutilated and crushed bodies; besides those who

Having treated in the preceding book of the nature of

History of the New World.

Further regarding the Indies, and continuing in this endeavor, and in the following sections of this first part, I set out to record the most notable and well-known things I have been able to learn about them — both those that are common to and of the same kind as those of Europe, as well as those particular and proper to this new world, of which, before it was discovered by us Spaniards, those of Europe had no knowledge. In order to proceed with clarity and distinction, it seemed right to me to divide them into four kinds and classes, following the division that philosophers make of all bodies composed of the four elements, which they call perfect mixed bodies: that is to say, the inanimate, such as metals, which are commonly generated in the bowels of the earth and lack life; the animated but insensible bodies, which include all the kinds of plants; the sensitive and irrational animate things, which encompass all the kinds of brute animals, whether of the land, water, or air; and finally the rational composite beings, who are the native peoples of these Western Indies and the New World. I follow in these ranks the order that nature observes in proceeding from the imperfect to the perfect. And I shall treat first in this book of the mixed bodies belonging to the first rank and member of the division, and in the following books, of the other three.

First Part. Book 3.
The common homeland of inanimate mixed bodies is the element of earth; where, setting aside those which the Creator produced at the beginning, when he gave being and perfection to the world, it is a settled doctrine among philosophers that through the power of general causes and the particular qualities of diverse soils, new ones are continually being generated afresh from the same matter, of all kinds and species: some drying and hardening, some by cold, others by heat; with the power of the matter itself and of the other three elements contributing to their generation. The specific difference follows the variety of the mixture from which they are formed, and the power of the element that predominates in such generation, and no less that of the star that exerts its influence, and with which the body produced has the greatest affinity and sympathy.
So that if in the mixture a greater portion of earth than of the other elements is present, a heavy, dry, hard, dense, and dark body will be generated, such as iron. And if air and water are present in the same proportion, clear and transparent minerals will be produced, such as diamonds, sapphires, and other precious stones. In the same way, if in the mixture there is a greater quantity of earth and water than of air and fire, and the earth and water with equal forces and faculties notably obscure the other two elements, minerals of a fluid nature will be generated, soft, heavy, and somewhat clear and lustrous, as

History of the New World.

They are gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and mercury: always contributing to the generation of the most precious metals the most perfect, purest, and most refined matter; and on the contrary, the most foul or impure matter to that of the imperfect and base metals. Together with the mixture of the elements, the virtue of the celestial bodies influences them, as has been stated; without which nothing in this lower world can be born, live, or thrive. For this reason, both alchemists and astrologers assign to each species of metal its own planet, which presides over, guards, and generates it, and gives it all its activity and force. And in the generation of all kinds of stones, it is likewise a well-founded opinion that each species of stone inclines toward one of the fixed stars, which gives it its strength and vigor.

And no more nor less than the generation of inanimate things, which belong to the first order and class of natural bodies, the elementary forces combine with celestial influences; so too they concur in the production of those of other grades, each according to what its nature requires. Of the mixture of the four elements with the influences of the celestial bodies, which concur in the generation of natural bodies, the Indians had no knowledge, nor of the other uses pertaining to the natural sciences.

Chapter 3: On Sulfur Stone

The abundance of sulfur found throughout the Indies is very great, particularly in the Kingdom of Peru — not only in the volcanoes that spout fire, but also in innumerable mineral deposits; from these there commonly flow springs of hot water carrying the very smell of sulfur, whose water is for the most part chalky and whitish in taste, and which congeals into stone. One kind of sulfur stone is extracted mixed with earth, and requires refining in order to purify it; another vein of it occurs in entire masses, pure and refined, requiring no treatment at all — this second kind is golden in color, very lustrous, and almost transparent. Similar to this is the sulfur stone that forms from the waters of a spring that flows in the province of Collao. The Indians made use of sulfur stone, and by burning it they used it only to treat the mange of their llamas and sheep of the land. The Spaniards make from it a great deal of very fine gunpowder, and they put it to all the same uses as in Europe.

Chapter 4. On Salt.

Just as the kingdom of Peru is the most abundant in metals, chiefly silver, of any we know today in the world, so too it is rich in natural salt deposits; for it seems God provided them in such abundance in a place where salt is so often needed to process silver metals, consuming an incredible quantity of salt. And there is no province or city that lacks it; for from the great amounts extracted in some lands, it is distributed to others; and none is so distant from some salt works that it cannot easily be supplied by land or sea with what it needs.

Authors who write on the subject describe three kinds of salt: namely sea salt, mineral salt, and that which is made from the water of certain springs. All of these are found in these Indies in very great abundance. And of two of them — sea salt and salt from brackish springs — both natural and artificial forms are found. For beyond the sea salt made from seawater by human industry, in some places the sea overflows with its tides and floods, casting far beyond the limits of its shores a great quantity of water, which with the heat of the sun congeals into excellent salt. And in other places they extract it in large stones from beneath the water of the same sea, from a certain earth where it is found solidified.
Beyond this

First Part. Book 3.

Beyond this, there are three ways in which salt is made from spring water: two of them by human industry, collecting the said water in pools where it is evaporated by the heat of the sun, and the other by boiling it in pots over fire until it becomes recognizable; the third way is that the same brackish water from many springs and lakes evaporates on its own.

There are three other ways found in this land by which salt is made from water. One is that in certain places salt is made from fresh water, by boiling in it the saltpeter gathered from the surface of the earth that the sea once covered, and also by means of a certain herb that has this virtue. In the province of Venezuela, the Indians made salt from the ash of the shoots of certain palms, which, although it was very white, was sticky and bitter in the manner of saltpeter. In the province of Popayan, they boil the herb mentioned above, and from the water in which it was soaked they make salt by evaporating it over fire.

Of the other two methods, one involves rainwater that collects in pools, and by the particular quality of the soil where it settles, it is converted into salt by the heat of the sun. But the one that causes me the most wonder is that found in a river in the province of Tucuman, for although its water is fresh, from the riverbed they extract great slabs of very white and fine salt. In other places a channel of fresh water is directed through salty ground, and after standing for some time it rises up, and

History of the New World.
it remains in very perfect salt.
All the different kinds of salt mentioned up to this point come from water, naturally, or through human skill; apart from those that yield mineral salt, of which there are many in the kingdom of Peru, both in the coastal lands and in the inland regions.
This salt is extracted by force of drill-bits, wedges, and sledgehammers of iron, and it comes in three varieties: one is granular salt, another is salt in stone form, and of this latter kind there is one they call "compass" salt, which is so smooth and transparent as crystal, while the other is less so, because it has some dark veins running through it.
The salt mines found in the coastal lands differ from those in the mountain ranges further inland, in that the coastal ones, being close to the sea, are ordinarily covered with sand, beneath which the salt lies not in veins, but rather like a continuous slab or flagstone forming a crust over the earth.
But the inland salt mines are enclosed in rugged mountain ranges, where between the earth and the crags run veins of salt, which continue unbroken, just like those of other metal-bearing minerals.
Even though the Indians are so fond of salt that among the strictest practices observed in their time of paganism was abstaining from it, they nonetheless consumed very little of it in...

To add to what we call it, having so few things to season it with: they could find the dried meat that they made, and the fish that they cured for keeping and carrying from one place to another, without a single grain of salt. They did this in the following way: if the meat or fish was to be kept for any length of time, they would roast it on a Barbacoa, and afterwards bind it with fibers and rushes in the hot lowlands. But those of Peru, both for short and long keeping, would dry and cure the meat and fish in the sun on the coast of the sea, and in the frost in the cold highlands. And even in the stews and dishes they ate, they did not always add salt to season them; instead, when they ate, they would place a lump of salt next to the plate, which served as their salt cellar, and from time to time they would lick it with their tongue, giving the flavor of salt to the palate rather than to the dish. And sometimes, when many were eating together and there was no more than one lump of salt on the table for everyone, it would go around from hand to hand, each one licking it in turn. Salt is called by two names in the two general languages of Peru: cachi in Quechua, and haque in Aymara.

Chapter 5. On saltpeter and alum stone.
The Indians of Peru call saltpeter yn in the general language, yuca; but it is what grows on the surface of

History of the New World

the land in salty places, because they knew no other kind of it. Saltpeter is very harmful to buildings, particularly in coastal towns such as the ports of Callao and Pisco, because it eats away the foundations of houses unless they are built of hard stone. And for the properties that are near the sea, because if care is not taken to remove the saltpeter from them, they become barren. The Indians did not know of saltpeter for gunpowder, nor did they know how to process it; which the Spaniards do by distilling the water in which it appears, and letting it settle in clay vessels, at the bottom of which the saltpeter congeals like grains of transparent salt. It is found in many parts of this kingdom of Peru in no small abundance, from which very good gunpowder is made; particularly the finest comes from the provinces of Quito. In lands that lack snow, the Spaniards cool water with saltpeter.

Of alum stone there are found in these Indies four or five species. In New Spain they make it very white, bright, and transparent, which the dyers use in their dyes, and it serves for the cures for which it is said to be brought from Spain.

Chapter 6. On certain clays and potting earths from which pottery is made.

From the varied mixture of the elements and the influences of the heavens, so many diverse soils are formed, differing from one another in color and quality, as we observe: of which there are as many varieties in this New World as in the other parts of the Old. The best known of all are the earths from which pottery is made, and all manner of clay vessels, being so necessary for the use of the people. All manner of clay from which pottery is made is called by the Indians of this kingdom, in their language, saño; and all potting earth in general, llanta. Many varieties of clays and potting earths of all colors are found in this land, and in some places very precious ones, from which curious jars and other drinking vessels are made for holding water, as is the case in the city of Cuzco, in the province of Chuncito, from where they are carried to many places, being much esteemed as a very fine clay. In this archbishopric of Lima, the clays of the valley of Ica and of the valley of Jipi are held in no lesser esteem; from the latter, white vessels are made that keep the water cool.
But all those mentioned are surpassed by those from the Diocese of Natá in Panama, from where many are brought to this city of Lima, very finely made and of various shapes. However, of late there has been found in the kingdom of Chile

History of the New World.
such fine clay that it surpasses that of Nata: jars made from it are brought to this city of Lima, which are so precious that they are sent from here as gifts to Spain, because they can compete with the best from there in smell, luster, and color of the clay.
The Indians did not make much use of clay vessels, because they never learned to make bricks or roof tiles; nor throughout all these Indies is there any record of there ever having been any of this kind; nor throughout all the land have I found a single piece of brick, nor a fragment of tile: nor among the ruins of ancient buildings is there any trace of mortar, nor any memory among the Indians that there ever was any. Nor did they make the varieties of earthenware that we use; but only pots and jugs different from one another in being larger or smaller, and in certain figures and decorations that they carved on them; and some small flat plates in the manner of patens. The other vessels that correspond to those which the Spaniards are accustomed to make from clay, they made from silver, gold, wood, and dried gourds: nor in their ancient tombs, where they buried with their dead all their foods and drinks, were any other vessels found beyond those mentioned. Nor did they arrive at the invention of glazing; all their clay vessels were unglazed, nor did they fire them as perfectly as we do, because they had no kilns for this purpose, nor for any other use: in the ground they made a hole, and in it they did not fire them except with dung and straw; and today they still fire them in this manner; although for this purpose the livestock brought from Spain helps them not a little, especially cattle, which the

It provides firewood, which they use in this ministry. The quantities of clay pots used by the Spaniards are excellent, since those made by Indians withstand fire. They also had neither a wheel nor any other instrument with which to make these vessels, other than their hands, which is why it took them a long time to form them evenly; and yet they still make them in their own way, and finish them just as well as if they had been made on a wheel.

After the Spaniards settled this land, everything that is made of clay in Spain is made here as well, including as much brick and tile as is needed for our buildings; many turned out a variety of vessels: particularly a great quantity of one-arroba jars in which wine is transported — it is estimated that five hundred thousand are newly made each year in the vineyards — and also a good number of half-arroba glazed small jars for oil, brandy, rose water, and other liquors that are stored in them.

As for small basins and large earthen jars, which in Spain are made of clay, they are little used in these Indies; in their place they use bateas, which are made of hard and valuable wood. The Spaniards have adopted this practice from the Indians, who — particularly those living in hot and mountainous lands — always used them. They make them from the trunks of very thick trees, most commonly cedar, and some are so large that they hold ten arrobas of water or more, and are big enough for a man to bathe in them.

Fine glazed pottery is also made there, which is no less worthy than that of Talavera, because in recent years people have taken to making it in the Chinese style, and it comes out very similar to it; particularly that which is made in the city of Puebla de los Angeles in New Spain, and in the city of Lima, which is very good, with fine glaze and colors. Likewise, very handsome tiles are made, which previously used to be brought from Spain, though it is true that those made here do not equal the finest colors of the Spanish ones.

Chapter 7. On Pasa, and other varieties.

Morada.
Casa is what the Indians of Peru call a certain kind of clay, which is white with some brownish spots, something like a flavor quality; it is cold in nature, and they use it because it is very pleasing to them, and dissolved in water they season their potatoes and other roots with it, dipping them in it as if it were a sauce. For this reason it is sold in the markets of all towns. Its powders, which are soft and gentle, applied to hemorrhoids are useful for drying them out and consuming them. Mixed with vinegar or quince juice they work against attacks of gout. They serve to remove stains, and are often used in place of soap, because the lather they raise cleans clothing. For this reason the Indians wash their hair with it, noting that it kills lice, and that if those who suffer from bloody dysentery eat it, it stops it.

Contaya is another species of white earth, good for

First Part, Book 3.
for plastering and whitening walls. Carpa is another clay, or red-colored earth, used in torments and on the floors of houses. Chau is another clay from which roof tiles and bricks are made, and poto-colored things, which women are inclined to eat. All these names come from the Aymara language, which is the general language of the provinces of the Collao in the kingdom of Peru.

Chapter 8. On Millu.

Millu is a type of earth similar in its astringency, and almost in color, to copperas; there are two varieties of it, one with which they dye the garments here, and another that is red. Millu is a powerfully strong substance, because beyond its astringency, it is purgative and biting; for which reason its powders cure scrofula. Whoever has eaten a small lump of sugar with this earth will dry out sores on any part of the body; and finally, with millu, saltpeter, and alum, a very medicinal strong water is made. The name millu comes from the Aymara language.

Chapter 9. On Tacu.

Tacu is what the Indians of Peru call, in the Aymara language, the earth that is properly Armenian Bole; and it is commonly administered as such: which we may properly call Indian Bole. Tacu is found in the rich mountain of Potosí, and in other metal mines, especially iron mines, among different varieties; the first is a reddish earth

History of the New World

There is a blood-red variety, used by painters and principally by gilders. The second is liver-colored: flatter and more common, and used by the Indians to cure certain illnesses. It is yellow. The Indians sell it in the plazas in loaves and rolls, and they make use of it to treat bloody dysentery by drinking its powder in chicha, which is their wine. This earth is useful, and especially when burned it dries any wound; and when unburned, mixed with vinegar, rosewater, or plantain, it is beneficial in treating inflammation.

A variety of tau is a certain earth which in New Spain they call sigillata, of which there is a vein in the town of Tepeotlan, a few leagues from Mexico City. It is good for the liver, grayish and shiny; when drunk dissolved in water it proved effective against dysentery.

Chapter 10. On copperas, and on the other colored earths.

In many parts of the Indies there are mines of fine copperas, from which ink for writing is made with great ease, so that one need only add the ground copperas with a little tara, also ground, into cold water and stir it naturally; and then, once the copperas has been added, it becomes very uniform in the ink, which turns black with a slight blue tinge. From this I conclude that it must be distinguished from that which is brought from

First Part. Book 3.
ña. Further evidence of this is that the ink made here with local materials is not as fine as that which curious people make with materials from Castile, that is, with the copperas and galls brought from there. This local copperas is called in the general language of Peru, tolpa.

There is also found that yellow earth much used by painters called ochre, which in the Aymara language is called puelle. And another kind of gilded earth called in the same Aymara language, Yitu, which painters also use. There is likewise red ochre in many places, which the Indians of Peru call Puco-alpa.

In New Spain there is found in veins a white earth, which is commonly used as white lead, and for painting; the Indian women use it for spinning cotton, taking it between their fingers, which makes them smoother so they can spin with greater ease.

Another kind of white earth is found in New Spain in the hollows of the rocks, which is given to drink to patients suffering from fevers.

And another yellow earth is found, which painters use; with which the Indian women commonly paint their faces, making themselves look fiercer. And likewise the Mexican Indians would smear their bodies with it when they went to war, in order to strike fear into their enemies.

Chapter 11. On Tepetate

It is a kind of earth that seems half soil and half stone, because it is neither entirely soil nor entirely stone, though it shares properties of both: it is soft like earth, yet resists water, which never softens it the way it does rock. Some call it "female stone," and in New Spain they call it Tepetate, which makes up the greater part of the ground of that kingdom, both in the mountains and in many plains and low areas, though this does not always impede the fertility of the region; because where the tepetate is exposed, the soil is entirely unfruitful; and where it is covered with earth, if the tepetate beneath is thick, it ends up robbing the waters when the land is cultivated, as has happened on the heights and hillsides around Mexico City, or even diminishing what is sown. Tepetate comes in various colors; for the most part it is reddish, though it is also found very white. A tepetate surface makes good ground for roads that run over it, because no matter how much it rains it does not turn to mud, but rather hardens so that water does not seep through or penetrate it. It is also good for cutting irrigation channels, ditches, and millraces into it, because it saves on lime and stone; and whatever is built of this material is so firm and secure that it never collapses. There is one tepetate harder than others: in the valley of Piura near Lima there are small hills of nothing but very white tepetate, which when ground up is commonly used to clean silver plates, and for this purpose alone it is brought from that city of Lima.

Chapter 12. On Sand.

There are various kinds of sand found in Peru, found along the shores of the sea and the rivers, as well as in many other places on the surface and in the depths of the earth. In these things the variety shows itself mainly in the following ways: one is color, and another is whether the sand is finer or coarser; and for the smelted and washed silver metals there is, beyond that, a great quantity of sand. On the coast of the sea at Pisco and Callao there is much sand made of broken and ground shells; it is white and is mixed with salt for use in construction. Apart from this sand, there is found in many places a black and fine grit, which is commonly sprinkled over fresh writing instead of blotting sand; and there is so much of it in Peru that there is no place that lacks it for this purpose, since everyone can obtain this fine grit.

For the same purpose there serve two other types that we may call fine grit. One is marcasite, which is found in many rivers and which in color and brilliance resembles gold dust, and has deceived more than a few Indians into thinking it was gold. The others from Charcas resemble silver filings. From these last two, the sand used in inkwells and urinals is commonly supplied.

In the province of Florida there is a certain deposit of very fine, white sand that silversmiths in New Spain use for whitening silver. In a river of New Spain there is also found a white sand that is good for treating fevers.

History of the New World

The uses for which we employ sand are in the making of lime and stone buildings: all that is consumed in this city of Lima for this purpose is extracted from the area nearby; and that which is used in the port of Callao is gathered from the seashore, which is coarser, and is preferred by the masons, and all of it that went into the construction of the city wall and the fortifications of that port was of this kind. The fine and subtle sand, without separating the air bubbles: the ordinary kind is not coarse enough for working marble; the coarsest is used to pave the street corners to avoid mud when it rains; for this purpose I myself saw a layer of sand spread on the streets of a garden, so that one could walk through them right after a rainfall without anything hindering one.

For none of these uses did the Indians ever use sand, for they marked with lime and sand what they made for their buildings, nor did they make use of it to work marble, nor to make clocks, for they never had any of sand, nor of wheels, nor of sun; nor even less to sprinkle over writings, since they never had any. Only in one thing do I find that the Indians of the coast of Peru made use of sand, which was to preserve maize, keeping it stored mixed with fine sand; and from them the Spaniards learned to preserve wheat in this manner.

Entering into the subject of quarries, minerals, and all manner of stones, I place first the most common ones, which in general

On many shores of the sea, and on most of the rivers, and also inland in places far from the coast and rivers, one finds in abundance the most common and ordinary stones, which are the smooth, flint-like ones, beautiful in all sizes. They tend to extract some from the larger rivers when they run swollen and muddy; although these are difficult to work because of their great hardness, they are very attractive and prized, particularly for decorative vessels. There are many coastal lands whose entire depth is made of stone of this kind, as we see in the high bluffs along rivers as well as along the seacoast, from which many stones are commonly broken loose by earthquakes and roll down to the bottom. The soil of this entire valley of Lima is composed of gravel, sand, and rubble, except for the surface layer, which is a little soil that tends to be from one to two varas thick, more or less. And so from the wells dug in this city, much of this stone is extracted, ranging in size from a hazelnut up to the size of a head, and some much larger, weighing three or four arrobas. The same is true of the stones from the rivers, which include very large and very small ones. The Spaniards make use of these kinds of stones to pave streets and the courtyards of houses; the large cobblestones are used in the foundations of buildings; the white ones are ground by potters to make the glaze for earthenware; and finally, in seaports the cobblestones serve as ballast for ships, and it is the best ballast of all.

The Indians did not have many uses for these pebbles, because they had no ships to ballast with them, nor did they know how to pave the streets and floors of the houses in their towns, since in the ruins of these we have found no such use: they only used the round stones as mortars and tools for working cut stone, and as ammunition in war to throw with their slings, at which they were very skilled. Some of these pebble-stones are very fine flints. We can also include in this category of stones certain slabs as hard as the pebbles, which are commonly found loose, very flat and smooth, two to three palms in diameter, on which the Indians grind their maize and other things.

Chapter 14. On stones used in construction.

Every kind of freestone and granite, which is easy to work, is what we call suitable for ashlar buildings, and there are choice quarries of it throughout these Indies; some stones are found very light and porous, in the manner of pumice, or pumice stone, which does not sink in water, and which is marvelous for construction, not only for walls and fortresses: similar to it there are many other kinds of light and spongy stones of all colors.
In the city of Arequipa there is a quarry of stone

White and so soft that it can be worked with a knife, it is
very cavernous, and has some cavities so large
that a fist fits inside them, and they are usually filled with ash
from what the volcanoes throw out: which leads one to suppose
that all that stone is congealed ash, and proof
of this is found in the fact that inside the very same

In the diocese of the said city of Arequipa, and in many

the lightest and most spongy of all; the fire volcanoes throw out these stones
when they erupt, and they come out glowing

Also used in buildings are grindstones,
and the Indians had no other use for them, because they had no

iron tools with which to sharpen them: in the highlands of this kingdom there are so many quarries of this stone that in some places I have seen entire mountain ranges of it stretching for many leagues, as in the province of Chucuito, diocese of Chuquiabo, and in the town of Moho in the same diocese. But the best whetstones found in this kingdom are those taken from the point of Santa Elena, diocese of Quito.
The region around Cusco is very well supplied with good quarries; and so too is that of Guamanga: in this second one there is found, among others, a kind of colorful stone of very pleasing appearance, which is composed of very tightly bound layers, thin and even, whose joints along the edges show stripes of the same slightly darker color, and they split easily into very flat and even slabs. About the thickness of a finger, or as one might wish. There is another quarry in the same city of very soft black stone, made up of grains the size of peppercorns, which crumble apart easily: and another kind of stone very white and soft to work.
The quarried stone used in this city of Lima is brought by sea and land from many places, such as Cañete, Arica, Silicaya, and Panama. That of Silicaya is of very pleasing appearance on account of its agreeable color, which is like a rose hue; it has good grain and is easy to work: but because the quarry is far from this city and the road is poor, only small stones are brought in

mule veins. The stone from Arica is white and good both

From Panama, very large stones are brought by sea, from

All the hills of this valley of Lima are of rocks, crags,

see hills that have continuous veins embedded among
