from one to two palms in thickness. These stones, selected in this way, are good for fine masonry work, because they have two flat and smooth faces: and it was with stones of this sort that the wall of the port of Callao was built. Others of the same kind, though very thin, because they come in layers like sheets, of a thickness ranging from a real de a ocho up to one, two, or four fingers wide, from which flagstones and very thin, flat slates are cut for paving floors: and the Indians used to cover with them the terraces of their houses and their burial places. It is indeed true that in these same hills around the city of Lima there are quarries of stone that can be worked, as well as on the island of Callao, from which the stone was taken to carve the gateways of the wall; and the quarry at the hill of Sulco, two leagues from the city of Lima, from which the stone was taken to build the bridge over the river and the council houses, but it is so hard and tough that whatever is worked from it costs a great deal of money.
The Indians of Peru call all types of good workable quarry stone cheu rumi: they made use of it for the same purposes as we do, except for channeling water, which they never achieved: and since they lacked iron tools, they shaped it with other very hard and heavy small stones, which in their language they call vini:

Chapter 15. On various flints.

In all places, particularly in the highlands and cold lands,
many kinds of fine flints are found;
these the Indians used very well and valued greatly, even
though not for striking fire, but used them instead of
knives and other tools. Flints of all colors are found,
and a kind of stone that looks like flint, as red as coral,
greatly esteemed by the Indians, which
they call Mullu, and from it they make strings of beads
that the Indian women wear around their necks as ornament. Among the gravel-
beds of rivers and along the seacoast many are found
that are perfect flints, such as certain pebbles
very hard that are brought from the river of Guayaquil, of a dark yellow
color. But where the greatest abundance of flints I
have ever seen is in the province of the Mixteca in New
Spain; in which nearly every stone encountered
along the road was choice flint. In the plaza of
Mexico some very fine white flints are sold, and
together with them a kind of tinder is sold, which
is the best I have ever seen in my life, which they extract
from the bark of certain trees.

The stone of the grape of Paraguay which is formed from earth
is so tough a flint that it greatly wears down the steel
striker. Also a fine flint is the wood found beneath the

water turns into stone
Chapter 16. On limestone.

Limestone quarries are not found equally in all places, nor in warm lands, and more often only in certain areas where, with somewhat greater effort, one climbs from the lowlands where it is not found. Throughout the highlands of the Kingdom of Peru, one finds abundant quarries of this stone here and there, particularly in the territory of the city of Cuzco, where the Indians used to build even the terrace walls of the fields and estates from this stone.
Beyond the ordinary quarries that the land produces, we find in this land two other very particular kinds of limestone. One is extracted in the diocese of Arequipa; it is a kind of crust that the land produces on its surface, about a palm's width thick, more or less. It is found in flat terrain and on hillsides, sometimes exposed on the very surface of the ground, and other times buried and covered by one, two, or more spans of earth, so that by clearing away the soil above, this crust is uncovered. Beneath it the ground is as it comes in places. The lime made from this stone is very strong, though not so white.

History of the New World

Another type of limestone is found on some islands of the kingdom's seas, as in the valley of Pisa, and in other places. This kind does not form on land, but rather in the sea, and when the waves rage they cast it onto the shores in pieces of various sizes, from medium up to four arrobas and more in weight. Once dried out, and the foam having settled, it resembles pumice stone, tending toward an ashen color, and is so soft that it easily crumbles. It has a strange property, which is that it soaks up and drinks whatever water is poured on it. The lime made from it is very white, but not as strong as the first kind.
In the city of Puebla de los Angeles, in New Spain, lime is made from a certain stone that congeals from water; it is good and white. In the valley of Ichacay, near this city of Lima, there are two or three ravines close to the sea, from which a certain water runs that gradually turns into stone of a reddish color, well-formed, and almost transparent, from which a lime so white is made that it is brought to this city to whitewash buildings.

In the province of Nicaragua, and in other coastal lands where limestone is scarce, lime is made from seashells, and this can hold its own against all others. Even so, the best, strongest, and most abundantly produced lime comes from ordinary limestone, which is very hard, solid, and heavy, of which there is great abundance in the valley of Lima, in a small range of hills about a quarter of a league from the city, where the early settlers found it, to the
North

Since the city was founded, although in the early days they did not use as much lime in the buildings as they do now — for when I came to Lima some thirty-three years ago there was no more than one lime kiln, and at present there are forty — they can barely keep up with the construction work being done. And from this point forward we build at great expense, working with lime and stone, which we consider essential. Also, within the last twenty-five years, other quarries of this stone have been found in the hills near the town of la te, half a league from the city, and the lime from these quarries is considered better than that from the first ones.

The most useful method that has been found for cutting stone from these quarries is with powder charges: a small hole is made in a large stone, and into it are packed tightly about three or four pounds of gunpowder, and when it is lit, it produces a blast as great as that of an artillery piece, and the entire stone, even one as large as a room, cracks and breaks into many pieces. We have found in this city that the mortar made from this lime, when used in damp places such as irrigation channels or cisterns where water beats against it, becomes as hard as bronze; but in buildings in the dry inland areas where it does not rain, it does not set as well — so much so that when an old building is demolished, the lime is found to be almost as loose as ash. For this reason, in new construction using lime and stone, the work is continuously wetted and moistened so that it sets better, and experience has shown this method to be very beneficial. A fanega of lime sells in this city of Lima for eight reales, and in other parts of the kingdom the price is no more or less, depending on its abundance there.

History of the New World.
Chapter 17. On gypsum stone.

Quarries of gypsum stone are found less commonly than those of lime, particularly in warm lands. In the cold highlands there are great hills of it, and some mines of selenite, such as those in the district of Guamanga and Cuzco. In the valleys of the lowlands a kind of gypsum is also found, particularly in those that are abundant in vineyards, such as the valley of Vitor in the diocese of Arequipa, and that of Pisco in the Archbishopric of Lima; it seems that God provided so far in advance for the need that those valleys would have for gypsum for the benefit of the great quantity of wine that is presently produced in them.

The Indians of the kingdom of Peru had not attained the use of lime and gypsum in their buildings; for they did not know how to make mortar from lime and sand, nor how to build with gypsum, which certainly would have been of the greatest utility for them in those times, and would have saved the Spaniards great expense had they known lime and used it in their constructions. For all the irrigation channels, sea walls, bridges, and other works that they built in the time of their paganism from dry stone could have been made with lime and sand mortar, which would have made them more durable and they would not have fallen into ruin so quickly; the repair of which costs much money and labor. The Mexican Indians did attain the use of lime, although they did not mix it with sand, but rather with a ground stone they call Tezonte; and they did not slake it, but instead piled up the stone and set it on fire.

First Part. Book 3.
Chapter 18. On the marbles and alabasters
found in the Indies.

In none of the ancient stone buildings that we see in this kingdom of Peru, made by the Inca kings, nor in those of New Spain built by the Mexican kings, has there ever been found anything carved from marble, alabaster, jasper, or porphyry, despite the fact that these Indies have many quarries of these kinds of stone. The Indians of this kingdom of Peru were accustomed only to making from stones some small vessels for everyday use, such as mortars and other things of that sort. The varieties of precious marbles found in this land are many, particularly in the cold highlands of this kingdom of Peru, where there are very rich quarries of marble of every color.

In the diocese of Chuquisaca there is extracted a kind of marble so excellent that a stonemason who worked in that Royal building of San Lorenzo in the Royal [Escorial] told me that no marble as fine as this one had been used in that precious edifice. It is white as snow, lustrous and almost transparent, without any stain or vein to mar it. And I saw in the city of Chuquisaca in the year sixteen hundred and [ten or fifteen], carved from this marble, a pillar of a fountain, almost as round and turned as the body of a man; it bore [illegible] in such a way that with the

Chapter 20. On stone that is formed by water.

In the town of Huancavelica, diocese of Guamanga, a hot spring flows forth in a quantity roughly equal to the body of a man, more or less. This water runs down to the river, and along the stretch where most of it passes, it turns earth into stone. Other springs of this kind are also found in other parts of the kingdom, and in New Spain. The stone produced by this water is whitish and porous, very good for construction, of which many buildings in the aforementioned town of Huancavelica are made; and the entire city of Puebla de los Angeles in New Spain is built of stone formed by water, from which salt is also made, by which it settles; and the limestone of the valley of Chancay, as already noted, was likewise formed by water; and in many other places similar springs are found, whose water ordinarily flows out hot, somewhat thick, and whitish. Chapter 22. On the stone that serves as firewood.

In the New Kingdom of Granada there is a hill of black and resinous stone, which burns in fire like wood, and people commonly use it for lime in the following manner: they place these stones in the kiln mixed together with limestone, and beneath them a small amount of firewood to start the fire, and once it begins to burn, these stones catch fire and gradually burn until they are consumed, the ash of which will be mixed in with the lime and serves blended with it, because it is a kind of lime.

Chapter 23. On the lodestone.

There are so many lodestone deposits in Peru that, due to their abundance, they have no value or esteem, for there are very large hills made entirely of this stone, from which pieces of whatever size one wishes are taken to carry to Spain and other places. I have observed some things about the nature of this stone, the first being that although it has magnetic power throughout all its parts

History of the New World.

The power to attract iron is not with equal force, but rather on one side it tends to have greater ability than on the other. The second thing is that it does not face North from all sides, because in any of these stones, whatever their size, there are to be found a head and feet; one side faces North, and the opposite faces South. And it is very credible that this diversity arises from the position it held in the mine or quarry where it was formed: such that the part of the stone that while in the mine faced North always retains that inclination, and imparts it to the iron it touches; and the part that faced South retains its corresponding property, which it then imprints upon the iron that is touched by it.

From these two properties relating to the two poles that this stone possesses on its different sides, arises the difficulty in working it of determining which part faces North and which faces South. These stones are commonly worked into an oval shape, making one point at the part that inclines toward the North and the other at the part toward the South. And taking two such stones after they have been worked, one can test what I have described by tying each one by its middle to a thread and hanging them near one another: for when hung in this way at a proper distance, the points of each that face North will come together, attracting one to the other; and the same happens with the points that incline toward the South. But if we try to join in this manner the point of the

First part, book 3, page 167

one that faces North with the tip of the other that faces South; we will not find any repugnance or division between the stones, because they themselves, by their own virtue, separate and unite among themselves.

And the same sympathy on one part, and antipathy on the other, that we experience in these stones among themselves, we also observe in the nautical compass needle, which is touched by them: for if one brings close to a needle that has been touched with the tip of the stone that inclines to the North, and applies the lodestone at the tip that faces North, it will attract the needle and draw it close to itself; but if one brings the lodestone close to the same needle from the other tip that faces South, it repels it. To such a degree that if one turns the stone around the needle, the needle likewise keeps turning, fleeing from the stone, because it was touched with the tip opposite to the one being applied. And so the lodestone, with its hidden virtue — one of which is iron, and the other the black sand used in sand-shakers — to clean this sand when it has mixed with earth, one need only pass the lodestone over it, because the sand immediately sticks to it, leaving behind the earth with which it was mixed. The Indians never came to know the remarkable virtue of this stone, because they had no iron on which to test it, and although they could have conducted the experiment with the sand that

Chapter 29. On copaquira

Copaquiri is what the Indians of Peru call verdigris in the Aymara language. And because of the resemblance that the stone I describe here bears to it, they give it the same name, and the Spaniards, corrupting the word, call it copaquira, and piedra de los lipes, because it is found only in the province of the Lipes, which belongs to the Archbishopric of Charcas. Copaquira is a bluish-green stone, and transparent, which is extracted from a mineral deposit found in the said province of the Lipes, whose veins are no thicker than a finger, although some loose pockets of medium-sized stones of four, six, and more pounds are sometimes found. In the same mineral deposit one also finds alum stone, and the Indians who extract the copaquira affirm that upon deepening the veins two fathoms, they find rock salt of a very white and transparent kind.

This stone appears in all its properties to be the true copperas, or Roman Vitriol, which Doctor Laguna describes for us. It is so prized that it is not only distributed throughout all the Indies, but great quantities are also sent to Europe. Its temperament is so...

it is felt that it reaches the fourth degree, with dry and altering properties, and its effects are most admirable. Because when its powders are applied to any cancerous or pestilential sore, however horrible they may be, they consume the malice, correcting the humors, drying them out, and cleansing the wound in such a way that afterwards with any cleansing medicine it fills with flesh and heals easily. And if this stone is burned, its powders cleanse gently, promote new flesh, and even cicatrize with moderate drying. Beyond this, the powders of this stone unburned, mixed with tallow from a male animal, and applied to a painful tooth, remove the pain. And likewise applying this medicine to any tumor it dissolves it. Finally, a cautery is made from its powders that eats away superfluous flesh and kills it without much pain.

Chapter 25. On the Haquimasi.

The stone called in Peru Haquimasi resembles in some way what Dioscorides calls Budaypea, although it is whiter and without those small protuberances shaped like acorns with which the Judaic stone forms certain points. This stone is found in great abundance in many parts of Peru, because it is common there, and the Indians recognize it easily: running through it are many small fine wavy veins, somewhat split. The Indians use it

History of the New World.

Ground stone, taken in water or in chicha, serves to stop loose bowels and the excessive bleeding that occurs in women after childbirth, or on account of excess menstruation. It is also useful taken in the same way against blood that passes through the urine. Beyond this, its powders applied to fresh wounds have the power to close and dry them. Taken with the powders of bezoar stone and of contrajerva in orange-blossom water, they work against poison, heart ailments, melancholy, and all contagious illness, and thus the Indians of Peru use them. Furthermore, these powders ground very fine and taken on an empty stomach with a little wine and the juice of limes or small lemons dissolve stones in the bladder and kidneys; and mixed with those of the herb called chapichapi, which will be discussed later, they have the power to clean and smooth the teeth. Finally, there are many other cures performed with the powders of this stone, mixed with egg whites and applied from twenty-four to twenty-four hours, at night, to swollen parts of the head, or to recent tumors, and to the very great pains in it, and a great lack of sense — all these ailments are relieved with ease.

The Indians of Peru call corauari a green stone, which the Indians of the province of the Lipez bring

Chapter 29. On the Bezoar Stone.

The bezoar stone is formed from layers, or rinds, like the husks of acorns, one upon another; of which the outermost is very smooth and lustrous. These stones are found in different sizes, from as small as chickpeas up to the size of a hen's egg; and some (though rare) as large as a fist, weighing one pound or more. The shape they take is highly varied; for some are round, others oval, and flat, and of as many different forms as the pebbles of rivers. They likewise differ in color; some are found black, others brown, whitish, ash-colored, golden-blonde, olive-colored more or less dark, and eggplant-colored: and those most prized and considered most perfect are those of an olive color, or the color of an unripe eggplant. Among the Western Indians, and especially in the kingdom of Peru, where these stones are most widely used, they form in the stomach of three species of animals, all of which are ruminants: namely the vicuña, the deer, and the llama, or sheep of the land. The stones produced by vicuñas are held in the highest esteem, next come those of the deer, and lastly those of the llamas and guanacos; whose stones are very small, and tend toward a black color with some golden speckles. Usually one finds in the stomach of each of these animals one or more stones, and in some

History of the New World

...twos, birds, fours, and more. And it is indeed true that in all
animals of each species, bezoar stones are always found; because it sometimes happens that of as many as are killed, one finds no more than one or two of them.

Regarding the cause of these stones forming in the stomachs
of the aforementioned animals, I find great variety among the authors
who have written on this subject: I will say what I think, setting
aside the opinions of others. Two causes, primarily,
are those that contribute to the formation of these
stones: the one, which we may call the material cause, is the healthful
plant matter the animals eat, not as ordinary fodder,
but as medicine and antidote against venom, when
they find themselves wounded or harmed by something that aggravates
and distresses their stomachs. The other, which is the efficient cause, is the
natural constitution of the animals themselves. And what persuades
me that such an herb is the material cause of their production
is that the very same animals that produce them in some
lands do not produce them in others; and this occurs not in lands far
apart, but within the same province, as we
have experienced in the province of the Collao, which being
all of the same climate and weather, in some parts
a great quantity of bezoar stones is found, as in the
district of the Pacajes; and in other parts very few, and in
still other parts, none at all; even though the animals that produce them
are raised throughout all the Collao, and indeed throughout all of Peru.

Part One, Book 3. 171

If bezoar stones are generated from the herb that they call by that name, wherever the same pastures are found, one would expect to find the bezoar stones equally; which we do not see to be the case. And what I say here is also the opinion of the Indians themselves, paying attention to which herb it is that the bezoar animals eat, saying that a medium-sized shrub two or three feet tall called Tola in the Quechua language, and Sopo in another tongue, which is well known to all, is said to be a medicine and beneficial for this kind of livestock. And when we ask the Indians from some land where these stones are not produced for bezoar stones, they answer us that there are none there, because there is no Tola in that land. Whether they are right or not that this is the herb from which the bezoar stones are generated, I will not undertake to determine; but experience greatly supports it, for in all the places where Tola is found in abundance, many bezoar stones are produced, and where the herb does not grow, none are found.

The second point, that the natural constitution of the animal plays a part in generating these stones, I hold to be very certain and beyond doubt. Because we see that apart from the vicunas and the other animals mentioned, no other creature produces them, not even those that are native to this land, nor those brought from Castile, it being very probable that they sometimes eat the same herb. In this way it is proved that the constitution and nature of the animal greatly aids in the formation of the stones through the virtue that they possess; which does not appear to be solely

History of the New World

The question is whether the herb from which they are formed matters; because when it and this had very great virtue, it being broken down in the animal's stomach, and being converted into another substance, as it is converted, it would have to lose it, or at least a great part of it. And so it occurred to me that the virtue and faculty that bezoar stones have come to them from the herb from which they are formed, and from what the animal communicates to them, which with its virtue and natural heat was the efficient cause of their production.

The principle and foundation upon which all bezoar stones are formed, large and small, is whatever the animal feels irritating or troubling its stomach; that which has wounded it, or what it happened to eat mixed in with the grass it grazes upon. And so when we break apart these stones, we find inside them, beneath the outermost layer, some hairs, straws, little stones; some thorn, or piece of a branch, or some other similar thing. For all brute animals being guided by the instinct given them by the Author of Nature toward what can help or harm them, as soon as the animal that produces bezoar stones feels itself wounded or inwardly hurt, it seeks a remedy for its ailment in some herb that counteracts all poison, which it knows, and from which it usually benefits in its times of need, eating of it; and it is from this that bezoar stones acquire, being formed from such herb, the property of being antidotes to poisons. Which herb, when eaten, comes to

what wounds the stomach of the animal, wrapping around it and embracing it thus; and as it hardens with the warmth of the stomach, it comes to form the hook, or first layer of the stone; and as the animal goes on enduring more and more hardship; and as the healing herb works, layers form one upon another, until the stone reaches its full size, at which point the animal dies, and the hunters kill it.

I do not wish to fail to record here the memory of the most strange and remarkable bezoar stone that has been found in Peru since the Spaniards discovered those lands; which was sold in the town of Potosí for two hundred and fifty pesos; and it was acquired by don Pedro Sorelo de Ulloa, who was the magistrate of that town, and acting governor of the kingdom of Chile: the stone was about one span in length, and was as thick through the middle as a hen's egg; and it had running lengthwise through it a piece of an arrow, in such a manner that on one side the arrowhead protruded, which was made of bone in the shape of a harpoon; and on the other side a piece of the same arrow. This caused very great wonder, considering that for the arrow to have entered the stomach of the animal, where this stone formed around the piece that remained inside, it must necessarily have broken it into a great quantity; and that despite all this the animal did not die, but rather, finding itself wounded, proceeded to w

of the healthy and medicinal herb, with which it so prevailed over the piece of earth that it had in its stomach, this bezoar stone so rare and admirable. Of no less marvelous origin I have news, affirmed to me by a trustworthy friar who saw it alive, which had at its center, beneath the first layer, a musket ball, over which the bezoar stone had formed.

Not a few have doubted whether these bezoar stones from Peru have such great virtue against poisons and other ailments, as is publicly claimed of them; for which reason it seemed good to me to record here an experiment performed by the viceroy of these lands, who was at that time governor of the province of Chucuito around the year sixteen hundred and some days, and what he did was take two equal chickens, and gave to each one an equal quantity of corrosive sublimate, and then made one of them drink powders of bezoar stone, of which that one survived, and the other soon died, upon whom the antidote had not been administered. By this experiment it was clearly shown how certain is the virtue of these bezoar stones; which, when good, serve as antidotes against all poisons, whether from the bites of vipers or other animals; and against typhus and plague-buboes. They also serve against all melancholy and afflictions of the heart, and for all pestilential fevers; and their powders are applied in poultices and cordials. And beyond this, whenever needed, no

The most remarkable stone of all those that have come to my attention is the one we call the coconut of Paraguay: it has been given this

the Spaniards named them for having the shape of a gourd, and they grow in the

inside; they grow beneath the earth, and because

and the pores of the shell tighten in such a way that the air
enclosed within cannot communicate with that
outside, it is inevitable that as it warms or cools with

alteration it receives within itself, it causes the shell of
the stone, or coco, to burst; even though it is so hard and strong, because

It would do the same even if it were harder than diamond. For when this stone bursts from beneath the ground, it flies out with such force and impulse that it breaks into two or three pieces, making a report louder than that of a musket; at the sound of which the Indians come running to find the stone, which they recognize by it.

These stones are greatly prized, and even more so when a large piece is found from which a drinking vessel can be made; for a whole one has never been found intact: and when they burst they tend to yield the greater part of the vessel whole; which can be presented to any great lord; and for this reason alone the inhabitants of Paraguay prize and seek out these stones so much: I saw one that had been worked only slightly at the foot to serve as a base, which was taken to the Kingdom of Peru in the year sixteen hundred and seven to be presented to the Pope, and it was a piece that well deserved to be placed in the hands of so great a monarch; which he esteemed greatly for its great antiquity. They say that these stones have the virtue, when one drinks from them, of relieving melancholy and sadness in a man; beyond this, the powders of these precious stones, given to drink in orange-blossom water, in addition to the effects already mentioned, are good against heart ailments, or epilepsy; and drunk with spirits, they have the power to restore the vital spirits.

Chapter 31: On Emeralds.

The finest emeralds that have been found in America are those from the province of Puerto Viejo, in the diocese of Quito, which fell outside the domain of the Inca kings of Peru. It was on account of these stones that the first Spaniards who came to the conquest of that kingdom gave the name "Province of the Emeralds" to that land. However, these were very few, because the mine from which the Indians extracted those that the Spaniards found on them and with which they adorned themselves has not been discovered to this day — although being barbarians, they knew and prized these rich stones for their beauty and brilliance. The land most abundant in them, and which has flooded the world with them and caused them to lose much of the value and esteem that people held them in when they were rare, is the New Kingdom of Granada, where there is a mine of perfect and excellent emeralds that has been worked for many years, from which are taken those that are sent to Spain and distributed throughout all these Indies.

These imperfect stones are somewhat whitish, and not as smooth and transparent as the fine ones; which shows that this imperfect emerald is so either because it has not yet reached perfection, or because of a defect in the material, which the natural agent did not find sufficiently pure and ready in that place. Among the imperfect and common ones, some come closer than others to the quality of the perfect and precious ones. But the entire vein, composed of both types, shows a continuous line within the rock in which it is embedded, rather than merely adjoining it.

Those he found there: which his Indians extracted and made use of in the same ways as we do. Had they not been so lacking in instruments for the purpose, they would have valued the pearls more, but they burned them with saltpeter, and they came out dark and scorched.

The pearls grew in certain sea shells called hiifas, shaped like olmones, about as large as a hand, a little more or less, and nearly round. On the side where one shell joins the other, as with olmones, there is something like a hinge or pivot, by which the creature that is born and lives inside opens and closes; it extends outward from where they are attached, clinging to the rocks, and sea urchins, which are a dark, clayish mass, as thick as a finger of the hand, serve to pry them loose. The outer surface of the pearl oysters is rough and coarse, covered with a kind of bark or dark crust like the olmones, while the inside is smooth and white, with a luster somewhat harder than nacre, tending toward a sky-blue color — a fine thing in a rough stone — and the lustrous dark exterior, once removed, leaves them as smooth and lustrous as the inside, and almost transparent. From them very fine spoons are made, which we call nacre spoons, and which the black pearl divers sell — a small privilege their masters allow them to ease the excessive toil they endure in that occupation. Although the flesh of the creature found inside these shells is tender and whiter than

that of the ohtones is not as good a food as they are, and the other kinds of seafood. Pearls grow embedded in the flesh of the oysters like knots in a board, and upon opening them one can tell whether they contain any or not, because not all of them do.

Pearls differ greatly from one another in size, shape, color, and luster; and sometimes two are found together, lodged in the same shell; and when they happen to find many of great value, the divers go down for them from four to twelve fathoms deep, and although there may be more at greater depth, they cannot be retrieved. On the coast of Panama some are known to surface and remain stranded on sandbars, owing to the very large tides and currents; and at such times the oysters open to receive the rays of the sun, as I myself have witnessed. Since the Spanish began the pearl fishery in these Indies, it is carried out in the North Sea along the entire coast of the provinces of Santa Marta and Venezuela, and in the South Sea along the coast of Tierra Firme and the Pearl Islands. It is a great and important enterprise above all for the residents of the Río de la Hacha and of Margarita; it is a rich and substantial trade, but one that requires men of means, for whoever undertakes it must outfit the venture with twenty or thirty slave divers and two or three salaried Spaniards — one to serve as steward and overseer of the fishermen, keeping account of what is brought up, and another to serve as coxswain and to pilot the vessel. Chapter 33. On other precious stones, of various colors, and virtues found in these Indies.

By precious stones I understand all those that are clear and shining, although many of them are not held in such high price by name, such as crystal, topaz, garnet, and others of this kind. Some are of the opinion that crystal is formed from water alone, frozen by excessive cold without any mixture of earth; which, if it were true, one would have to find in these Indies a greater supply of crystal than in any other part of the world, because there are lands so cold that they are always covered by many fathoms of snow, and where plains are discovered and caverns, and where it never rains water in its proper form, but rather when it falls upon the earth it is congealed into hail and snow. And I believe that those who held this opinion were led to it by seeing that crystal mines are ordinarily found in very cold places and lands, where that which is found in these Indies also occurs.

But I hold it as most probable that crystal, like the other transparent and clear stones, is produced like the others with a mixture of some portion of very clean and purified earth. Chapter 34. On Metals.

In such a manner did the sovereign Creator enrich and make fruitful our common mother the earth, that not only does she produce upon her surface innumerable kinds of herbs and plants for the nourishment of men and animals, but also within her bowels and deepest recesses she holds a great variety of metals, all ordered for the benefit of human life. For some are used by men to cure their illnesses, others to defend themselves from their enemies; others for vessels and all manner of tools and instruments that human ingenuity has invented; and others finally for the adornment and elegance of their persons and dwellings. Seven are the different species into which all kinds of metals are divided, namely: gold, silver, quicksilver, copper, iron, tin, and lead. In the formation of each one of these, its corresponding planet exerts its influence, communicating its force and affinity to each one or that metal with which it has the most analogy and affinity.

History of the New World.

Gold receives from the sun all the good qualities it possesses; over silver, the moon predominates. Mercury, whose nature is unstable and changeable, has special care over quicksilver, and thus both are restless and inconstant. Venus governs copper; Mars governs iron; Jupiter governs tin; and finally, heavy and cold Saturn governs lead.

Metals are generally born in rough, sterile, unfruitful lands; in gloomy, uninhabitable climates. Yet the greed for gold and silver populates them and makes them pleasant and well-supplied. But in lands of good climate, abundant in provisions, minerals are rarely found. The author of nature distributes his gifts in such a way that, by exchanging their riches and products with one another, all may be enriched and supplied. Although it is true that there are also pleasant, healthy, and abundant places that also produce metals, these are very few in comparison with the great wealth produced by the sterile and rugged lands. Because the greater part of the West Indies has the most favorable conditions for the generation of minerals, they are found there in much greater quantity than in other regions; particularly in the Kingdom of Peru, whose rugged mountains and desolate moors are all the more abundant in metals the more sterile they are and the more lacking in the fruits necessary for the sustenance of men and animals. And this is principally because the wisdom of the eternal Lord has seen fit to grant to rest

First part, book 3.
to enrich so much those remote lands, populated by barbarous and idolatrous peoples, so that by drawing in and bringing along barbarous men, and in the process civilizing them into proper society according to their customs and ways, and ordering them to receive the true religion of the true God, which they had been ignorant of: which is so greatly true that the manifest experience of it requires no further proof. For we see that the most remote provinces, of the harshest and most rigorous climate of that kingdom, which are those included in the district of the Royal Audiencia de los Charcas, surrounded by settlements populated by Spaniards, and supplied with whatever provisions are needed for their sustenance, along with the peoples, and especially the incomparable wealth of mines found therein, principally those of the famous hill of Potosí and the town of Oruro; whose territories, among the most barren and rugged of Peru, have not only been settled by Spaniards, but who, on occasion of providing labor for the mines, have devoted many of themselves to agriculture, and have founded very large and productive estates, not only in lands inhabited by Indians, but in many valleys that they have opened up, which were previously uninhabitable wastelands. So that the provisions, flour, meats, wine, timber, and other produce that used to be brought to Potosí from distant places, a hundred, two hundred, or more leagues away, are now so abundantly supplied from the surrounding valleys that from them the city is provisioned with victuals.

The gold that is found pure would be in hills and hillsides of earth, buried within it, and not as some think in veins attached to rocks, from which they wish to deduce that it was scattered and dragged there by the rays of the sun: as if, were that the case, wherever gold is found underground, one would only need to dig deeper to strike the vein; but it was not so, because in the province of Carabaya, at two hundred leagues distant, it lay scattered within the earth of certain hills whose foundation from top to bottom reaches some forty fathoms in depth, being bare earth, in which no veins of gold are found, nor any trace of them. And another reason is that the gold of mines was never found in veins, but rather in small pieces or nuggets, scattered and embedded in the rocks, and cannot be extracted from them except after being ground and turned to powder, mixing the metal with mercury to aid the process, which by its power separates it from the dross. And what is understood from this is that all the gold found in rivers derives from the hills and hillsides in which it lies buried; from there the rains come with their force and the rush of the current carries it away, already loosened from the earth and sand, and bears it downward; for which reason it is usually found in great quantity in the streams that descend from the mountains, not...

The mines of pure gold in dust and nuggets are called Lavaderos (washing places), because the earth in which it has settled is washed out, without any other processing than carrying it away from there. Those who wash gold in this manner are ordinarily slaves of the mine owners, although in the early days Indians were the ones who did the washing. Each person extracts some two or three grains of gold per day.

In many other lands there are abundant mines and gold-washing sites, but no extraction takes place for lack of workers. The Indians of Peru call gold Cori in Quechua, and Chique in Aymara.

Chapter 37. On Silver.

Although gold is so excellent and precious that by quantity it far exceeds in value a great deal of silver, nevertheless the greatest wealth extracted from these Indies at present consists principally in silver, because the silver mines are far more numerous and incomparably more abundant than those of gold: for what is extracted each year from this metal, with all the wealth that comes from it, amounts to only a tenth part of the value that results from silver; because this exceeds twelve million pesos, and at most one million in gold, more or less, throughout all of America. The Indians had knowledge of and use of

History of the New World

Silver was used primarily among the Peruvians, and was so common among them that nobles and commoners alike had many pieces, vessels, and jewelry of silver, and they even combined it with other metals — the place that silver now holds suits it well, ranking it above all others except gold.

It is ordinarily found in rough and barren lands, in cold high plains, in hills, ridges, and snowy mountain ranges, in rocky, scrubby, and rugged terrain, and some also in small hillocks and flat ground. Ordinarily more so in iron-bearing and humid areas than in lowlands, being farther from water. Ordinarily all the mining hills are barren of trees, not entirely of earth nor of bare rock, but partly of earth and partly of stone, of reddish, brown, or whitish color; those that have some of these characteristics are called by miners hills of good cloth, because mines are usually found in them. All the cold lands, mountain ranges, and highlands of Peru are paved with silver, for there is scarcely a hill anywhere that does not contain it in some quantity, large or small. From now until the end of the world, the inhabitants will not lack for mines to work. New ones are discovered every day, and so many are worked, that despite the great attention given at the time to the extraordinary wealth of Peru after it was discovered, the silver then extracted was not even a quarter of what is extracted today.

Silver is the opposite of gold, for the greater part of what is found is pure, perfect, and refined, as if it were

First Part. Book 3.

As stated in the preceding chapter, pure and clean silver is so rare that no great account is made of it, and most of what is extracted comes from ore. Even so, some clean and refined silver is occasionally found that requires no processing, which is called hammered silver. To separate it from the earth and dross with which it is mixed, nothing more is needed than to shake it and give it a few blows with a hammer. Most of the time it appears like frost, and other times it is wrapped in the manner of a thin thread of fine silver, coiling around many turns as if it had been wound through it, passing through many parts. Likewise, large and small points of perfect and pure silver are found embedded and clustered within the very same stones. Other pieces of silver are found the size of a hand, in the form of plumes, and others that look like nothing so much as a honeycomb after the honey has been removed, and I found there, along with many other shapes, many that I myself have seen. This hammered silver is not found in fixed veins, but rather in loose formations within the earth and low-grade ore of the mines.

The silver that is born in mineral deposits incorporated within rocks, although it is all one and the same, when it comes to refining and improving it, yields its full grade; and it is worthy of wonder to see how many are the ores in which it is produced. For some are black, others yellow, brown, chestnut-colored, ruddy, and of every color; some extremely hard and famously flinty, and others soft, tender, and very brittle. Some are smooth and sticky, and others on the contrary dry, clean, and crumbly. Some minerals are lustrous, others [illegible], others [illegible], and others have [illegible]

that the metal is stone, and in parts as hard or harder than the building stone of a house, and it differs from it so much in color and other properties that any miner could distinguish it. Wherever fixed veins are discovered, it is certain that others lie nearby, because they are born from one another, like branches of a tree. And not infrequently, when two veins are encountered at great depth, which at the surface had been very far apart, one is found to have merged with the other, or to have given out, each continuing on its own course — which tends to cause miners many disputes. Some veins emerge above the ground, raising up a crag or ridge of the same thickness, and yield good metal, just as what lies deep within. Others are covered by one fathom more or less, and these are called capped veins. Some have their richness near the surface of the earth and as they go deeper they thin out and are lost, already much diminished in grade. These are called head mines. Others — and these are the hardest — yield rich metal at thirty and forty fathoms depth, even though at the surface they may appear poor.

The mines that run shallow, along the openings of the earth, are usually worked by open-cut, making a trench the width of the vein. Although these are very few compared to those that descend into the abyss, which are the most difficult to work, because as one follows the metals, the earth must be broken and drilled

First Part. Book 3.
up to where it meets with no more than the concavity and width of what the vein carries; and if it is so narrow that a person cannot fit through the opening left for working, part of the wall-rock is broken away. The rock that lies across from it they call "cajas" [wall-rock], which commonly contains no silver. Going deep into the mines, they set up supports at intervals so that the walls do not give way, and these supports are pieces of the hardest wood they leave unbroken, so that they serve them as props. They reinforce the ore body as the mine progresses, making recesses, which are dry-stone walls from one side to the other, as bracing against the force of the mine.
The tools with which they break and extract the ores are iron bars of thirty to forty pounds in weight, tipped with steel; they also use certain chisels or long nails, about a third of a vara more or less, likewise steel-tipped, which they call "fámulos," with which, together with a hammer, they dislodge the ore that remains stuck to the walls, which they call "respaldos"; and they also shape the chimneys. When ore so hard is encountered that the bars cannot break it, they use wedges, and a mallet, or hardwood. When the vein is worked straight down, plumb toward the bottom, it is called "labor de apoyo"; and if it is worked level, that is, directly in front of the worker, it is called "labor de frontón"; a chimney that goes straight upward is called so; and one that goes at an angle, like a millstone groove, they call "labor de chiflón." Such difficulties...

The most useful of all these works is that of the chimney shaft, because it rises perpendicularly, and has platforms built along its way, or barbacoas, where the drilling workers climb up to work.
In the main ore-bodies of many hills they cut passages called socavones that run through the veins, and through them one enters to cross into the mines, and extracts the metals; of which the owner of the socavon takes a certain portion, when it is used to cross into the mines of others.
These socavones are passages cut through the hills at level grade, going in straight, like a street, more than one man's height tall, and two varas wide: they are cut through solid rock, and go into the innards of a hill two hundred paces and more, as was said above; when they are very long, air-shafts are made in them, because without these the candles go out inside, and the men run short of air: the making of one of the longest socavones, when it is cut through rock, can cost from twenty to thirty thousand pesos; and it happens that after a miner has spent all that money, he gets nothing of value from it.
In these socavones and in the deep mines, one does not feel the storms of heaven with their thunder and lightning; for which reason miners usually take shelter in them as a safe refuge in such storms. When the mines are deep and go straight down, one descends into them by means of ladders made of leather ropes.

First Part, Book 3.

degree with two crossbars, and steps of wood; each ladder has three ropes, two on the sides, and one in the middle: they are wide enough that two or three persons can descend and ascend at the same time. These ladders with bars, poles, and rungs are called collapos, ayerali, and other names in the local tongue, of many states in depth.

The hills are riddled and full of holes, like caves and lairs of wild beasts, which descend to the depths of the abyss, one hundred, two hundred, and more fathoms deep: where those who work cutting and processing the metals never come out whether it is day or night, lighting themselves with tallow candles, never ceasing that labor, relieving one another so that some may rest while others work. They endure incredible hardship and fatigue; because beyond never breathing the pure, clean air that exists above the surface of the earth, what goes down is heavy with the smoke of candles, and the foul vapors that the minerals exhale, which tend to harm them and are dangerous, since some come from sulfur stone and vitriol: the fatigue of breaking rocks with such heavy iron crowbars is very great, and carrying the metals such long distances up such dangerous ladders, that merely gripping and holding onto them is work enough for a short man, let alone carrying two or three arrobas of weight on one's back, and a candle in hand to light the way

was ordinary, and the walls of the mine would collapse, and from

Once the metals are brought to the surface, they are placed in small
enclosures, which are made at the mouth of the mine, in the manner of troughs,
which they call canchos; and there in the sunlight they go about
breaking them with a hammer, and sorting, and separating those that
are of the ore veins, from the useless stones. All the work
comes back to breaking them apart, and drawing from the deep recesses of
the earth the rough metals, and crude stones; in which is found

Chapter 38. On the processing of silver by
smelting.

From the mines the ores are carried in llama trains,

First Part, Book 3.

Those that we call llamas of the land, when they arrive to benefit their plant, some are processed with mercury and others by smelting. The processing with fire is of two kinds: one in Guayrás, and the other in reverberatory furnaces. Only the richest ores are purified in this way, since the others are too base, and if they are mixed with some alloy that makes them profitable and combined. And there are ores among them so porous but coarse, that they often yield fifty pesos, a hundred, or two hundred per hundredweight.

To smelt them, they are placed on hillsides and slopes, where the winds blow most strongly, in large clay braziers called guayrás, with burning charcoal and the ore inside; and as they melt, the fire consumes the slag and purifies the silver. Everything that the Indians of Peru extracted in ancient times was done by this method of smelting, because they never knew any other process; and in this way they made use without trouble of the very rich ores. And for many years the Spaniards used no other process there, until it was that during the viceroyalty of Don Francisco de Toledo the mercury amalgamation method was introduced.

The reverberatory smelting is done by placing the ores in furnaces shaped like bread ovens, except that the opening through which the fire is fed is no more than half a man's height from the floor of the furnace, and built into it is a small enclosed firebox where the firewood is placed and lit, whose flame, entering through the mouth of the furnace, strikes the entire vault and ceiling; and by this heat the ores are melted within it.

History of the New World

comes out from below the flame - in front of the opening the furnace has another very small one, from which begins the chimney, which rises somewhat higher than the furnace, through which the smoke exits. Outside of these two openings everything else must be sealed on all sides while it burns. Its floor, very firmly made, the part below beaten with a tamper hardening the metal, and it sinks through it, and for this reason they make it of a mixture of burnt and ground timbers, charcoal, and sand. This they press and pack down with an iron hammer, and for each furnace load, or metal smelting, a new floor is made.

They place many metals into this furnace just as they take them from the mine without grinding them, which are stones and pebbles of about one or two fists in size, larger and smaller, and each furnace load usually holds fifty quintals. They give it fire without ceasing for forty hours more or less. The wood that burns is small brushwood, which raises a great flame. With the force of the fire they are broken down and melted, the metal stones, in such a way that they are converted into a liquid the color of fire, as fluid and porous as when honey is highly purified for making sugar. It raises a foam in the manner that any kind of liquid does when it boils, about a finger's width in thickness, more or less. When this mass is entirely melted, the metals separate from one another, each taking the place that its nature demands, so that the silver and lead mixed together sink to the bottom, and above them

contained the tin, and above and on top of all, the least heavy ones float together with the other mixtures from various metals, such as copperas, sulfur, and other various compounds that are incorporated within the metals themselves.

When they are already well melted, in such a way that one can stir and turn them with a thick iron rod — set there as a stone to break them apart — an opening is made on one side of the furnace level with the surface of the metals, a small mouth through which there exits and flows for a good distance, after falling to the ground, the metal from above, which contains no silver, but is entirely slag and a mixture of various metals. And this opening or gap is scraped downward until the refiners can see that all the slag has come out — in which matter they have such great skill that if a single drop of silver should begin to come out mixed with the slag, they recognize it and stop it. This slag that rises to the top of the molten metal is tough and black, with a slight reddish tinge; and upon cooling, which happens very quickly, it becomes so glassy that it breaks easily, and is heavy and shiny. Once the slag has been removed in this way, they attend to the silver metal, which is still mixed with lead and other compounds, and they draw it out in the same manner as the slag, opening the mouth of the furnace down to its floor, through which it flows out melted and falls to the ground. After it has come out it retains the smell of lead, and

History of the New World

The miners call this metal from the first smelting "crude": from this crude metal there comes out, from six to ten quintals out of the hundred that were put into the furnace, and the rest was lost to smoke and slag.

In the second smelting and fusion they load the furnace with another fifty quintals of crude metal: which amounts to five or six batches from the first: and they smelt this second batch in the same manner as the first, and those who do it give it fire for no more than thirty hours, more or less: after it is well melted, the chiuia is drawn off as in the first time; which is of the same color and qualities as the first, except that it somewhat resembles tin in color. This second fusion they call adulterating the crude metal: from it a sheet is extracted composed of lead and silver with very little ore and slag. The less lead it contains, the more silver it has, and vice versa. To then separate the silver from the lead, and finish purifying it, a third smelting or fusion is given, for a period of twelve hours more or less, according to what the metal requires: which metal is smelted in the third and final smelting in a furnace somewhat smaller than the first, of the same shape: and when everything is well melted, a small crack and opening is made in the furnace, through which flows

First Part, Book 3.
the slag, and so that it all comes out, and the silver remains clean and refined; and on the other side of the furnace, opposite the opening where the slag comes out, some bellows are placed, and because the wind blows out the lead, which from one side with some slag moves like foam, floating on top of the silver; in the same way that when we drink we must blow away the foam from the wine. The slag that comes out of this third smelting they call greta, which contains two of every three parts of lead, which afterward with a little treatment is refined and purified. Once removed, what remains on the floor of the furnace is the silver, clean and refined to full assay.
With this process, the silver that is contained in all kinds of ores — rich, poor, coarse, and hard — is given its value, without losing a whit. And in order that they melt and flow easily, care is taken to mix with the ores a seventieth part of what is a lead-like metal; which, although it tends to be poor and of low grade, still serves mixed in with the others to make them run. The quantity of silver extracted by this process varies depending on whether the ores are rich or poor. From a single furnace load at the smelting works that I was able to observe in Oruro in the year sixteen hundred and six or eight, in which entered a considerable quantity from the first melt and smelting, amounting to some fifty quintals, that is to say two hundred and fifty of crude ore, there were extracted six hundred and fifty marks of silver.

History of the New World

Of pure silver. The ores from which silver was extracted were chaplato, broche, and negrillo; the latter was very rich, but harder to work, as all negrillos are. And the poroche was so poor that when refined, it yielded barely a pestle per quintal in the smelting process that I describe — one fifth of the negrillo ore; and the other four parts went to poroche. And although in terms of noise and labor the smelting process is similar to that using mercury, since it is not necessary to grind the ores, they weigh the same without mercury: even so it has its drawbacks, and the profit is not very great; since it is necessary to rebuild the furnaces almost entirely for each smelting, and so much firewood is consumed, that a refiner in Oruro certified to me that he spent six thousand pesos on firewood each year; and that those who made a profit from it earned one hundred pesos per week.

Chapter 39. On the mercury refining process.

The mercury refining process yields much greater wealth than smelting, because it is more abundant and universal; through it all the silver is extracted from the ores however low-grade and poor they may be. When the ore yields two ounces or more per quintal, a profit can be made from refining it; and below this there is very little or no profit, particularly in the mining settlements that do not have assigned Indians under royal warrant and repartimiento, or mita as they call it in Peru. A reasonable yield is four ounces; and those that yield

First part, book 3.

From this point upward they are considered rich metals, and the more they yield, the richer they are. When I was living in Oruro in the year sixteen hundred and eighteen, many ores were being processed at eight ounces per quintal; and some of the richest yielded as much as thirty marks per quintal: these were extracted in small quantities from very narrow veins. The greatest richness that has been drawn from the said mines of Oruro has been half silver, so that from one quintal of metal it has happened that twenty marks of pure, clean silver were obtained. At other times metals have been found that yielded a third, or a quarter part silver; and more commonly one comes across two, three, and four marks. But the most common are those of about four ounces per quintal, more or less.

In order for the mercury to bond with and separate the silver from the waste, the ores are first ground in certain mills, or water-driven mills in the manner of fulling mills, in the following way. The water for one mill is of greater volume than what a single millstone requires; it strikes with a drop of thirty to forty feet, and thus rushes with great force upon the wheel, which is set up like that of a fulling mill, and is so large that it measures twenty-two feet in diameter if it has one axle-head, and twenty-six if it has two; and because a very thick beam is called a single-headed mill, when the axle of it

History of the New World.
A wheel on one side alone raises a row of stamps and grinds; and with two heads, when grinding on both sides, each one raising its own row of stamps. The number of stamps on each head runs from six to ten. These stamps are made of very hard and heavy wood, squared off to two palms in circumference, and nine to ten feet in length. Each one has at its end an iron striking-plate with which it crushes the ore. One stamp weighs several arrobas, and the largest may weigh four or five, so that each stamp comes to weigh ten or twelve arrobas in total. The stamps are arranged in a row, together and raised upright. They rest upon a great beam called the mortar, which is covered with thick iron plates called tejos. The axle of the wheel lifts these stamps one after another to a height of three or four palms, and as they fall they deliver a terrible blow upon the ore. On each side of the mortar stand two or three Indians who do not stop feeding ore into the mortar while the stamps rise; and even though some of these ores are stones as hard as flint, the heavy blow of the stamps breaks them down and grinds them like flour. A mill of one head can grind in a natural day from one hundred and fifty to two hundred quintals of ore; and double that if the mill has two heads.
Once the ore is ground, they keep it in sieves of thread

First Part. Book 3.

of iron, or of wire, very thin, through which the powder comes out as fine and
delicate as wheat flour sifted through a very fine sieve.
Two or three sieves are used to sift all the metal ground by
a single-head mill; they are placed near the north
with a new adjustment, and a person carries the grains, so that
the dust does not fly through the channel, and it returns to pass through the sieves again.
On top of each sieve there is a hopper like that of a wheat mill,
from which the ground metal falls. All
the powder that comes out of the mortar and sieves is such that those who
work there cover their nostrils with cotton or wool,
and place long leather pouches over their mouths,
so as not to swallow with their breath that powder, which, being composed of
various metals, is very harmful. At the beginning when the silver
refining process with mercury was discovered, a few small mills were built,
which were driven by mules and horses
like millstones: but now all of them in Peru run on water.
Those that stand on the banks of rivers always grind
with the water from them; and where there are no rivers they build large reservoirs

as needed.

It costs two thousand pesos to build a single-head mill;
and if it is a two-head mill, from fifteen to twenty thousand; and to
operate a mill well one needs a steward,
an ore refiner, a carpenter, and up to fifty
Indians, if it is a single-head mill; and one hundred, if it has two heads.
