When the owner of a mill grinds metals belonging to others, the cost for each mill of thirty to forty thousand pesos — this being for a single-head mill — and if it has two heads, sixty thousand. But if he grinds his own metals, combining the costs of the mine work with those of the mill, it comes to double. If the metals are not very poor, but of middling quality, the owner of a two-headed mill saves from twenty to thirty thousand pesos per year, and half that if the mill has only one head. In each mill there is a very large house with many rooms and quarters, both for offices and for lodging all the people who work there, so that each mill looks like a small town.

The sifted powder of the metals is placed in stone-built bins, raised like small granaries, holding about four hundredweight each, with as much water as is needed until it forms a soft mud that can be stirred and kneaded easily. The treatment given to the metals in these bins varies according to their properties. But all of them generally receive salt and mercury; and beyond that, some are also given copper metal, others processed iron, tin, lime, magistral, and other materials. Into each bin, six hundredweight of salt and from one and a half to two hundredweight of mercury are added. In Oruro they further add from two to twenty pounds of tin; and in Potosí they use iron and copper. Once this mixture is made, prepared in the manner described, they turn it over and work it through four to six times, kneading it very well with their feet; and each day lifting

First Part. Book 3.

from four to six passes until the mercury is fully incorporated with the silver: this is achieved through the heat of the sun. For this reason, depending on different times of the year, the process takes more or fewer days, and to check its progress, the refiner tests it several times a day, carrying with him whatever tools he needs. The time commonly spent on this process is from eight to fifteen days. Some mercury is consumed in the process, and the more so the richer the ores are. It is ordinary to lose as much mercury as the pure silver extracted — four to six pounds more or less, depending on the quality of the ores.

After the mercury has been incorporated with the metal, they remove it from the bins and place it in large wooden vats, where it is washed. A pipe of water enters the vat, and as much flows out as enters, carrying with it the finer earthy particles, while the coarser and heavier material sinks to the bottom together with the mercury and silver. The water in the vat is stirred by a paddle shaped like a wheel spoke, which they call a molinete, with arms at the end like a cart wheel, driven by the flow of water. This, with its rapid motion, swirls the metal around and dissolves it, causing the earth and slag to separate, while the mass of mercury and silver settles to the bottom of the vat. Other washing stations are smaller; in them three bins are washed each day, and half a bin is placed in each vat. Those using wheels and running water wash more gently, and each vat takes one bin of metal. To better collect the silver, more mercury is added to the vat while washing the metals. Besides the mass of silver and mercury, three things come out of the vat:

History of the New World

Types of metals called lamas, relave, and relavillo.
The lamas and relavillo are the finest and most delicate parts of the metal, and the water it carries with it runs off as described above. These are collected in large pools, the relavillo in some smaller basins where it settles. There is a channel through which the bars enter the basins. The relave is the coarser metal, like grains. It remains on the floor of the amalgamation vat and on top of the amalgam, and because it comes out very clean and washed, these different types of metals resulting from the washing still retain some silver, and for this reason they are collected to extract it through various processes.

For the relave and relavillo, a person goes along throwing handfuls into the sluices, which are small channels made in the style of gutters lined with coarse cloth or old pieces of fabric. When the water carries the earth through, the amalgam of mercury and silver remains stuck to the cloth, and by gently washing it, it is gathered up.

The lamas are burned in small furnaces made of clay vessels called caperucas, and each furnace holds thirty caperucas. Twenty or more furnaces are placed together in a row, in which two cajones are burned at once. They are fired for six hours, and the mercury that had combined with the lamas is found stuck to the lids of the caperucas. The lamas that come out poorly processed are re-treated in vats with mercury, and the lamas that come out of these are called relamos. Some of these are burned in large reverberatory furnaces, where two fires keep them for two nights and days. They reduce by a quarter, which is the impure material and the mercury that was in them, which the fire consumes; that

First Part. Book 3.

giving them again of re-burned material like ground brick, which they are accustomed to throw into the vats of metal in place of iron, because they clean and dry the metals.
Chapter 40. Of the piñas and bars of silver.

The metal having been washed, and the mercury that has bonded with the silver — which they call pella — separated from the earth and dross: they pour it into coarse linen cloths, and by pressing the pella they beat out a portion of the mercury with blows: because there now remains no other task to be done with the silver than to separate it from its most intimate companion, the mercury. Once pressed in this manner, the pella is left loose and soft, and very similar to the touch of sieved ash or condensed snow. From it they form the piñas, pouring it into molds shaped like pine cones or small sugar loaves, and pressing it into them: the piñas come out of the mold still somewhat soft, because the pella is pliable and soft, with a hole in the middle so that the mercury can escape more easily. For this purpose they place them in small furnaces, each one over its hole, covered with a clay cap made in the shape of a sugar loaf mold or a still: there they apply fire with charcoal, by means of which the mercury exits through a tube like that of an alembic, which the covers have: and each piña uses two arrobas of charcoal to de-mercurize: which, once de-mercurized, is left free and solid, but very spongy, and so much so, if they weigh them, that before de-mercurizing, what it has is no more than one fifth, or thereabouts, of the weight it had with the mercury. Afterward they are given another round of fire to refine them further, re-burning every ten piñas with four arrobas of charcoal, with which the processing of

History of the New World
the silver, and it remains pure and refined, made into ingots of thirty, forty, and more marks each.
From the time the metals are cut from the vein until the silver reaches the perfection we have described, it has so many enemies and thieves — or better said, greedy and eager ones — that by one means or another they take the better part of it, which is astonishing. For the Indians who work in the mine, upon seeing the ore (which they call the rich metal stone) set it aside and steal it; those who carry it out of the mine also cast their eye on the best pieces, and if they can do so safely, they steal them; those who transport it to the mill have the same bad habits. And the Indians who work in the mills do not sleep either: and after the metal is washed and the amalgam extracted, so much is lost through greed, since what is used at that point is a morsel of greater substance and lesser cost. So that when the mine owner comes to collect his silver in the clear, it has already been well skimmed by all those through whose hands it passes; and these thefts are so cleverly concealed up to that point that no loss can be detected in the estate's accounts.
The manner of assaying and taxing the silver is as follows: the owner delivers the ingots to the assayer, who melts them and makes bars; and in order to assay the bars and determine their fineness, he takes from each one a small piece with a steel punch shaped like a fingernail, which according to the ordinance must weigh two tomines, although it always runs over, and the owners make nothing of the excess, given the abundance and richness of the land. That piece, or bit of silver, is brought before the officials, and after purifying and refining it in the fire, and by the weight, and

First Part. Book 3.
shrinkage that the assayers recognize, who are always
very expert silversmiths, the quality of each entire bar, and they mark it
together with the number, running the size of the die across it, from the first one
that is assayed at each mining settlement, where there is
a Royal House, until the last one that is taxed in the same year.
These marks are made with steel punches, in which are cut
the necessary letters and numbers.

The silver from the mines of the king and not of Peru has a standard quality
commonly of two thousand three hundred and eighty maravedis
per mark; and although silver of higher quality is found, and on the contrary
the whole thing causes trouble, extracting it, if not called upon by the Royal
treasury; so that the mark comes to contain two thousand four
hundred maravedis: no more is placed on the bars closer to
two thousand three hundred and eighty, so that those who buy them may have
profit. But when the silver contains less, it is deducted from the two thousand three hundred and eighty mara-
vedis.

After the bars have been assayed by the method described, in order
to pay the King his dues from them, on the days dedicated
for the payment of the royal fifth, which usually falls each week,
the assayer takes what he has assayed to the accounting office,
where the Royal House is located, recording it in a ledger he keeps
for each owner; and with the Royal officials present
in their tribunal, the weighmaster weighs each one, and
states the number, quality, and weight of each. All of which

History of the New World

Two junior officials write together in two ledgers, and having placed in the margin of each entry the name of the owner of the bars, and written their assay marks; each one separately, because they tend to be of different grades, weight, and number; they reduce them to maravedis, and adding up the total value of all of them; one and a half percent is taken out for the fees of the smelter and assayer: and from what remains the fifth is taken; and joining the one with the other, it is collected in the same bars in which the fifth is taken, bringing together the royal officials with the owners, giving and receiving from them the reales that are to be said; each assayed peso being reduced from four hundred and fifty maravedis of the standard in Potosi, and Oruro, where the grace of the fifths applies, to twelve and a half reales; which is the value it has there, and thus the Viceroy Don Francisco de Toledo, because the small coins that are to be said are the fees, and the surplus, that such an assayed peso may hold until it becomes reales.

Having paid the duties to the King, they stamp upon the bars the die and mark that the Royal officials hold in their possession, which are opened in steel in the manner of chisels bearing the Royal arms, which they stamp by force of hammer upon the bars, and these testify that the fifth and other duties have been paid: so that all silver found outside without these marks shall be known as unquinted; and may be seized as forfeit, which is the penalty for those who do not pay the fifth, in accordance with what

First Part, Book 3.
An ordinance made by His Majesty, applied uniformly to the bars, which retain the full value of their assay quality: so that even though they are returned to the owner minus the fees extracted from them in terms of quantity, the greater value and price remain, so that they are equivalent to what was paid to the king in duties.

Chapter 42. On Mercury.

The mercury mines of this kingdom of Peru are held to be of equal importance to those of silver, because these mercury mines serve without being worked, and if some had not been worked, so great a quantity of silver as is now extracted could not have been obtained. In various parts of the Indies, mercury ores have been found, but not rich enough to be profitably processed. Above all, in the town of Huancavelica, in the diocese of Huamanga, the richest deposits of this ore were found, and because they have been worked for many years now, they have yielded endless riches, and for their sake that town was populated, whose residents have no other trade or livelihood than the working of these mines. The hill from which these ores are extracted is adjacent to the town, and in it each miner has built his hut where they process the ores, and there are many groups of Indians who come by mita to work in these mines, and they rotate every two months. Once the ores are removed from the mines to these camps, they are carried from there on trains of llamas or local sheep to the smelting settlements to be stored.

History of the New World

The mining settlement is located about one league, give or take, from the mountain, in the most convenient and sheltered areas, chosen because water was found there in abundance, and close to said place fuel for the smelting works: the discovery of which was the principal cause of all this wealth, because had God not provided such an abundance of ichu grass throughout the surrounding highlands, the mercury ores could not have been processed, since there is no firewood for many leagues around these mines with which to smelt them.

For the processing of this metal, each miner has his own smelting site, with its furnaces and necessary equipment. The method of processing and smelting these metals has changed several times; the one used before the current method was adopted was called de jabetas: whereby the metal, broken into small pieces, was smelted in certain clay pots or vessels. But the present process is much easier, more manageable, and more refined — it consists of placing the metals just as they come from the mine, without breaking them up, into furnaces of a particular design. This method was discovered during the time of the Viceroy, the Count of Chinchon, and its inventor was well rewarded with a generous income granted to him by the Viceroy.

The mercury ore that the Peruvian Indians call llimpi is the finest from which they extract vermilion. And although the Indians made use of llimpi for paint

First Part. Book 3.
themselves, they did not know how to extract copper from it, nor was this metal known throughout this new world until the Spaniards arrived and made it known to the Indians. How the mines were found, and the history they have had up to the present time, we write at length in the second part, in the description of the provinces of the kingdom of Peru.

Chapter 42. On Copper.

There are found greater quantities of copper mines in this kingdom, and in many other parts of the Indies, than of silver or other metals. The Indians extracted it in great quantities in ancient times; for which reason many mines worked long ago can still be seen today. Because as they lacked iron, they forged from this metal their weapons, tools, and instruments for agriculture, and for some other trades; and they made no less use of it in certain medicinal applications. At present, the Spaniards work some of these mines, extracting from them all the copper consumed in the Indies, and some that is sent to Spain. All the copper of the kingdom of Peru is of very fine quality, most notably that which is taken from the province of the city of Los Charcos, and that of the kingdom of Chile, from where all that is spent in the City of Lima is brought, to cast artillery, bells, and for all the other uses it serves, both as instruments and in medicine.

History of the New World

Almost all the copper of the kingdom ordinarily has some mixture of gold, and more than any other metal it is very easy to refine, because at the first smelting it comes out pure and perfect. To process it they place the raw metal in a furnace just as it comes from the mine, often in small pieces, alternating a layer of charcoal and a layer of metal; they then apply fire until it melts, the dross separates and rises to the top, and the copper sinks to the bottom. They draw off all the slag through a channel, and after it the clean copper by itself, which upon falling to the ground and meeting the air forms into large sheets. Only the river metal mines are worked; and from the combined ores one gets a fifth part of pure copper, others a quarter, and those that go to refining get as much as half — these are considered very prosperous. In the New Kingdom of Granada there are mines where pure copper is found already calcined, so that it need not be passed through fire to be refined. The metals from the mines of Paria yield a quarter part of clean, already calcined copper. The Indians of the kingdom call copper in the general language Anca.

Chapter 43. On Iron

It is a remarkable thing that, although the nations of the New World knew the mines of most metals, worked them, and made use of them in many ways, none has been found that had any use of iron or knew of it; nor do we find among the Indians any memory of or name for this metal — even though there are as many mineral deposits of it throughout the mountains as anywhere. In place of iron for their weapons and tools they used wood

First Part. Book 3.
                                                                                    201
wooden beams, of copper, flints, and fish bones, never imagining anything better: and since nothing of such utility can replace arms and other instruments for human life's service so well-suited and perfect as iron, they labored greatly at whatever work they undertook that required strong iron tools.

Their ignorance of the strength and power of iron caused them at first to hold our weapons in contempt, for when fighting hand to hand with the Spaniards in wars, they would grasp the lances and swords as if they were their own clubs and wooden sticks, until they learned at great cost the severity of those arms, as the sharp edges cut their hands, which filled them with as much fear as they had previously had boldness. And after they came to know iron's great usefulness, it is remarkable how well it has come into use not only among Christian and friendly Indians, but also among the heathen who are at war and have learned of it: these latter desire nothing more, and so when they go out to trade, they want nothing in exchange for their goods but knives, scissors, machetes, hatchets, and other iron tools; and when the Spaniards are reluctant to give them these things, they obtain them from the Christian Indians on their borders, with whom they are accustomed to trade.

While a priest was in a province of heathen Indians, into which he had entered out of zeal for their conversion (as he himself told me), he happened to fall into conversation with an Indian who was making arrows with a butcher's knife; and coming to speak of the arms of the Spaniards, and of the

History of the New World
Indians, the barbarian told him; that although it is true that your weapons are stronger than ours, they are still not so well suited for war; because to arm one of your soldiers it takes many men, one to make the arquebus, another the cap, another the powder, and so on with all the other things needed to put it in order. But to arm an Indian, no one else is needed to help him, for see here how quickly I have made arrows enough to fight for a long time; and I myself make the bow and the string. The priest asked him whether, before they had the use of knives, they had made those weapons with the same ease; and the Indian replied that no; and that the use of the knives that the Spaniards had brought them was so beneficial to them; that arrows and weapons which an Indian formerly could not make in a whole week with great effort, he now made with little effort in a single day; from which one can see the harm there is in giving such weapons to warring Indians, because even if they do not immediately fight with them, giving them the instruments with which they can more easily supply themselves with their own causes no less damage.
Although in many parts of America there are many iron mines, the Spaniards have not taken to working them, since it is a commodity that costs less when brought from Spain; and so they prefer to put the labor it would cost them to work iron mines into working those of silver and gold, from which they draw greater wealth. Only in the province of Paraguay have they managed to obtain some iron from which they made wedges for the Indians, but

First part. Book 3.
they have already stopped working it; because they consider it cheaper to
buy the labor from Spain.

Chapter 44. On tin.

Only one tin mine is worked in Peru, and as I am in
formed, no other is known in all the kingdom, but it is so pro
mising that although it has been many years since work began on it, it
promises great duration: it is located in the province of Caranollos, diocese
of Charcas. They manage to extract a thousand quintals of clean tin
per year, which is what is consumed throughout the kingdom
for the uses for which it is needed, such as in the alloy of
bronze for casting artillery and bells; for the many
plates that are made from this metal, and other things; and also
some is carried out of the kingdom, particularly
to New Spain because they have none there.

The mine and metal of tin are very different from the other
minerals of the kingdom; because it is not a fixed vein, but rather
masses, which the miners call mantles; and the raw metal
extracted from it is not rock, but very fine
sand: among it one usually finds silver ore.
Tin is processed in the following manner: once this sand is taken from the mine,
it is washed in a channel made for
this purpose with pools at intervals; where, being heavier,
it settles on top of the metal, and the water carries away

§ 50 The ore. After washing it is left clean without slag: which they cast into some furnaces over burning charcoal, and blowing hard with bellows it melts, and distills through the floor of the furnaces, which is perforated for this purpose. In this mine that I have mentioned there is a water-powered engine that raises the bellows. This metal commonly comes mixed with a quarter part of clean, pure tin; and the richest tends to come in at one third. The Indians in ancient times made very little use of this metal, because they did not know how to alloy it with copper to make bronze, nor did they have the uses for which we employ it, such as the glazing of pottery and others; they call it in the general language of Peru, chayanta.

Chapter 45. On Lead.

Lead is found together with silver, as these two metals are commonly mixed, and for this reason I can truthfully say that wherever there are silver mines, there are also lead mines. And so they usually extract it from the silver ores that are processed by smelting, it being the slag that is finally separated from the silver. There are also many mines of lead alone, which is processed by smelting it by itself; and some are very rich, notably one in the town of Juli, diocese of Chuquiabo, and another in the province of Sonqo, archdiocese of Guamanga. Because of this there is great abundance of lead throughout this entire kingdom; although

First Part. Book 4.

The Indians in their paganism made little use of it, and did not learn to make white lead from it, as the Spaniards do now. The name that lead has in the general language of Peru is titi.

History of the New World: First Part, Book Four.

Chapter 1. On how the native plants of this New World are to be distinguished from those that have been brought from Spain and from other regions.

Among the mixed things composed of corruptible matter and form, the family of plants holds second place in order. This will be treated in this book and in the following ones. Regarding what presents itself here, there is a considerable difficulty, which although it did not arise in the preceding book — where bitumen and animate things were discussed — it does arise in what is to be noted from here forward; which is the need to distinguish the plants that were found in this New World from those that the Spaniards have brought from the lands that settled it, whether from Spain or from other foreign lands. This difficulty arises, first, from the abundance with which these foreign plants have taken hold and spread throughout this land, now growing in many places across the fields and wastelands without any cultivation by men. Wherefore

History of the New World

Some have come to us as strangers or pilgrims, as much as the natives of the land: and regarding the many herbs and other plants that are found in these Indies, which being common and of the same species as those of Spain, one may doubt whether they were found here or were brought to them from others, of which there is no doubt that they came from Europe. To resolve the doubt and clarify this difficulty, two paths present themselves: the first is to see whether the thing in question has its own name in the languages of its native peoples; for since they are so curious and knowledgeable in agriculture and the knowledge of plants, that there is no herb, however small, nor however undesirable it may be, to which they have not given a name, as is natural to this land — it seems a clear indication that any plant which lacks a name among them is not native to the Indies; and on the contrary, that which has a name in their languages is native to here.

To make this as generally true as possible, certain warnings are added: the first is that not every word found with a proper name in the natural language of some Indian nation should straightforwardly be taken as an indication that it is native to the land, as it may be that the Indians gave it such a name based on some resemblance. And the second is that such a word must carry the meaning that properly signifies that name; as we see in this kingdom of Peru, where certain words from the general language are known to have not existed in this land before the Spaniards settled it — such as the word for hen, Atamalpa; for mirror, quilpi; and for shears, quelcani: which words primarily signify other things, for the first signifies an Inca king; the second

First Part. Book 9.

no, any glassy and transparent thing, and the third, to draw.
Therefore, in order to resolve this difficulty, one must look at whether the thing in question has its own proper name in the language of the Indians.
Because since the languages of the native peoples are so many that almost every town speaks its own, and even among those, each one has as many languages as there are factions and lineages living among them; and the topic of which there is doubt; had its name in this land before the Spaniards came to it, in each of its languages its most proper name: and if in other places only a single name is found taken from some Indian language, it is clear evidence that the Indians applied it to it by transference, as can be seen in the three names mentioned, and in many others that could be brought forward to confirm this truth. Sometimes I was led and helped to ascertain some things about which there could be doubt.

The second thing to be noted is that just because one does not find the proper name in the province where one happens to be, it should not therefore be inferred that it did not exist in the Indies: because there are many cases in which the Spaniards have carried things from one province to another within the same Indies, renaming in the lands to which they were transplanted things with the names those same things had in the provinces from which they are native, going by the names of the lands from which they were transplanted — something about which I could bring much evidence here, which I omit to avoid prolixity: where it is to be noted that just as it is not a certain argument to find a given name in one of the languages of the Indians in order to infer that such a thing is native to the Indies, in the same way it is likewise not sufficient proof to affirm

History of the New World

nothing has ever been brought from Spain except the names in our
Spanish language. Because almost all the things proper to the
Indies, apart from the proper names that the natives have in their own
languages, the Spaniards have given the names of
those things with which they bear some resemblance or anal
ogy.

The second path to bringing to light the truth of what
we are discussing is much more reliable than the first;
and it is that at the time the author writes there cannot be more years, not
withstanding that past the first century of the discovery
and conquest of the kingdom, one will not find the clarity in this mat
ter that we see today within our reach. And this is the path
that I have followed in most of the doubts that in the treatise
on plants, and other natural things of the land have arisen
for me. Namely, having informed myself diligently
from ancient persons, both Indians and Spaniards: because of the for
mer I have dealt with and spoken to many who knew the
times of the Inca kings, before the Spaniards discov
ered and settled this kingdom of Peru. For having entered
it at the sixty-eighth year of its discovery
and conquest; and in the city of Lima at the sixty-fourth
year of its founding; I encountered many old Indians, who when
the Spaniards entered the land, were already young men
of age and discernment. For these old Indians have such
knowledge of the things that existed in the land before
the coming of the Spaniards, that when some of them were
questioned they answered me without hesitation, and moreover

First part. Book 4. 205

asking me about the plants, saying: Father, there is no doubt about this, these plants are ours, and you Spaniards brought them, those which we did not know, nor did we have them; in the same manner, before, in the same way they responded about the animals, and about the other things about which I asked them. Beyond this I managed to know and speak with some old Spaniards among the first settlers of the land, and with nearly all the sons of the conquerors; who have such knowledge of the plants and products brought from Spain that they take pride in those which their forebears brought, keeping the information in their memory.

It is worth noting here that since Spaniards commonly give to the plants, fruits, and other natural things of America the names that the Indians of the provinces where they reside had given them; and many of these are general and common throughout all the Indies, it comes from this that one and the same fruit has many different names in various lands; which tends to cause great confusion for those who in Europe read accounts of the natural things of the New World: because it happens that when the same thing is set down in various accounts written in different provinces many times under different names, one who has no knowledge of what I am explaining here will be misled, thinking that things written with different words are distinct things. And this same error is found in matters of greater importance, such as provinces and cities. For I have seen a map made in Europe in which the city of

History of the New World

Chuquiabo had been named twice before under different names, an error I must not fail to point out as I go along, because as it became customary to name that city by three names — which are Chuquiabo, Pueblonuevo, and La Paz — whoever encountered two of them, thinking that each signified a different city, came to make three cities out of one, led astray by the variety of names. This example being set out, one can see how easy it is to fall into the same error in other matters.

In order to remove the occasion and stumbling block of falling into such a mistake for whoever reads this history, we shall observe two or three precautions. The first is that for each plant and animal I shall give a brief description, portraying with the greatest accuracy possible both the parts of the plant and its fruit, so that by the description given for each thing one may distinguish one from another, without being confused and misled by the variety of names that would otherwise lead one astray. In providing this description I shall not trouble myself with determining whether the thing in question is the same as what the ancient authors describe, such as Pliny, Dioscorides, and others, because I judge that endeavor to be beyond reach given the difficulty we find in ascertaining which species of plants those authors are depicting, even though some of them are well known to all. Whoever reads the description I give of each thing

First Part. Book 4.
206

Comparing it with that of the ancient authors, one may settle this matter, having seen what is said of the one and the other.

The second observation is that one and the same plant, in different lands, owing to the various climates thereof, has great diversity within itself in the size of the plant itself, its leaf, and its fruit; in the time of fruiting, and in other qualities. And such diversity is at times so great that it has happened to me almost not to recognize plants I had known, upon seeing them in different lands and climates. For which reason I will describe each plant according to the most common form it takes in this kingdom of Peru.

Every sort of plant is divided among genera or classes: the first in herbs and vegetables, which shall comprise all those plants that complete their course in one year, and whose stalks and branches are tender and not of woody matter; then shrubs and small trees, to which genus belong all those plants that in duration and nature are of hard, woody material comparable to trees, yet do not rise from the ground as high, nor form a trunk as thick and tall as they; and finally, in all the lineages of trees, in whose class fall all those plants that form a tall and strong trunk, whose timbers serve most notably against fire, and are used in the framing of buildings, in the construction of ships, and in other uses of the like kind. Each of the three classes and ranks of plants will have its own book, as follows.

placing in it, in the first class, all the different
kinds of plants and vegetables that were found in the Indies.
The plant that the Indians of Peru call Mallqui —
the use they made of the fruit of all of them was to sustain themselves,
some serving them as bread, others as food, and making from
them their drinks and wines. They ate some green, and

Something that has caused no little wonder, and I am certain
will cause the same in whoever reads this,
is to see that the plants and herbs found across this vast
land that fills Spain
are all wild, and most of them without fruit; and that

The plant and herb most commonly found

First Part. Book 4. 207

In all parts of the world there is the rush, which grows two or ten years on the banks of lagoons, rivers, marshes, and swamps, in many varieties, all of which produce the totora abundantly. The first and largest species of rush is the cattail; the Indians of Peru call it totora, as do the Spaniards; and the Mexicans call it Tale. In the provinces of the Collao that lie along the shores of the great lake of Chucuito, where it grows abundantly, it serves as fodder for cattle, particularly a certain variety of it that is triangular in shape, and whose roots, which are white and tender, the Colla Indians eat; they call this root couri, and they display many bundles of them in the plazas of their towns for this purpose, as they do with other foodstuffs. From the cattail, the Indians of Peru make mats and rafts, not only to cross rivers but also to go out to sea in them; especially from the totora, which they call l'amo, or the large and triangular rush. The ash of the cattail helps them with all flows of blood and to dry wounds. There are many other varieties of rushes; some are shorter and thinner than totora, from which grows a great bulrush in the lake of Mexico, and they serve in that city in place of paper for animals, and they call it there zacate. Others are round, called min min in Peru. Among them are found large and small ones of all the varieties that grow in Spain. The sea rush, so called by the Indians, and by Garcia, has a square stem.

History of the New World

In some places the Indians make curious mats of thin, long rushes, especially in this city of Lima and in the town of Lambayeque, in the diocese of Trujillo. These mats are called here petates, which is a Mexican name; and they make them in all sizes, as rugs are made, and they serve the same purpose as rugs on the pedestals of altars and on the platforms where women sit. They are also placed underneath small rugs, and travelers use them to cover their saddlebags and the loads of their animals, because they protect them from the rain. In short, rush mats are better than those made in New Spain from palm leaves, because they are more durable, and even when folded like a rug they do not break.

In the province of Chachapoyas, in the diocese of Trujillo, there grows in the countryside a species of rush no larger than an asparagus, called in that land sipanti. Although it is always green, it does not give off its scent until split down the middle, at which point it smells as fragrant as a pastille. It is placed among clothes so that they take on its scent. There is also another three-sided rush of aromatic scent, though not very strong, called by the Indians vermilcu or ayaras; swallowed it is harmful, but used in tobacco it removes the bad smell of it and refreshes the brain.

The strawberry of Chile, acuella, grows well in that kingdom, and for that reason the Spaniards gave it that name. The Chilean Indians call it in their language cuellen, and from it they make

First Part. Book 4.
chicha, which is their wine. This plant is what they call in Spain the strawberry, which is well known in the mountains of Oviedo, and in many other parts of Old Castile; only the one from the Indies is larger than the one that grows in Spain, because some strawberries are as large as walnuts: it is a very tasty and delicious fruit; and although in Chile it grows wild and in uncultivated places, in the other parts of these lands, principally in Peru, where it has been transplanted, it is cultivated and has spread so widely that it is almost universal throughout the Indies, since it has been taken as far as New Spain, where I saw it in a garden near Mexico City: it does better in temperate and cold lands than in warm ones, yet it grows well in the gardens of this city of Lima.
Great abundance of wild lupins is found throughout the countryside, which the Indians call Tañi; and this plant grows so vigorously that in some places it reaches the height of a man, and ordinarily serves as firewood. The following herbs are also found: white and red amaranth, which are a very common food of the Indians: and in the city of Guamanga very fine nougats are made without sugar from the seeds of the white amaranth: purslane; watercress not as pungent as that of Spain, particularly those of the larger kind, of which there are two varieties; the larger ones produce a small yellow flower shaped like that of the claro and somewhat smaller; eaten raw this herb gives a good breath, and its juice

It is useful and attracts all inflammation of certain plants, some without spines and others more delicate with small milky shoots, stone or hard surface, which is a wild herb that sheds its leaves, and small branches that produce three small leaves joined at the base of the stalk like roscorabones: chicory: wild lettuce: various kinds of nettles, large and small, which do not grow in the lowlands but only in the highlands; and the natives of Lima who have not left it do not know nettles; some nettles are dark green, with taller stems and leaves, others smaller with a light green color, small leaves, curled, and reddish, whose base is the most thorny; among others one finds dead nettles, which do not sting those who touch them; the Indians make use of nettles for many cures.

The mora plant, of a somewhat lighter green color, in herb form; it is used as a remedy: it is placed on wounds; it is found in the province of Nicaragua, called by a name understood there: Berbino. The plant called in Spain "monk's ear," with a thick, round leaf, quite solid, used by those with strong constitutions because they tend to treat themselves with it. Grama grass grows in such abundance in the valleys of the coast of Peru that it costs the farmers a great deal of money, especially the wine producers, to clear it from their fields; it grows in parts two to three nodes high, and it serves to melt the glass that is prepared for carrying from one place to another. The plant called Mugo, which grows on rocks, and on the trunks and branches of trees, hanging from them like hair, or more like sheets of lichen in great quantity; the Indians, when they feel tired and weak in their muscles, tend to bathe in the decoction of this plant, which they say makes them feel well.

Also the plant from which glass is made, which grows ordinarily on the sea floor; the Indians had no use for it because they did not know how to make glass, nor was any such thing found anywhere in the New World; and it was one of the things that most amazed them when the Spaniards brought it; and even more so when they saw a small glass full of rich, golden wine. Today in Peru glass is found, not much, but of very fine quality; and in New Spain as well.

The holy thistle, called caribcho by the Indians, grows in all temperate lands; it has a yellow flower and a new seed resembling that of the radish, which serves everyone here as a safe purgative. Wherever one wishes, one can find grasses among them. The plant called rabo del lobo grows abundantly in swamps and humid places. The plant called bola grows in cultivated lands, and it bears a yellow flower; the juice of this plant is used to cure the sickness of the valley. Sarsaparilla; horehound; all kinds of mushrooms, large and small, among which some are poisonous and not edible.

All these plants are well known to the Indians, and they have given them names in their language; it is not surprising that all of them are wild and uncultivated, since they had no inclination to make gardens and transplant them by planting them in their fields; yet they made use of all of them for their sustenance, as well as for curing their illnesses and ailments. Another very common one is artemisia, which common people usually call altomisa; it grows in such great quantities on the estates of this valley of Lima that they burn it in the lime and brick kilns. Of wild mallows there are two species; not those we call locas, which bear large flowers, white and purple, for these are garden

Chapter 3. On Maize.

Thus I found throughout all these Indies no wheat, nor any other kind of grain of those that grow in ears in Europe. The Creator gave only three kinds of seeds to the natives of this land to serve them as bread, which are maize, quinoa, and chia.
Of these, maize is so widespread throughout all of America, both on the mainland and on the islands adjacent to it, just as wheat is in Europe. The maize plant is already well known in Spain under the name of Indian wheat. Its leaves resemble those of cane, except that they are wider and not as rough. The stalk — the cane of maize — rises most commonly to about one estado in height, and grows as thick as a thumb, more or less. It has, at equal intervals, knots like common cane. It is tender and weak, and breaks easily. Between the leaves it puts forth ears or plumes of a color between white and red, with many small filaments. It produces its fruit not at the top, as most other plants do, but around the stalk, and each plant or cane yields from one

History of the New World.

One finds four choclos (this is what they call in Peru the ears or cobs of maize) — each cob, after being husked, is as thick as a wrist, and some are of extraordinary length, ordinarily quite long, and from here on down. The cob is covered with husks or layers of leaves, rough and leathery; and between them and the grain there are many threads like hairs the color of maize, which, surpassing the length of the cob, emerge from its tip in a bundle as thick as a finger. The grains of maize are the size of chickpeas, not perfectly round; they are arranged on the cob in rows lengthwise, in great order like the seeds of a pomegranate, and so tightly packed together that to shell a cob the labor is to pry out one grain, since once one is removed it makes room for the rest.

Maize is a crop so versatile that it grows not only in temperate lands, but also in many others of various climates, such as cold and hot lands, dry and humid ones, in mountains and in plains, in winter and in summer, under irrigation and dependent on rainfall. Between it and wheat there is this difference: all lands that bear wheat also bear maize, but those that are too cold to produce wheat will likewise not produce maize. Though in this respect wheat has an advantage over maize in tolerating cold better; because in temperate lands that lean more toward cold than heat, sowing

together. It grows so quickly in some places that within three or four months, and sometimes even within two, it is sown and harvested. There are many varieties of maize, because first of all it comes in all colors: light, dark, yellow, purple, light red, dirty, and mixed with various colors. It also differs in flavor and in the size of the kernels; the largest ones found are somewhat smaller than broad beans. One kind is very tender, with very white flour, and mild; another is very hard, which the Indians call muruchi, and the Spaniards call morocho, which is the one that the canalizaduras ordinarily use. Given these differences, the Indians have their own names for each.

Maize is the most suitable grain-bread that has been found for these people of such limited industry, because of the little effort it requires to prepare it to the point where it can serve as sustenance, not having the trouble that wheat requires — reaping, threshing, milling, and all the other labors that men must go through before it reaches the goodness of bread. For from the moment the ear of corn is in milk it serves as nourishment for days; and they eat maize in many ways, either as whole grain or ground: as whole grain, they eat it green while still in milk, before it dries, or roasted in the embers, or boiled in water, and in both ways it is tasty; and together with any kind of fruit, green ears of corn are sold in the plazas, some raw and others cooked. Because the raw ones are usually added to stews, particularly

a flat stone, another small stone, and on that same stone the dough is kneaded and bread is made, without salt, leavening, or any other ingredient than a little cold water.

In New Spain they boil the maize in lime or lye to hull it, and then, as soon as it is done boiling, they grind it on a Metate, which is an instrument made of two stones, one long one about half a vara, and another about a third of that, and another small, round, and long one like a German rolling pin. In this way thin little rounds are made, which are toasted or cooked on clay dishes placed over the fire. This is the most prized bread the Indians make from maize; in Peru it is called tanta, and in New Spain Tlascale. These tortillas are not made the same way everywhere: in New Spain they are made thin, the width of a horseshoe's edge; in Tierra Firme, as large as what they call Arepas; those found in Peru were like those of New Spain. They must be eaten hot, because when they cool they become tough like wet leather and lose their flavor. On one occasion when in an Indian village of Beneyu we ran out of bread, the priest ordered the Indian women to make us maize tortillas as they used to make them in the old days for their chiefs. And they made them so delicious and fine that they seemed like pan-fried pastries, because they had kneaded the maize flour with eggs and lard. In the port of Santa Elena, diocese of Quito, the best are made

to see them in the leaves, or husks of the corn cob, and for this purpose alone they tend to place these leaves in the hands throughout all of New Spain. But in the city of Lima they wrap them in banana leaves. The Spanish have learned greatly to appreciate them, because they make them with more care and curiosity than the native Indians themselves. The other way of grinding the corn to make it into flour is to place it dry on a large flat stone, and grind it with another medium stone, which goes from one person to two mills. At present much is ground in our wheat mills; since the Indians in ancient times had no sieves, they sifted the flour only for people of distinction, such as the Caciques, using a cotton cloth, in which the fine flour or flower of the flour would stick, and the coarse part was separated from it by hand; but now they use our sieves. They also make from corn flour, besides the bread called torta, or rough pieces they call Yanos: porridges, or maçamuría, which in New Spain they call Atole, and other uses.

Chapter 4. On chicha made from Maize.

Under the name chicha are included all
the drinks that the native people of the New World
use in place of wine; and because they get drunk very frequently,
a vice to which they are so inclined that neither
the benefit of having been converted to our holy faith, nor their
dealings and communication with the Spaniards, nor the punishments
inflicted upon them by their masters and the Justices, to make them
give it up; although in some provinces there has been some
improvement; in general, in all places they are no less
given to drinking and frequent drunkenness than in
the time of their paganism. Chicha is made from many seeds,
each nation adapting to those seeds and fruits
which their land produces most abundantly, to
make chicha from them; some chichas are made from oca and yuca

First part, book 4. 215
and from other roots: others from quinoa, and from the fruit of the molle tree: the Indians of Tucuman make it from carob; those of Chile from fish; those of Tierra Firme from pineapples; the Mexicans from Maguey, the wine they call Pulque; and that called in different provinces by various fruits and vegetables, which seems as if all the inhabitants of America were inspired against water, given how they refuse to drink it pure. But the best chicha of all, and the one most generally drunk in this land, which like a precious wine holds first place among all other drinks of the Indians, is that which is made from maize.
This is made in many ways, and what differentiates one from another is that some chichas are stronger than others, and of different colors: for chicha is made that is red, white, yellow, ash-colored, and other colors. One very strong kind called Sora is made from maize that is first buried for several days until it ferments; another from roasted maize; another from chewed maize, and in other ways. The most ordinary kind that the Indians of Peru drink is that made from chewed maize; for which one sees not only in their own towns, but also in many Spanish ones where there is a gathering of Indians, such as Potosí, Oruro, and others, vessels set out in the plazas made from old jars,

History of the New World

and boys sitting chew maize: which alone is enough to disgust the Spaniards just by watching it; no less so does it disgust the Indians to drink a beverage made in such an unclean manner. They do not chew all of the maize from which the chicha is made; only a portion of it, which mixed with the rest serves as a kind of leavening. This the Indians consider so necessary to give the chicha its proper quality, that when the maize is ground for this purpose in our water mills, they chew the flour until it is moistened in the mouth and formed into a dough; and they fill their small portion of this mixture of chewed maize and flour, apart from what they gain by swallowing whatever they wish to satisfy their hunger.

The Spaniards also are accustomed to making chicha from maize as a treat, but they do it with more cleanliness and skill than the Indians: it is a wholesome, fresh, and pleasant drink, and it is made in the following way. One almud of maize is taken (more or less according to the quantity of chicha to be made) and it is ground and its flour sifted; this flour is then kneaded with a little warm, not hot, water, adding a little salt: the dough must be worked very well in such a way that it is neither too thin, nor watery, nor too dry; but rather that it holds together somewhat. Once this is done, the dough is left to stand overnight; and in the morning it is placed into

First part, Book 4:
a vessel that can hold one arroba of water; and into it shall be poured about six quartillos of very boiling water, and with a large spoon it shall be stirred so that the dough and water become lukewarm; and then successively lukewarm water is added until it reaches a full arroba, and it is stirred again so that everything combines. Then the vessel is covered, and left like that for twenty-four hours; once these have passed, the water that has settled and become clear is drawn off and poured into another vessel, from which about six quartillos of it are taken; this, with a pound and a half of sugar, must boil a little, and this sugared water is mixed back in with the rest, and after it has become lukewarm it must be quickly poured into the vessel from which it is to be served for drinking, covering it with a cloth so that the foam that must come out does not obstruct the serving of the chicha. If the vessel into which the new fermented batch of the drink is poured already has some chicha in it, it will be ready to drink within two days, and if not, it will take seven or eight days to ferment and mature.
Every type of chicha as a beverage is beneficial against illness and retention of urine; and against gravel and stones in the kidneys and bladder: for which reason these ailments are never found among the Indians, both old and new converts, because of their custom of drinking chicha. Taking half a quartillo of it on an empty stomach, even steeped overnight with pieces of half a white onion and a little sugar, it removes the burning sensation

Of the kidneys, or at least it tempers and reduces so that it does not chafe or cause sores in the urinary tract. Taking half a quartillo of this beverage warm on an empty stomach, when it is not too sour or unripe, is beneficial against ulceration and against all retention of urine and pain in the side. The sediment or lees of the dough used to make chicha also serves a purpose, because when applied to gouty feet, it removes the burning and eases the pain. The name chicha does not come from this kingdom; I believe the Spaniards took it from the language of the island of Hispaniola. In the Quechua language of Peru it is called Aca, and in Aymara, Chila.

Chapter 5. On Quinoa.

Quinoa is a plant very similar to pigweed. It grows about two thirds of a vara in height, more or less. Its leaf is like that of pigweed, except that near the stem it is wider and not as pointed. It produces its seed at the top of the stalk in small clusters like those of pigweed. The seed is about the size of mustard grains, or somewhat larger, not perfectly round but rather somewhat flat. This seed tolerates cold better than any other plant grown in these Indies, whether those native to this land or those brought from Spain, because it grows in lands so cold that all other plants, even barley, freeze. There are two species of quinoa, no more and no less than those of pigweed: one white and one golden. When this

First Part. Book 4. 217

This herb while tender, before it goes to seed, is eaten cooked like chard and spinach, though only the white variety and not the red, because eating the red causes urinary problems.
The seed of quinoa comes in as many different colors as maize, for there is white, yellow, purple, red, and ash-colored quinoa: one wild variety and one domestic, and one that dyes. The best of all is the white, and it and the fine grains are used like rice, and ground into flour they make bread like maize arepas. From the other colored quinoas they make chicha, most notably from the ash-colored one called cañahua, whose chicha is very potent in causing intoxication, and turns sour when it has gone too far. The stalks and leaves of quinoa, cooked and eaten with oil, vinegar, and sugar, have the property of softening the bowels. Its juice, or taken with a few drops of vinegar, is good against inflammations, and with the addition of sugar it makes a good gargle for inflammations of the gout. The seed of the herb cooked in water with milk, or with pot drippings, increases milk in new mothers, and it has been found by experience — and I have seen it used myself — that it is very beneficial for any kind of fall or injury to take a bowl of warm polenta, or of the seed of quinoa, so as to lessen the harm that could result from such falls. From the cane or stalk of quinoa, when burned, the Indians make an ash which they call

that they eat as a relish with coca. In the Quechua language it is

Chapter 6. On chia.

Chia is native to New Spain. The plant
is very similar to that of quinoa, and its leaves are seen
dried. It puts out a spike similar to that of quinoa, and on
it the seed, which is very similar in shape to sesame,
except that it is smaller and black in color. The Indians of
New Spain grind this seed and add it to atole, or ma-
camorra, and it gives it a good flavor.

Chapter 7. On yuca.

Since all of America was a land lacking the grain
species and seeds of Europe, from which their settlers drew sustenance,
as well as the meat of domestic animals, until the Spaniards
brought to it wheat, and all manner of vegetables, and
domestic livestock from Spain: God supplied the lack of these
things by endowing this new world with many and diverse
fruits and vegetables, principally an infinite variety
of roots, which served as sustenance for the Indians.
Of these, the most widespread, and that which sustains a great
part of the Indies, is yuca, which the natives of warm
lands have never ceased to call cacabi: because

First Part - Book 9.
Not a few parts of it are eaten by the Spaniards. Yuca is a plant that grows two estados tall, more or less, and sends up a stalk, or straight rod, round, solid, and as thick as a finger of the hand. From the ground all the way up to the crown it is covered with leaves, which do not weigh it down, and it is made all the more beautiful and handsome by these leaves being very fine to look at. They are attached to the stalk by a long stem, very similar to that of a grapevine leaf — very red in color, round, smooth, and no thicker than a slender reed. The leaf itself closely resembles that of hemp; it has the shape of a star with seven or nine points, cleft down to the stem and nearly equal, making it round overall. Each point resembles in shape and width the leaf of a peach tree, except that it is not so channeled. They have a deep green color that is quite striking. When the plant is covered with leaves, since they are all so equal, it ends up being as broad in circumference as the width of a man's body from top to bottom, which makes it so pleasing in appearance that, for its good looks, people often plant it in gardens. The leaves fall off over time, beginning from the lowest ones, and where they were attached to the stalk they leave small knobs or nodes, which is why the stalk is very knotted in those places.
The way it is sown or planted is by sticking into the ground pieces of the stalk from those that have been uprooted. These pieces soon take root, each one sending out two or three shoots, and as they grow upward, they spread out and

History of the New World

going, and putting forth its fruit, which are roots like white turnips, tender and watery, some as thick and long as an arm, and they are sometimes known to grow so large that I myself have seen a yuca a fathom in length, and where it is thickest, as big around as a man's leg; they have a rough, tough skin of a dark brownish-tawny color, and inside they are very white. From each plant one can take four to eight roots, more or less, depending on the fertility of the soil that produces them; they take a year to ripen, and they become much better if left for a year and a half.

There are two kinds of yuca, one sweet and one bitter; the sweet one is eaten like sweet potatoes, boiled or roasted, and is often put into the pot in place of turnips, and in any form it has a good flavor, and even if eaten raw it does no harm. This kind is called on the island of Española "Boniata," meaning without poison, in contrast to the other kind, which is so poisonous that any animal that eats it before it is pressed out will die without remedy; and the same fate befalls whoever drinks the juice that comes out when it is pressed. From this poisonous yuca cassava bread is generally made, and they make it in the following way: after these yucas are ground up they are grated on rough stones, and then, once grated, they are placed in a long, narrow sack about the width of a thigh called a cibucan, made from soft tree bark, in the manner of a press; and then

So, placing it [the yuca], one puts it in this tall bag, and at the other end a great weight is placed, which causes it to spread and compress the yuca. And after it has been pressed down for as long as it takes to be well squeezed, so that all that poisonous juice, which is like whey, comes out, they remove it, and what remains looks like squeezed almonds. These they place in the buren, which is a flat earthenware pan as large as a sieve, set over the fire and sealed with clay so that no flame escapes. And although when it is poured in it is loose and moist like wet bran, it curdles together, and they turn it so that it cooks better. In the time it takes to fry an egg, each cake of it is well formed. These cakes they then put out in the sun for one or two days to dry out, and they end up as stiff as a board, even though when taken off the fire they were soft and greasy. These cazabi cakes keep without spoiling, as if new, for more than a year, and at sea they make up for the lack of hardtack. Two kinds of cazabi are made: one very thin one called jaujau for refined people, which is very white, tender, and crumbles easily; and another thicker and more compact one for common people. And speaking of the cakes of one and the other, it seems to me that the saying is verified here: "for want of bread, cakes will do," because in lands where wheat bread cannot be had it cannot really be eaten with pleasure, nor is it appetizing, no matter how much some may wish to praise it.

Chapter 8. On the Sweet Potato.

The sweet potato is a root very well known not only throughout the Indies,
but also in Spain; and it is among the most prized
foods that the Indians had. The plant is small, and its
branches spread out over the ground without rising very high;
each plant produces many shoots or stems, which are
round, smooth, and purple; and they grow like tendrils
spread out over the ground. The leaf of the shoot
grows on a stalk as long as that of a vine leaf,
but more slender, tender, and purple in color; the leaf is
wider near the stem than at the other end, and ends in

three points, the two on the sides a little shorter than the middle one; the small veins of the leaf are green on the upper side and purple on the underside. From each plant one can extract four to twelve roots, more or less depending on how fertile the soil is. Sweet potatoes differ from one another in size and shape; most commonly they are somewhat thicker in the middle than at the tips; some are elongated and tapered at both ends, others are round, oval, or flattened; some are as thick as a man's arm and half a yard long, and from there downward. They are very tender and floury, and they also come in different colors: purple, yellow, white, red, and mottled.

There are among them different varieties: the first retains the common name of batata, and it surpasses the others just as the camuesa apple surpasses other apples. The second is the kind found in Peru, which we call camotes, and which holds second place in quality; although in some places the camotes are so good that they are in no way inferior to the best batatas, such as those from Payta in the diocese of [illegible], and from the valley of the same city of Trujillo. The third kind of sweet potato is inferior; it is the one that on the island of Hispaniola they call ages, and the Spaniards name them ñames. The ages grow in a very short time, and for that reason they are commonly planted in large quantities to feed slaves and servants. From a single plant one can extract twelve or fourteen roots, and sometimes twenty; the age is bland and of little regard,

It grows as large as a medium-sized turnip, which can sit upright: on the outside it is earth-colored, and when the skin is removed it remains white, with some purple spots, like jasper.

The sweet potatoes are eaten boiled and roasted over coals, and they taste like roasted chestnuts; they are also used to make delicious stews and fritters. Although this plant's root resembles a turnip or radish, forming a head where the root meets the leaves, from each node there grow and extend underground many small tendrils or thin threads, resembling the plant's rootlets, and at the tip of each one of these a root grows. In this same manner grow almost all the edible roots found in the Indies, such as yuca, potatoes, ocas, peanuts, and many others. The green leaf of the sweet potato, or camote, mashed and mixed with lard without salt and placed on chiggers, kills them and relieves the pain and discomfort they cause. This root is called batata in the language of Hispaniola; in Peru it is called Apichu in the Quechua language; and in Aymara, sutucu. The Spaniards call it camote, which is a name from the Mexican language.
